AGG-F01.claim: A state-space model pools polls over a campaign: a hidden level of support that moves as a random walk, observed through polls that each add sampling error and a firm-specific bias (house effect). The pooled estimate is less biased and more precise than any single poll. Level and house effects cannot both be learned from polls alone. Jackman pinned the trajectory to the actual result, and says real-time tracking needs a priori restrictions on the house effects.
AGG-F01.quant: Australia 2004, five poll series. Measurement model y_i ~ N(a_t + d_j, s_i^2), with s_i set from each poll's n (p. 508). Two-party-preferred house effects (Table 1, p. 513): ANU/ninemsn internet poll -5.7 pp [-7.3, -4.2]; Roy Morgan (face to face) -4.9; Newspoll -2.9; ACNielsen -1.1; Galaxy +0.1 [-2.0, 1.8]. Mean of the three phone polls about -1.3 (2PP) and -0.1 (first preferences). The largest house effects track interview mode. Full text read. Venue note: Australian Journal of Political Science, not the American JPS.
AGG-F01.model_link: fit(): weekly random-walk latent plus delta (firm x list house effects). delta_c is centred across firms for each list, which is the real-time restriction Jackman says is needed. So the industry-wide error cannot be learned inside the fit, and it enters at projection (correlated bloc swing, family shocks, per-list residual).

AGG-F02.claim: Linzer's dynamic Bayesian model uses a binomial likelihood on decided respondents only, excludes undecideds, uses a reverse random walk, and has no house-effect terms. He argues firm-specific corrections are impractical when most firms publish few polls. He also argues that deflating sample sizes to absorb over-dispersion makes the model underestimate how much opinion moves, which worsens overconfidence in the forecast.
AGG-F02.quant: p.132: variance of poll results 3-5x the variance of the latent trend (sd about 1.7-2.2x); 98% of daily latent changes < 0.5 pp; p.126 overconfidence from deflating n described as minimal.
AGG-F02.model_link: s.23 sampling floor (BAYES_FLOOR, off): the eight-cycle harness rejected a uniform binomial-times-DEFF floor (pooled MAE 1.66 -> 1.71). Linzer gives the same verdict on uniform noise inflation from US data. The mechanism differs: in this model the floor widened intervals rather than narrowing them. CEC filings renormalised to the party sum = Linzer's exclusion of undecideds.

AGG-F03.claim: The Economist 2020 model (Linzer lineage, in Stan) layers poll-level adjustments over a random-walk latent with correlated states. The adjustments are pollster house effects, mode (phone vs online), population (likely voters vs adults), and a time-varying partisan non-response adjustment modelled as an autoregressive process. It also has poll-level and state-level polling-error terms for measurement error beyond the stated margin of error. Priors were tuned by cross-validation on past cycles.
AGG-F03.quant: Preprint pp.2-4: about 3% polling error per poll as starting prior; cross-validation (2008, 2012, 2016, early 2020) applies to the state-level random-walk innovation SD priors only; error terms are national and (correlated) state polling-error terms.
AGG-F03.model_link: s_obs x lam (estimated excess noise per list and firm) is the poll-level error term. The house-effect drift (s.21, linear) is a simpler cousin of their AR non-response term. The model has no explicit mode term: mode enters only through DEFF, and the floor that uses DEFF is off.

AGG-F04.claim: The reference multiparty dynamic Bayesian model has five parts. (1) A multinomial likelihood using each poll's n. (2) An additive-log-ratio latent with the last party as baseline. (3) House effects that sum to zero across parties within each firm, and across firms. (4) A backward random walk. (5) A FULL innovation covariance W = diag(sigma) Omega diag(sigma) with an LKJ(50) prior, so parties' latent movements may covary.
AGG-F04.quant: p.258: W = diag(sigma) Omega diag(sigma), Omega ~ LKJ(50); sigma_j ~ N+(0, 0.1) per day; fn 9: 0.1 log-ratio step moves 0.50 to 0.52.
AGG-F04.model_link: Latent z. Until 15 Oct it was ALR with an independent HalfNormal(0.06) weekly tau per coordinate and no covariance. A full covariance is what makes ALR independent of the reference choice. The shipped CLR latent (s.46) is also independent per list, so it has no within-bloc covariance in the walk (Challenge 2).

AGG-F05.claim: The Jackman dynamic linear model carries over to multiparty systems (Germany, Sweden) and gives reasonable forecasts despite system complexity and the emergence of new parties. Adding a seasonal component for cyclical swings in party support significantly lowers early-campaign forecast error.
AGG-F05.quant: Seasonal component, one month out: Germany 2013 about 8% lower error (avg 1.52 pts, 'measurable, but inconsistent'); Sweden 2014 1.28 -> 1.06 pts (about 17%). One election per country.
AGG-F05.model_link: Supports a state-space poll model for a multiparty system. Informs the campaign volatility calendar (campaign_vol_weight), a deterministic counterpart to a cyclical term.

AGG-F06.claim: Across US state-level polls, total error is about twice what reported margins imply. The model writes poll variance as p(1-p)/n + tau_r^2, an additive election-level excess variance. Poll bias is alpha_r + beta_r t, an election-level bias that may change linearly in time. Firm house effects are left out of the mean, so they enter the variance. The shared bias persists however many polls are averaged.
AGG-F06.quant: p.611: tau_j^2 ~ N+(0, sigma_tau^2), sigma_tau ~ N+(0, 0.05^2), on the probability scale (excess variance); alpha_j, beta_j on the logit scale.
AGG-F06.model_link: Industry (election-level) bias is shared by all firms and cannot be averaged away, so it lives in the projection's correlated bloc swing and family shocks. Their linear-in-time bias matches the house-effect drift (s.21). Their additive excess-variance form, binomial plus tau^2, is the template for any revived floor (Challenge 4).

AGG-F07.claim: Applying the Shirani-Mehr model, with more temporal flexibility, to a multiparty system: German poll errors are dominated by biases common to the whole industry. Variance is about twice what margins of error imply, and there is little evidence of house or mode effects.
AGG-F07.quant: Variance 1.5-3x nominal (conclusion; about 2x in the abstract); house effects 'generally weak compared to the election-day biases'; mean absolute election-day bias 1.5 pts (0.9 Greens/Linke to 3.2 CDU/CSU).
AGG-F07.model_link: Supports a multiparty excess-variance term and industry shocks at projection. Contrast: the Israeli fit finds firm drifts of up to about 3 seats end to end (s.21: Tatika/Likud -2.95, Filber/UTJ -1.88). House effects are a larger share of error in Israel than in Germany, so the house-effect layer is a local necessity rather than a universal one.

AGG-F08.claim: A multilevel decomposition of Spanish poll errors has four parts: a time-invariant house effect that persists ACROSS elections, an election-level bias common to all firms, a common linear trend, and idiosyncratic error with party covariances. Estimated house effects lined up with sponsors' politics. Sigma Dos (for El Mundo) leaned to the PP, Invymark (for La Sexta) to the PSOE, and the public CIS showed none. Declared margins of error understated the true uncertainty.
AGG-F08.quant: 157 polls within 30 days of the 1996-2011 Congressional elections. In one cycle, firms collectively missed the PSOE-PP differential by 7 pp. arXiv version (1612.03073) read, pp. 9-10 and 14-15.
AGG-F08.model_link: Here, house effects are re-learned inside each 240-day window from a zero-mean group prior, and only firm PRECISION carries over from past cycles (the lam scorecard). Montalvo et al. carry the signed lean across elections too (Challenge 7).

AGG-F09.claim: Across the three 2019-20 Israeli elections, media-sponsored polls were biased in line with the sponsoring outlet's stance on Netanyahu. Polls commissioned by anti-Netanyahu outlets consistently underestimated the seats the pro-Netanyahu bloc won.
AGG-F09.quant: Abstract only: polls commissioned by anti-Netanyahu outlets consistently underestimated the pro-Netanyahu bloc's seats (2019-20). Per-outlet magnitudes and any pro-Netanyahu-outlet effect unverified.
AGG-F09.model_link: Israeli evidence for firm/sponsor house effects (delta; correlation groups in pollster_meta.csv), and for leans at the BLOC level rather than list by list. The firm-level delta absorbs sponsor effects only where each firm has one sponsor.

AGG-F10.claim: Israeli law requires anyone who conducts an election poll for publication or broadcast to send the Central Elections Committee a copy of the results. The filing must state the sampling method, initial sample size, populations sampled, how many people were asked, took part, refused or were ineligible, the interview dates and hours, and the margin of error. The CEC posts filings as received.
AGG-F10.quant: s.16E(e)(1)-(3) as cited; copy held for public inspection on request (posting is CEC practice, not a statutory duty). Filing n is not used by the fit; n_resp comes from firm filing medians (FIRM_N_DEFAULT).
AGG-F10.model_link: _merge_cec: filed raw shares displace seat-derived table numbers. Filing n feeds n_resp, and the filed undecided share feeds u_c (beta_u) and the undecided pool (U_POOL). The method and response fields are an untapped source for firm-level design information (Challenge 4).

AGG-F11.claim: Polls are not independent. In the 2012 Republican primaries, automated (IVR) polls were as accurate as live-interviewer polls when a traditional poll had already been published in the state, and markedly worse when none had. That suggests pollsters take cues from each other. If so, a poll of polls is misleadingly precise.
AGG-F11.quant: 159 polls released after the 2012 New Hampshire primary. Overall IVR-vs-human difference -0.256 (n.s.). IVR polls with no prior human poll in the state had an average absolute error 3.229 points larger (p. 335). Authors call it suggestive, not conclusive. Full text read.
AGG-F11.model_link: The likelihood treats polls as conditionally independent given the latent and house effects. Herding was measured (dossier s.12: final-window dispersion 0.88x mid-campaign, 0.6-0.9x sampling noise) and deliberately left out to avoid double counting with the backtest-calibrated shocks. Effective sample size is still overstated inside the fit (Challenge 5).

AGG-F12.claim: US state presidential polls in 2000-2008 did not behave like random samples. Standardised errors against the result were far more dispersed than sampling theory implies, and they were biased. Treating undecided respondents as ignorable (dropping them proportionally) removed most of the raw shortfall. The authors suggest pollsters may avoid publishing 'atypical' polls. NOTE for the brief: this paper documents OVER-dispersion against the outcome, not panel smoothness. It does not support the s.23 stickiness diagnosis.
AGG-F12.quant: Jan 2009 author draft, Table 1: N = 1,857 polls (text: 1,761); variance of standardised errors 1.58-4.38 raw/adjusted (adjusted alone 1.58-3.20) vs 1 under random sampling; Rep -3.48 -> 0.03, Dem -4.57 -> -1.04 pp after proportional undecided allocation; wrong winner 19.2-20.7% of polls. Published AER version not opened.
AGG-F12.model_link: Supports proportional renormalisation of filings (raw_pct / party sum) as the baseline undecided treatment, and an estimated excess-variance term. It is NOT evidence for a floor driven by panel smoothness.

AGG-F13.claim: A pollster's accuracy is only modestly predictable. Past accuracy correlates with future accuracy, but a firm's record is mostly noise until it has about 30 graded polls. The best firms are about 1 point better than average. Methodology and transparency standards predict accuracy and serve as the prior that records are shrunk toward.
AGG-F13.quant: Firms in AAPOR-TI or NCPP (membership as of 6 June 2010): 4.6 vs 5.5 points (1998-2009), 4.0 vs 5.2 (2012). Roper archive is a 2014 methodology-score criterion only.
AGG-F13.model_link: lam prior from the 8-cycle scorecard. q is shrunk to the industry median by n_cycles/(n_cycles+3), and only the FINAL pre-election poll per cycle is graded (s.23). That is at most 8 graded polls per firm, far below the ~30 at which 538 lets a record dominate. A firm with 8 cycles keeps 73% of its own record (Challenge 6).

AGG-F14.claim: The current Silver Bulletin pollster ratings penalise herding directly. If a firm's Average Distance from the Polling Average (ADPA) is below the theoretical minimum implied by its polls' sampling error, a penalty is added to its accuracy score before the predictive rating is computed. Ratings are mean-reverted by number of polls, with older polls discounted, and transparency earns a bonus.
AGG-F14.quant: January 2026 update (14 Jan 2026), read. The page does not state the penalty or bonus sizes.
AGG-F14.model_link: s.23 found this symptom within firms: NB-bloc scatter around each firm's own trend was 0.43-0.67 seats, against a binomial 2-3 seats. The fix tried was a likelihood floor, which the harness rejected. An ADPA-type herding penalty on the lam PRIOR is the ratings-side alternative (Challenge 5).

AGG-F15.claim: Bootstrap design effects for the 2015 UK final polls were mostly BELOW 1. Calibrating on past vote or party identification, which correlate strongly with current vote intention, made the estimates more efficient than simple random sampling. Without those variables, design effects were 1.04-1.68. Online opt-in panels did not show larger design effects than phone polls. The miss itself, a Conservative lead underestimated by about 7 points, came from unrepresentative samples: a shared bias, not variance.
AGG-F15.quant: Table 2, d2 (Con/Lab). Online panels 0.42-1.17: Opinium 0.42/0.47, YouGov 0.76/0.76, Panelbase 1.17/1.16. Phone 0.53-1.40: ICM 0.53/0.68, Ipsos-MORI 1.37/1.40. Without past-vote/party-ID calibration, 1.04-1.68. Accepted manuscript read (ora.ox.ac.uk).
AGG-F15.model_link: DEFF table (phone 1.0, mixed 1.1, opt-in online 1.3, SMS 1.4) is declared, not measured, and the best measured evidence does not order modes that way. s.23 also computed within-firm scatter on the NB-BLOC total, the quantity that past-vote calibration makes most stable, so some sub-binomial smoothness may be design efficiency, not stickiness (Challenge 4).

AGG-F16.claim: Across 28 benchmarks, online opt-in samples had about twice the error of probability-based panels. The excess was concentrated among young and Hispanic adults and traced to bogus respondents. It is a bias problem, not a sampling-variance problem.
AGG-F16.quant: Average absolute error 5.8 points for opt-in (three vendors: 6.4, 6.1, 5.0) vs 2.6 for probability panels (2.3, 3.0, 2.5). Ages 18-29: 11.2 vs 3.6; Hispanic adults: 10.8 vs 3.6. Six samples, 29,937 adults, June-July 2021. Report page read.
AGG-F16.model_link: Opt-in panel quality belongs in the precision prior (graded record, lam) and in house effects, not in a variance-only design effect. This backs the shipped choice of letting the graded record carry firm quality.

AGG-F17.claim: The AAPOR task force holds that the margin of sampling error does not apply to non-probability samples, and that precision there is a model-based quantity. Replicate-sample methods estimate variance but cannot detect bias. Treating such estimates as having no error is not acceptable either.
AGG-F17.quant: Full task-force report, pp. 82-83 (summary in JSSAM 1(2):90-143). Report read (aapor.org PDF).
AGG-F17.model_link: Supports estimating each list's and firm's noise from the data (s_obs, lam) rather than imposing sqrt(p(1-p)/n x DEFF) on opt-in panels as if they were probability samples.

AGG-F18.claim: Static allocation of undecided respondents, proportional or even, biased 2016 US polls and poll aggregates. Undecideds did not split in proportion to decided voters, and a probabilistic allocation that carries its own uncertainty does better. The problem grows with the undecided share.
AGG-F18.quant: US final-week undecided 2.7-5.1% (2004-2016) vs Israel 2026 U_POOL 9.65% of filed respondents (bayes_model._undecided_pool(), s.44); probabilistic allocation 'may be superior' (authors).
AGG-F18.model_link: Filed shares are renormalised proportionally (_merge_cec), beta_u widens noise for high-undecided polls, and the projection's measured undecided-lean layer (U_LEAN_PER_SIDE, Beta posterior) is a probabilistic allocation. Backs keeping that layer separate from the poll fit.

AGG-F19.claim: Replacing normal errors with Student-t errors gives robust likelihood-based inference. The degrees of freedom are a convenient robustness setting that can be estimated or fixed. In the multivariate t, one scale-mixing factor is shared by all components of an observation, so an aberrant observation is downweighted as a whole.
AGG-F19.quant: Abstract read via a bibliographic mirror. The common 'df = 4' default attributed to this paper is NOT verified.
AGG-F19.model_link: StudentT(nu=4) likelihood, applied independently to each poll x list cell on the share scale.

AGG-F20.claim: A logratio Student-t distribution puts heavy tails inside the simplex geometry. It is equivalent across logratio representations for estimation and outlier detection, and it flags outlying whole compositions better than classical robust methods.
AGG-F20.quant: Monte Carlo under scale contamination, with a leave-one-out procedure: higher AUC and near-perfect specificity against MCD and COMCoDa. Abstract read; full text not opened.
AGG-F20.model_link: The model's t is applied per list cell. A poll that is wrong as a whole (a mis-parsed filing, a different question, a composite list) is downweighted cell by cell, not coherently, and the cells it does not downweight still pull the latent (Challenge 3).

AGG-F21.claim: The logistic-normal family is closed under permutation of parts, as Aitchison (1986) proved: reordering the parts transforms (mu, Sigma) linearly. So the family is reference-free only when Sigma is unrestricted. A diagonal Sigma (independent coordinates) under one reference is generally not diagonal under another. Independent random walks per ALR coordinate are therefore a reference-specific assumption.
AGG-F21.quant: SORT 37(1):29-56 (2013): Property 4.3 p.45 (Sigma in ILR coordinates); closure under permutation p.49, attributed to Aitchison (1986). ALR non-invariance of a diagonal covariance: own derivation (off-diagonals become Var(y_j) after a reference change).
AGG-F21.model_link: Backs the CLR latent shipped 15 Oct (s.46). The ALR latent's reference was the last merged block; on today's data prepare_data() makes it 'beit_yisrael'. Its implied volatility was about a twentieth of any other list's. The refit moved Tzomet Beit Yisrael from 0.595% to 0.339%, toward its 0.30% polls (s.46): the 'frozen reference' measured.

AGG-F22.claim: An additive-log-ratio transformation can come measurably close to the full (isometric) logratio geometry if the reference part is well chosen. The first criterion is high Procrustes correlation with the exact geometry, the second is low variance of the log reference, and references with low abundance or many zeros should be avoided.
AGG-F22.quant: Procrustes correlations of 0.9991, 0.9974 and 0.9902 on three datasets with the chosen references. Full text read.
AGG-F22.model_link: The old ALR reference, a micro-list polled in few polls (MIN_LIST_POLLS = 3), was exactly the low-abundance, high-noise reference to avoid. The ALR path is still live: it is the refit-gate FALLBACK when CLR fails twice (s.46) and the research latent under BAYES_CLR=0. Its reference should be fixed to a large, stable list (Challenge 1).

AGG-F23.claim: Aitchison's pairwise and additive logratios are quasi-isometric in practice; exact isometry is not a prerequisite for good analysis. With a near-constant reference (geochemists use silica, the most abundant and stable part), ALRs behave like logs of their numerators. The centred log-ratio is the symmetric alternative: logs taken against the geometric mean, which sum to zero (D-1 free dimensions) and preserve all pairwise logratio distances.
AGG-F23.quant: Sections 3.3-3.4 (silica reference; CLR definition); quasi-isometry statements in the abstract, s.4.2 and s.7 (arXiv 2201.05197).
AGG-F23.model_link: Two literature-backed exits from reference dependence: CLR (symmetric, shipped) or ALR with a large, stable reference (for the fallback). Either removes the data-order dependence of merge_blocks().

AGG-F24.claim: PyMC provides a Normal distribution constrained to sum to zero along an axis, N(0, sigma^2 (I_K - J_K/K)), which has exactly K-1 free directions. Sigma must be shared across the constrained axis.
AGG-F24.quant: Documentation for pymc.ZeroSumNormal (stable docs, read 15 Oct 2026); n_zerosum_axes defaults to 1.
AGG-F24.model_link: The shipped CLR walk draws B free z0/steps and row-centres afterwards, so the row mean is a direction the likelihood cannot see. s.46: the default-seed CLR refit failed the gates (max r-hat 1.04, min ESS 98), and two harness windows showed bimodal endpoint shares attributed to that common-mode direction. A sum-to-zero parameterisation removes it (Challenge 1).

AGG-F25.claim: Unequal weights alone inflate the variance of a weighted mean by deffK = 1 + relvariance(w), the Kish design effect. The formula assumes weights unrelated to the outcome. Calibration on variables that predict the outcome can push the true design effect below 1 (cf. AGG-F15).
AGG-F25.quant: deffK = 1 + relvar(w) (PracTools deffK page, citing Kish 1992); stated conditions: equal stratum unit variances, not appropriate where unequal weighting is more efficient.
AGG-F25.model_link: The declared DEFF values (1.0-1.4) are in the range Kish's formula gives for moderately weighted samples, but heavily weighted opt-in panels can exceed them and past-vote calibration can undercut them. A firm-specific value should come from filed weights or from the data, not from mode.

ERR-F01.claim: Across 351 general elections in 45 countries (1942-2017), the average final-week poll miss per party is about two percentage points and has not grown over time; recent high-profile misses (UK 2015, US 2016) are within the historical norm. The authors infer that pollsters have adapted to falling response rates rather than that polling has got worse.
ERR-F01.quant: 30,916 polls, 351 elections, 45 countries, 1942-2017. The final-week model uses 220 elections in 32 countries (763 party observations). Final-week MAE per party: 2.1 (1940s-50s), 2.1 (1960s-70s), 2.0 since 2000. Year coefficient -0.001 (p=0.85, Table 3). About 4 pp at 150-200 days, about 3 at 50 days, under 2 on the eve. Table 2: presidential 2.70 vs legislative 1.83; PR 1.62 vs SMD 2.28; ENPP>3 1.71; parties <20% 1.29 vs >=20% 2.28.
ERR-F01.model_link: Overall scale of the election-day shock stack, and the choice to pool 2009-2022 with equal weight (no era trend in poll error).

ERR-F02.claim: Israel is not one of the 45 countries in the Jennings-Wlezien polling-error dataset, so no Israeli numbers can be taken from their 2016 or 2018 papers. The cross-national benchmarks are out of sample for Israel. The model's own eight-cycle record (2009-2022) is the only direct Israeli calibration. On that record, Israel's final-poll miss per list is smaller in points than the cross-national figure, as expected for a system of many small lists.
ERR-F02.quant: Own record (error_decomposition._frames(), FINAL_WINDOW 21 days): per-list final-window MAE 1.64 / 1.69 / 1.86 / 2.99 / 0.88 / 0.66 / 1.07 / 1.04 seats, mean 1.48 seats (about 1.1-1.2 pp of the vote). Cross-national comparators (JW 2018 Table 2): small parties 1.29 pp, ENPP>3 1.71 pp, all 2.03.
ERR-F02.model_link: Every election-day shock size (bloc_sd, family sd, residual base/slope) comes from the own Israeli record (error_decomposition.py). The literature can serve only as a prior or a sanity check, not as a direct Israeli estimate.

ERR-F03.claim: The authors' own summary of the pooled cross-national regression: final-week absolute error is larger for larger parties and for presidential elections, and smaller under proportional representation. Errors fall as election day approaches. A more fragmented party system, with smaller parties, should lower the average per-party error in points.
ERR-F03.quant: Party-level absolute error is regressed on election type, electoral system, effective number of parties, party size (vote share), candidate-centricity, incumbency and year (eq. 2, p. 4). Signs are reported (larger parties, larger errors; PR, smaller errors; no significant year effect), but no coefficients. Worked example: UK 2024 final-week MAE across 6 parties was 2.15 pp (total absolute error 12.89 / 6; p. 3).
ERR-F03.model_link: Per-list residual: sd = (1.83 + 0.044 x seats) x 0.9. The literature backs a size gradient. The shipped slope is shallow: a 4-seat list gets 69% of the sd of a 25-seat list. See ERR-F07 and ERR-F24.

ERR-F04.claim: Polls become steadily more informative about the vote over the election cycle, at different speeds in different institutional settings. Where the effective number of parties exceeds four, polls are less predictive at every horizon. The poll-vote fit barely improves over the final ~150 days and then sharpens over the last ~50 days. (Published as Jennings & Wlezien 2016, AJPS 60(1):219-233, doi 10.1111/ajps.12189, on 26,000+ polls, 45 countries and 312 cycles. Detailed figures come from the working paper.)
ERR-F04.quant: WORKING PAPER ONLY (superseded by AJPS 2016, which uses RMSE and splits at ENPP 3.5): 23,554 polls / 41 countries / 245 cycles; R2 >0.75 at 2.5 years, 0.9 at 4-5 months (p.15); ENPP>4 R2 about 0.15 lower one year out, flat over the final 150 days, rising over the final 50 (pp.17-18, Fig.10). AJPS 2016: 26,000+ polls, 45 countries, 312 cycles. Israel seat-based ENPP about 5-6.5 (2020-2022).
ERR-F04.model_link: Calendar-scaled forward random walk (campaign_vol_weight 1.13 / 1.25 / 0.64 by days out). The literature says fragmented systems keep real movement into the final 50 days, so at D-12 a non-trivial forward variance is appropriate.

ERR-F05.claim: Party characteristics matter more than institutions for how voter preferences evolve over the campaign. They largely mediate the institutional effects. This is the published basis for treating poll uncertainty as party-specific (size, novelty) rather than only country-specific.
ERR-F05.quant: 27,357 polls, 26 countries since 1942, 231 electoral cycles, 208 parties (abstract). The full text was not opened. The claim in the 2015 conference version that party size and party age matter most is UNVERIFIED (not opened).

ERR-F06.claim: In 608 US state-level races, total survey error in final-three-week polls is about twice what the reported margins of error imply. About half of it is an election-level bias shared by every poll of the race. That shared bias correlates across different races in the same state and year. Error barely changes between one month and one week before the election, so it is non-sampling error, not late opinion change.
ERR-F06.quant: Average absolute election-level bias (Table 1, p.612): Senate 2.1, governor 2.3, president 1.2 pp. The one-month vs one-week comparison uses the secondary 7,040-poll set (2004-2012). 'About half' is a derived share (about 1/2 Senate and governor, about 1/3 president), not a figure the paper states.
ERR-F06.model_link: Three links. (1) The bloc swing as a shared election-level shock correlated across lists. (2) Poll-level noise beyond n (design effects, per-firm lam). (3) The election-day stack does not decay with the calendar, while campaign events belong to the forward walk. The measured Israeli bloc sd of 3.36 seats (about 2.8 pp of bloc share) is the same order as the 2 pp election-level bias.

ERR-F07.claim: In a multiparty system (German Bundestag polls 1994-2021), the average absolute election-day bias of the poll average is 0.9-3.2 pp per party. In relative terms it is largest for the smallest parties (14-17% of their share). Total poll variance is 1.6-3.1x simple random sampling. House and mode effects are weak next to the common bias, which the authors read as industry-wide method problems or herding.
ERR-F07.quant: Absolute election-day bias 0.92-3.17 pp; relative bias 5-17% of share, highest for FDP, Left and Others (0.14-0.17), with no clear size pattern according to the authors (p.1031); variance ratio 1.6-3.1x SRS, average 2.3 (p.1032).
ERR-F07.model_link: This challenges the residual intercept for small lists. A 4-seat Israeli list (3.3%) gets a shipped sd of 1.81 seats (about 1.45 pp), or about 1.95 pp with the new-list x1.35, which is 44-59% of its share. The German relative bias for parties of 5-10% is 14-17%, which implies an sd of about 0.6-0.7 pp for a 3.3% party. It supports the bloc and family layers carrying the common error, and the house-effect correlation-group design (common bias is not identified from house effects).

ERR-F08.claim: The UK 2015 miss was an industry-wide error on the lead between the two main parties, about 6.5-7 points. Its primary cause was unrepresentative samples (too many Labour and too few Conservative voters) that weighting did not fix. Late swing contributed at most a small part.
ERR-F08.quant: Final polls had the Conservative-Labour lead near 0; the result was Con 37.7, Lab 31.2, a 6.5-point lead (Table 1, Introduction). The Summary says the error averaged about 7 points. Recontact-survey late swing was 0.6 points in the sample-size-weighted estimate (95% CI -0.2 to 1.6), 1.8 with equal weighting and -0.4 for final-poll respondents only (Table 3, Section 4.1). Also published as the 2016 Inquiry report to the British Polling Council and Market Research Society, which could not be opened (403).
ERR-F08.model_link: Bloc swing (an industry-wide error on the gap between the two main camps) and its tails. A single 6.5-point lead error is about 2 sd of US election-level bias. Supports fat tails (T_DF 5) on the bloc term.

ERR-F09.claim: A review of UK and US polling finds error constant over time but always well beyond stated margins of error. Large misses on the lead are frequent. Lying 'shy' voters are rarely a substantial cause. The usual causes are unrepresentative samples and weighting, then undecided voters breaking one way, and to a lesser extent late swing and turnout models.
ERR-F09.quant: UK Conservative-Labour lead errors of 5 points or more occurred in 1951, 1970, Oct 1974, 1983, 1992, 1997, 2001, 2015 and 2017. Only 1970, 1992 and 2015 were called 'misses', because the winner was wrong (section 'Is polling actually getting worse?'). No evidence of a Shy Tory effect in 2015 or a Shy Trump effect in 2016 (section 'Shy voters'). Undecideds broke one way in 1992, Scotland 2014, the US 2014 midterms and US 2016 ('Differential Don't Knows').
ERR-F09.model_link: Fat tails on the bloc swing: about 9 of ~20 UK elections since 1945 had a 5+ point lead error. Undecided-lean layer (certainty layer, U_LEAN_PER_SIDE). Argues against a structural 'shy right' mean shift.

ERR-F10.claim: US 2016: national polls were among the most accurate since 1936, while state polls missed by much more. Errors are 'somewhat correlated in any given election', but there is no consistent partisan direction from election to election.
ERR-F10.quant: National polls, final 13 days: average absolute error on the Clinton-Trump margin 2.2 pts, signed 1.3. Compare 2012 2.9, 2008 1.8, 2004 2.1, a 1936-2016 average of 4.4 and 2.7 since 1992. State polls: absolute 5.1, signed 3.0. Polls under-estimated Democrats in 2000 and 2012 and Trump in 2016 (Key findings, pp. 9-10). Published in condensed form as Kennedy et al. 2018, Public Opinion Quarterly 82(1):1-33, doi 10.1093/poq/nfx047.
ERR-F10.model_link: Mean-zero bloc swing (no structural partisan bias carried across cycles), with a within-cycle correlated component.

ERR-F11.claim: US 2020 had the largest poll error in 40 years for the national vote and in at least 20 years for state races. Every mode and sampling frame erred in the same direction. The error did not shrink in the final two weeks, the final week or the final three days.
ERR-F11.quant: Table 4 p.19 poll MAE history: 2002 4.8, 2004 3.4*, 2006 4.0, 2008 4.0*, 2010 4.8, 2012 3.8*, 2014 5.8, 2018 4.6, 2020 6.7 (6.2 incl. presidential); *rows include presidential polls; NCPP 2002-14, AAPOR 2018. The no-shrinkage finding is for presidential polls.
ERR-F11.model_link: Two links. (1) The election-day stack should not decay with the calendar: the error is a measurement error present on the eve. Late events belong in the forward walk (see challenge on EVENT_RISK). (2) Fat tails: a 40-year-maximum miss arrived 4 years after a 'fixed' 2016.

ERR-F12.claim: US 2024: polls were more accurate than in 2016 and 2020, but for the third straight presidential cycle they understated Republicans. Historically, same-direction errors rarely persist for more than a couple of consecutive presidential elections. Republican-affiliated pollsters were slightly more accurate, possibly because they habitually publish Republican-friendly numbers, which helps only in years when the average poll leans Democratic.
ERR-F12.quant: 611 polls in the final two weeks. Average absolute error on the two-party margin 3.3 pts (2020: 5.3; 2016: 5.2). National presidential 2.6, state presidential 3.0. Democratic margin overstated by 2.7 across offices (2020: 4.6; 2016: 3.1). Midterms: 2022 overstated Republicans by 0.6, 2018 overstated Democrats by 0.1 (Executive Summary, p. 4).
ERR-F12.model_link: Mean of the bloc swing. A run of same-sign errors can happen, so a zero mean is a prior, not a certainty. The point about partisan-affiliated pollsters maps onto the Filber / Direct Polls / Channel 14 correlation group: their apparent accuracy in one cycle is not evidence of method quality.

ERR-F13.claim: FiveThirtyEight's 2016 forecast drew errors from a Student-t rather than a normal distribution. The author reports that this changed the forecast only slightly; the correlation of errors across units mattered far more. Poll volatility is also tied to the share of undecided and minor-party voters.
ERR-F13.quant: A 1-in-1,000 event under the normal becomes about 1-in-180 under their t. Switching to normal moves Clinton from 85% to 87%. Treating state errors as independent gives Clinton 99.8% against 85% with correlation. Clinton plus Trump held about 85% of the national vote, against about 95% for Obama plus Romney at the same point in 2012, and more undecided voters historically meant more volatility (24 Oct 2016 post, as reposted on the author's Goodreads blog). The t's degrees of freedom are not stated.
ERR-F13.model_link: T_DF = 5 on the bloc and family shocks: fat tails are standard practice, but they should change the tail shape, not inflate the variance. Correlated bloc swing as the dominant term. The undecided share (N12 11.5%) as a volatility driver belongs in the forward or certainty layer.

ERR-F14.claim: Calibration of election forecasts cannot be checked well from a handful of elections. Units within an election (states, or here lists) are correlated, not independent. Tail behaviour cannot be checked from past data at all. Forecasters also face incentives that push them toward over- or under-confidence.
ERR-F14.quant: With 10 events forecast at 0.7, the standard error is 0.14, so 'any success rate between, say, 0.5 and 0.9' is consistent with calibration (Section 2.1). A 1-in-20 event is expected about once in 80 years of presidential elections. FiveThirtyEight's 20% events happened about 14% of the time and its 80% events about 88% (Section 3.2; few elections). State polls missed by about twice the stated margin of error (Section 1.2).
ERR-F14.model_link: Validation harness: 90% coverage of 0.97 (eve) on about 90 list-cycles from 8 correlated cycles. The gap from 0.90 is suggestive, not proof. The shipping rule (win every leave-one-cycle-out fold) is the right bar. Tail parameters (T_DF, EVENT_RISK) cannot be validated on the record.

ERR-F15.claim: The Economist's 2020 US model starts from a prior of about 3 points of polling error per poll, based on historical data. It adds national and state polling-error terms, with state errors correlated through a scaled correlation matrix. It explicitly does not model unforeseen events (a late COVID-19 outbreak, the death of a candidate).
ERR-F15.quant: HDSR s.2.5 / s.4 / s.5. Either cite the July 2020 preprint for 'not adjusted for a renewed COVID-19 outbreak in late October or the death of either candidate', or, keeping the DOI, use: 'conditional on both major candidates staying in the race, no major third-party challenge and no unprecedented turnout or vote-counting problems (Abstract); COVID-19 effects on turnout and ballot rejection not modelled (s.5).'
ERR-F15.model_link: EVENT_RISK 1.2 on the bloc swing. A leading published model leaves event risk out of the election-day error. When forecasters do add it, it is forward-looking uncertainty, not a scale-up of measured poll error.

ERR-F16.claim: A multiparty forecast built only on current polls was overconfident. The authors added an election-day error term per party, based on how far polls had missed in past elections, and the 95% intervals then covered 94% of results over four German elections. The model uses an additive-log-ratio latent with a backward random walk and correlated party innovations.
ERR-F16.quant: Additive log-ratio transform (p. 256). Backward random walk with full innovation covariance W and an LKJ prior on its correlations (pp. 257-258). Footnote 14 (p. 259): forecasts were 'overconfident' because the poll model relied only on current data; an extra error term based on past poll misses, following Hanretty et al. 2016, gave 94% coverage of 95% intervals for the last four German elections. 2017 final forecast: RMSE 1.88 pp, with 6 of 7 five-in-six intervals covering the result.
ERR-F16.model_link: This is the same architecture as the model: ALR latent (CLR proposed), a per-list election-day residual calibrated on historical misses, and full-board correlation. It supports the residual layer existing. It also shows the calibration target: about nominal coverage, not 97%.

ERR-F17.claim: A UK multiparty forecast (ALR state-space, house effects summing to zero across active pollsters) was badly overconfident in 2015. House-effect centring cannot detect an industry-wide error; that error must come from a separate election-day term. The historical weight on poll-implied swing rose from about 0.45 a year out to about 0.80 on the eve: polls over-state change ('swingback').
ERR-F17.quant: Highlights: 'Like other poll-based models, model displayed large total seat error (110 seats) and overconfident predictions.' ALR transform and multinomial poll likelihood; house effects identified by a zero mean across active firm-method combinations. Weight on poll-implied swing fitted on 8 elections from 1979, rising from about 0.45 to 0.80 over the final year (accepted manuscript, pp. 1-2).
ERR-F17.model_link: House effects with a sum-to-zero constraint (the bloc swing must carry industry bias). Fat tails. The forward walk has no mean reversion (swingback) term; see open questions.

ERR-F18.claim: In Israel's three 2019-20 elections, media-sponsored polls were biased in line with their outlet's stance on Netanyahu. Polls commissioned by anti-Netanyahu outlets consistently under-estimated the seats the pro-Netanyahu bloc won. This is the only peer-reviewed study of Israeli poll bias for the 2019-2022 era that this desk located.
ERR-F18.quant: Direction only (abstract): on average, polls commissioned by anti-Netanyahu outlets consistently under-estimated the pro-Netanyahu bloc's seats, Apr 2019 to Mar 2020; no effect sizes; no reported result for pro-Netanyahu outlets.
ERR-F18.model_link: House effects with outlet-aligned correlation groups (Filber / Direct / Channel 14 cluster; dossier s.1). The bias is outlet-specific and of opposite sign by camp, so it belongs in house effects, not in a mean shift of the bloc swing.

ERR-F19.claim: Israel 2015: the final polls had Likud trailing the Zionist Union, and Likud won by six seats. Pollsters attributed the gap mainly to late movement inside the right-wing bloc (from Jewish Home and Yachad to Likud after a final-weekend rally and Netanyahu's election-day 'droves' warning), not to a swing between blocs. Even the exit polls under-counted Likud.
ERR-F19.quant: Exit polls (Ch 1/2/10) Likud 27-28, ZU 27; result Likud 30, ZU 24. Final polls had Likud trailing or tied. Pollsters cite late movement within the right bloc (Jewish Home named; Yachad not mentioned) plus an exit-poll closing-time gap. Own record: Likud final-week 21.2 vs 30 (beat +8.8, actual-polled); bloc error -0.12 (polled-actual); 2019a Likud beat +6.8, bloc +0.39.
ERR-F19.model_link: Gevalt coupling (Likud <-> satellites, zero-sum) and the trailing-Likud conditional sourced from satellites (s.41). The large Israeli misses were within-bloc transfers, which a bloc-level swing cannot represent.

ERR-F20.claim: Israeli polling has structural coverage problems. Haredim respond less, especially to online polls. Arab citizens and post-Soviet immigrants are less willing to share opinions. Weekly TV polls use samples of about 500 and fix gaps by weighting after collection, which adds sampling error. Pollsters disclose little about their weighting.
ERR-F20.quant: Typical TV-poll n is about 500; the article states a margin of error above 4%, larger than the 3.25% threshold. Haredim are less likely to respond to online polls. Oversampling small groups is too expensive for weekly media polls (party pollsters do it). HaMadad (Channel 13) separates Jewish and Arab respondents. Israeli pollsters have historically done better on bloc totals than on individual parties.
ERR-F20.model_link: Two links. (1) Correlated haredi and Arab family shocks: own record shows the haredi family under-polled by 1.35 seats on average (sd 1.77; Shas beat its final polls by about 1.2 over six cycles). (2) Design effects on poll noise.

ERR-F21.claim: Arab-sector poll error is mainly a turnout problem: Arab turnout swings by double digits between consecutive elections. Balad's 2022 near-miss of the threshold turned on turnout, not on its share of Arab voters.
ERR-F21.quant: Rudnitzky 2022: 2021 44.6%, 2022 53.2% (+8.6 pp), 2013-2022 average 55.9%; Druze 48.7 vs 55.9. Double-digit swings need another source (e.g. IDI on 2019-2021: 49.2 / 59.2 / 64.8 / 44.6). The poll-error interpretation is the desk's.
ERR-F21.model_link: Graded Arab turnout term (T about 0.58, pass-through 0.247, intercept -0.634; dossier s.43) instead of an additive Arab family shock.

ERR-F22.claim: Near the 3.25% threshold, a small vote-share miss becomes a 4-5 seat miss. Seat-based error records therefore mix the vote-share error with the threshold's all-or-nothing rule. In 2022 Meretz missed by 0.09 pp of the vote and lost all its seats.
ERR-F22.quant: 2022 CEC: Meretz 150,793 votes = 3.16% (0.085 pp / 4,061 votes short of 3.25%); final-window poll average 4.43 seats is about 3.35-3.46% of the valid vote, so the vote-share miss was about 0.2-0.3 pp, booked as a +4.4 seat error.
ERR-F22.model_link: This challenges the residual calibration: error_decomposition fits the residual on seat errors that include eight threshold deaths, then applies that sd in vote-share space before Bader-Ofer applies the threshold again. Ties to the s.41 open item (re-grade on CEC vote shares).

ERR-F23.claim: Own record, 2009-2022: Israeli final-window polls show no systematic 'shy right' at bloc level. The right-plus-haredi lists were over-polled in five of eight cycles. The big right-wing under-counts were Likud-specific, in years when Likud trailed. Bloc-level error has sd 3.36 seats with a non-significant positive mean.
ERR-F23.quant: Bloc error (polled - actual, seats): mean +1.66, sd 3.36, RMS about zero 3.55, t 1.40, n=8; over-polled in 5 of 8. Likud final-week beat (actual - polled): trailing or tied +8.8 / +6.8 / -0.5; otherwise -3 (2013) to +1.9 (2020). Haredi family: raw -0.98 (sd 1.58); net of bloc swing -1.35 (sd 1.77). Arab: -0.32 (sd 1.45) net, raw -0.69 (sd 1.17).
ERR-F23.model_link: Bloc swing sd 3.36 (BLOC_SWING_SD) and its zero mean; the trailing-Likud conditional; family shocks. Cross-national work (ERR-F09/F10/F12) also finds no stable partisan direction, which backs the zero mean.

ERR-F24.claim: Own record, computed for this desk: Israeli list-level final-poll errors are strongly fat-tailed. The small-list residual is inflated by threshold deaths: lists of up to 8 seats that won seats miss with sd 1.22 seats, while the eight lists that died show +3.3 seat errors. Re-fitting size dependence on lists that won seats gives a steeper, lower line than the shipped one. Pollsters also spread less than pure sampling would imply (herding).
ERR-F24.quant: Won-seat lists (n=83): raw sd 2.09, excess kurtosis 4.1, t df 2.2; e2 kurtosis 4.6; e3 (the fitted residual) kurtosis 2.0. Like-for-like e3 refit on won-seat lists: 0.79 + 0.075 x seats (1.10 / 1.55 / 2.68 at 4 / 10 / 25). Shipped decompose() 1.83 + 0.044 is inflated by an index-aliasing bug; corrected full-sample fit 1.48 + 0.041 (x0.9: 1.48 / 1.70 / 2.25 vs shipped 1.80 / 2.04 / 2.63). Herding ratio 0.47-1.06 (median 0.66) of n=500 SRS spread.
ERR-F24.model_link: This challenges two things. (1) The Gaussian per-list residual (rng.standard_normal x sd_list). (2) Its shape: (1.83 + 0.044 x seats) x 0.9 is too wide for small lists and slightly narrow for the largest. It supports a fat-tailed form on the stack (T_DF 5). Herding means between-pollster spread understates true error, so industry-level shocks must be added.

SYS-F01.claim: The legal threshold is 3.25% of ALL valid votes, tested per list ('not less than'); only lists that pass take part in the allocation, and the quota is the INTEGER part of the passing lists' valid votes divided by 120; each list first receives the integer part of votes/quota.
SYS-F01.quant: s.81(a): 'not less than 3.25% (three and a quarter per cent) of all the valid votes'; s.81(b): quota = whole number of (sum of valid votes of participating lists)/120; s.81(c): seats = whole number of votes/quota. 2022: quota 36,227 (Kenig 2026, reproduced exactly from CEC counts).
SYS-F01.model_link: src/simulate.py THRESHOLD = 0.0325 and `passed = sh >= threshold` (also src/bayes_model.py project(), validate_bayes.allocate_vector): the comparison operator and the 3.25% value match the statute; see SYS-F15 for the denominator.

SYS-F02.claim: Remainder seats go one at a time to the largest 'list quotient' votes/(seats+1); an exact tie is broken by a lottery run by the CEC; and a list with no more than half of the participating valid votes stops receiving seats once it holds half of all seats. The model breaks ties by column order (np.argmax) and does not implement the majority clause.
SYS-F02.quant: s.81(d)(1)-(3) highest-averages iteration; s.81(d)(2) tie -> 'a lottery conducted by the Central Committee'; s.81(d)(4) majority clause (cap at 60 seats for a list with <=50% of participating votes). Exact ties on the CEC counts 2015-2022: 0 of 6 elections. In the model, shares are continuous floats, so exact ties have probability ~0; the largest 2026 list is ~19% (Likud mean share 0.190), so s.81(d)(4) is unreachable.
SYS-F02.model_link: src/simulate.py dhondt(): `i = int(np.argmax(quot))` (lowest index wins ties) - a formal deviation from the statutory lottery with no measurable consequence; 81(d)(4) absent.

SYS-F03.claim: Surplus-vote agreements ('linkage', התקשרות): a list may link with only ONE other list; written notice signed by both lists' agents must reach the CEC no later than the 11th day before election day; the CEC publishes the linkages by the 8th day. Linked lists act as one list ONLY in the remainder stage (combined votes and combined s.81(c) seats), and only if EACH passed the threshold on its own; their joint seats are then split between them by the same s.81 method.
SYS-F03.quant: s.67(a) one partner only; s.67(b) deadline day 11 = Friday 16 Oct 2026 for the 27 Oct election; s.67(c) publication by day 8 = 19 Oct 2026; s.82(a) 'provided that each of them by itself received the percentage of votes fixed in s.81(a)'; s.82(b) internal split by the s.81 method. Statutory amendment history of ss.67/81 includes 5733 (1973), the Bader-Ofer amendment.
SYS-F03.model_link: src/simulate.py SURPLUS_PAIRS (5 signed pairs, 'Deadline Oct 16'), form_factions() (pool only if passed[a] and passed[b]; a list pooled at most once), and the inner dhondt([votes[a], votes[b]], k): all three legal conditions are implemented correctly. The site's 'deadline October 16' is correct.

SYS-F04.claim: Bader-Ofer as legislated (integer quota, floor seats, highest averages, linked lists pooled for the remainder stage, internal split) is mathematically D'Hondt applied to 'factions' (pairs pooled), and the model's implementation reproduces every official seat allocation 2015-2022 exactly.
SYS-F04.quant: Desk re-implementation of ss.81-82 in exact integer arithmetic on CEC final counts with the registered agreements: equals the official seats in 6/6 elections (2015, 2019a, 2019s, 2020, 2021, 2022); simulate.dhondt + form_factions on the same counts equals the statutory result in 6/6; 0 ties. The CEC guide describes the floor stage 'then ... the Bader-Ofer method'; Kenig (IDI 2026) calls the remainder stage D'Hondt (2022: 7 remainder seats).
SYS-F04.model_link: src/simulate.py dhondt()/form_factions(); dossier s.25 ('reproduces the official 2022 allocation exactly') - extended here to all six 3.25%-era elections.

SYS-F05.claim: Only a handful of seats are decided at the remainder (surplus) stage: 3 to 8 per election in 2015-2022 (mean 5.3), not 6-9.
SYS-F05.quant: Seats awarded under s.81(d) (120 minus the sum of integer quotas): 2015 4 (quota 33,511), 2019a 7 (32,860), 2019s 3 (35,917), 2020 3 (37,943), 2021 8 (36,210), 2022 7 (36,227). IDI (Kenig 2026) independently gives 2022 quota 36,227 and '7 seats remained'.
SYS-F05.model_link: docs/priors_dossier.md s.1 table row 'Surplus pairs in Bader-Ofer': '~6-9 of 120 seats decided at the surplus stage'.

SYS-F06.claim: Surplus agreements moved exactly one seat in four of the six 3.25%-era elections; per pair, holding the other registered pairs fixed, 9 of 23 effective pairs (both partners passed) gained a seat.
SYS-F06.quant: Registered pairs vs no pairs (CEC counts): 2015 Kulanu +1 / Joint List -1; 2019a UTJ +1 / Likud -1; 2019s none; 2020 none; 2021 Meretz +1 / Likud -1; 2022 Likud +1 / Labor -1 (dossier's 'without pairs Likud 31, Labor 5' confirmed). Pair-by-pair marginal gains (+1): 2015 YB-Kulanu; 2019a Shas-UTJ; 2019s B&W-YB, Likud-Yamina; 2020 B&W-Labor-Gesher-Meretz; 2021 Yamina-New Hope, Labor-Meretz; 2022 YA-National Unity, Likud-RZ. Pairs that died because one partner failed: 2019a New Right-YB, 2019s Noam-Otzma, 2021 B&W-New Economic, 2022 Labor-Meretz.
SYS-F06.model_link: src/simulate.py SURPLUS_PAIRS / the pair layer; backs the site's description that pairs are a real but one-seat-sized mechanism.

SYS-F07.claim: The expected value of one effective surplus pair is about +0.4 seat (range +0.23 to +0.77), consistent with the model's own 2026 measurement (+1 seat in 30-35% of draws) and with D'Hondt's known large-list seat bias - but below the '+0.5 to +0.9 expected seats per pair' stated on the site.
SYS-F07.quant: Desk perturbation on the CEC counts 2015-2022 (each list +/- N(0, 0.15 pp), 400 draws, registered pairs with vs without the pair): mean expected gain +0.40 seat over 23 effective pairs (min 0.23 UTJ-Shas 2015, max 0.77 Labor-Meretz 2021). Model 2026 (dossier s.40, 8 Oct posterior): JL+Ra'am +1 in 30% of draws, Together+YB +1 in 35% (-1 in 1% each) => ~+0.3. Schuster et al.: the divisor method with rounding down (Jefferson/D'Hondt) 'exhibits noticeable seat biases in favor of larger parties'; Hamilton and Webster are ~unbiased.
SYS-F07.model_link: site/template.html 'Threshold and Bader-Ofer' chapter: 'worth a measured +0.5 to +0.9 expected seats per pair'; dossier s.1 table 'Measured value +0.5-0.9 expected seats per signed pair'.

SYS-F08.claim: The validation harness's historical surplus pairs are not the registered agreements in four of eight cycles, and with exact official vote counts they misallocate 8 list-seats across three of the six 3.25%-era cycles, so part of the graded seat error is seat-law error, not poll error.
SYS-F08.quant: PAST_PAIRS differs from the registered agreements in 7 of 8 cycles (all but 2020). On exact CEC counts it misallocates 8 list-seats (2015, 2019s, 2021). The shipped harness additionally drops 6 PAST_PAIRS entries via DECOMP renaming (pair_alias off).
SYS-F08.model_link: src/validate_model.py PAST_PAIRS ('approximations of the registered agreements'), consumed by validate_bayes.project_cycle; dossier 'Not established: the registered surplus agreements (item 4)'.

SYS-F09.claim: Wasted votes (lists below 3.25%) swing between under 1% and almost 9% of valid votes, and in the two high-waste elections they decided the majority: 2019a (New Right short by 1,454 votes) and 2022 (Meretz short by 4,062).
SYS-F09.quant: 2019a: New Right's 1,454-vote miss cost the NB-without-YB a majority (60 vs 62). 2022: waste enlarged the NB from ~61-62 to 64 but did not decide the majority (Meretz passing alone -> NB 62).
SYS-F09.model_link: Threshold layer of project(); backs the site sentence on vote-loss/seat-win asymmetry.

SYS-F10.claim: Israel's disproportionality is driven by threshold waste, not by the D'Hondt formula: the Gallagher least-squares index tracks the wasted-vote share almost one-for-one across the 3.25% era.
SYS-F10.model_link: Supports modelling the threshold explicitly per draw (seat totals are a nonlinear function of straddlers' fates) rather than a proportional seat mapping.

SYS-F11.claim: The 3.25% threshold was set by Amendment No. 62 to the Knesset Elections Law, passed 11 March 2014 and applied from the 2015 election; it replaced 2%.
SYS-F11.quant: Amendment 62 (Sefer HaHukim 5774 p.347; passed 9 Adar II 5774 = 11 March 2014) substitutes '3.25% (three and a quarter per cent)' in s.81(a). IDI (Kenig 2026): 'Since the 2015 election, the electoral threshold has been set at 3.25% of the valid votes.' Threshold in votes: 140,052 (2019a), 143,327 (2021), 154,855 (2022).

SYS-F13.claim: Israel is the textbook 'extreme' PR system (one 120-seat national district, closed lists), and the threshold rise did not durably cut fragmentation: the effective number of electoral parties fell from 8.68 (2013) to 5.19 (2020) and rebounded to 8.92 (2021) and 7.99 (2022).
SYS-F13.quant: Gallagher Eff Nv / Eff Ns: 2013 8.68/7.28; 2015 7.71/6.94; 2019a 6.33/5.24; 2019s 6.11/5.57; 2020 5.19/5.01; 2021 8.92/8.52; 2022 7.99/6.51. Rahat & Hazan: a closed-list PR system 'so proportional' that it produced a fragmented parliament (abstract); Hazan, Itzkovitch-Malka & Rahat (2017) treat Israel as 'a prototype of an extreme PR system' (abstract).
SYS-F13.model_link: Context for the many-straddler structure of 2026 (21 latent lists, 38 filed): a fragmented field under a 3.25% bar keeps several lists in the threshold band every cycle.

SYS-F14.claim: Invalid ballots are excluded from every denominator; they run at 0.5-1.0% of votes cast and are defined by statute (identifying marks, more than three identical slips or slips for different lists, non-official envelope, blank slips).
SYS-F14.quant: Invalid share of votes cast (CEC): 2015 1.03% (43,854), 2019a 0.71%, 2019s 0.64%, 2020 0.54%, 2021 0.59%, 2022 0.62% (29,851 of 4,794,593). 2013: 40,904 (about 1%) disqualified (Knesset RIC/CEC leaflet). Grounds: s.78(a); CEC guide: 'two or three ballots for the same list ... valid'; blank slips without list letters invalid. s.84 requires the published results to list invalid votes separately.
SYS-F14.model_link: Model shares are shares of valid votes (vote intention); invalid voting is correctly not modelled as a list. No change.

SYS-F15.claim: The threshold denominator in law is ALL valid votes, including votes for the many micro-lists the model does not carry; the model renormalises shares over its modelled lists, which makes its threshold effectively 3.25% x (1 - m) of valid votes - slightly lenient, by roughly 800-1,300 votes in 2026 terms.
SYS-F15.quant: Formal bias 3.25% x m = 0.009-0.028 pp (~430-1,330 votes at 4.76M valid). The net bias is unmeasured; the modelled small-list columns already hold 2.3-4.2% of projected share.
SYS-F15.model_link: src/bayes_model.py project(): shares /= shares.sum(axis=1) over modelled lists, MICRO_PRIORS empty since s.42, then `passed = sh >= THRESHOLD`; same in simulate_core and validate_bayes.allocate_vector (v/sum(v)). Note implied_share_obs reserves 1% for micro-lists in seat-derived observations (seats/120*(1-wasted-0.01)) while CEC filings are renormalised to 1 - the latent's denominator is ambiguous.

SYS-F16.claim: Double-envelope (outer-envelope) votes are cast by soldiers, voters at accessible stations, hospital patients, prisoners, diplomats, shelter residents and - new for 2026 - evacuees displaced since 7 October 2023; they are checked for double voting after polls close and counted centrally in the Knesset after the regular count, and the official results must be published within eight days.
SYS-F16.quant: ch. 10-3C (פרק י׳3ג, temporary provision for the 26th Knesset), ss.116יז10-116יז13; outer envelope at s.116יז12(c).
SYS-F16.model_link: Election-night engine (dossier s.2: publish 'election-night seats' vs 'final seats'); the new evacuee category is not in any 2019-2022 base rate.

SYS-F17.claim: Double envelopes were 5.5% of valid votes in April 2019 and 9.6% in 2021 and 2022 (462,807 cast in 2022) per the CEC's final files; the election-week figure of 'over 600,000 / over 12.5%' for 2022 is not borne out by the CEC record, so a 2026 expectation of 600-700k (12-13%) lacks an official basis.
SYS-F17.quant: CEC outer-envelope rows (cast / valid / % of all valid): 2019a 240,783 / 238,822 / 5.54%; 2019s 282,442 / 280,216 / 6.32%; 2020 330,209 / 327,702 / 7.14%; 2021 425,512 / 421,619 / 9.56%; 2022 462,807 / 458,714 / 9.63% (838 counting units). IDI series via ToI matches 2019a-2021 (5.5/6.3/7.2/9.6%) but ToI (2 Nov 2022) said 'over 600,000' ballots, 'over 12.5%', for 2022. Atmor, Friedberg & Kenig (2025) document that the special-vote share 'has increased significantly in the past decade' (abstract). Invalid rate inside envelopes 0.76-0.91%.
SYS-F17.model_link: docs/priors_dossier.md s.2 'Double envelopes: record 600-700k expected (~12-13% of votes)'; election-night engine sizing.

SYS-F18.claim: Double envelopes lean strongly away from Arab and haredi lists and toward right-religious lists; the lean is large in percentage points and stable in sign across five elections.
SYS-F18.quant: Double-envelope share minus regular-station share (pp, CEC): Arab lists - Joint List 2019s -6.75, 2020 -7.70, 2021 -2.40; Hadash-Ta'al 2019a -2.89, 2022 -2.26; Ra'am(-Balad) 2019a -2.29, 2021 -2.45, 2022 -2.57; Balad 2022 -1.46. Haredi - UTJ -2.0 to -2.6 every cycle; Shas -0.6 to -1.9. Right-religious - Zehut 2019a +4.09; URWP/Yamina +0.88 (2019a), +3.18, +3.34, +3.54 (2019s-2021); RZ 2021 +1.45, 2022 +5.10. Likud +2.9 to +3.5 in 2019-2020, ~0 in 2021-2022. Labor 2021 +2.25, 2022 +1.58; Meretz -0.2 to +0.7. Matches the IDI characterisation (young Jewish voters; favour right-wing and fringe lists; disadvantage haredi and Arab lists).
SYS-F18.model_link: Election-night engine; dossier s.2 double-envelope lean bullet ('haredi and Arab lists ~1/3-1/2 under their regular-station share') - supported for Arab lists (34-52% of their regular-station share), weaker for haredi lists (UTJ 56-67%, Shas 69-92%).

SYS-F19.claim: From the complete regular-station count to the final count, seats moved in every election but the net bloc shift was zero in four of five and -1 for the Netanyahu bloc in 2022; the envelope effect is a within-bloc and Arab-list effect, not a +0.5-1 seat drift to the right, and Meretz and Balad (2022) were already below 3.25% before any envelope was opened.
SYS-F19.quant: Final minus regular-only seats (statutory allocation with registered pairs, CEC counts): 2019a URWP +1, Likud -1; 2019s B&W +1, Likud +1, UTJ -1, YB -1; 2020 Likud +1, B&W +1, Shas -1, JL -1; 2021 Meretz +1, Ra'am -1; 2022 YB +1, UTJ -1. Straddlers regular% -> final%: Ra'am 2021 4.023 -> 3.788; Ra'am-Balad 2019a 3.461 -> 3.334; New Right 2019a 3.143 -> 3.216 (still short); Labor 2022 3.542 -> 3.694; Meretz 2022 3.169 -> 3.165; Balad 2022 3.049 -> 2.909. (Partial election-night counts differ from the complete regular count; not measured here.)
SYS-F19.model_link: docs/priors_dossier.md s.2: 'night->final drift ~+0.5-1 seat right' and 'Meretz/Balad 2022 died in the envelopes'; election-night engine.

STR-F01.claim: Cox's coordination theory treats deserting a non-viable option as a feature of every electoral system. For PR, though, the claim that strategic voting matters politically (the Leys-Sartori conjecture: low district magnitude, high thresholds, or other features that penalise small parties) is one Cox says rests on reasoning rather than systematic evidence. Israel elects 120 members from one national district, so the only wasted-vote trigger is the legal threshold. Desk inference: wasted-vote desertion should concentrate on lists projected near 3.25% and be weak elsewhere.
STR-F01.quant: Chapter 5, 'Strategic voting in multimember districts', pp. 99-122 (chapter DOI 10.1017/CBO9781139174954.007). The concluding chapter's M+1 rule caps viable lists at district magnitude + 1 and is an upper bound, not a point prediction. Israel M = 120 (Abramson et al. 2010, p. 76). Only the chapter abstract was read, so it gives no magnitude.
STR-F01.model_link: new_straddler band test (desertion only near the line); certainty-layer soft-support churn (applies to every list)

STR-F02.claim: Israeli election-study respondents whose favourite was a minor party were much less likely to intend to vote for it than major-party supporters were for theirs, and the defections went mainly to the large parties. In 2003 Likud received most of them. The authors find that in every election studied, smaller parties lose votes to major parties.
STR-F02.quant: Jewish respondents with a strict top preference, pre-election vote intention (INES). 1999: One Israel 94.7% and Likud 93.6% loyal vs 61.3% for those preferring Center/Meretz/Shas (n=83) (Table 3A, p.77). 2003: Labor 81.9% and Likud 90.2% vs 72.5% for six other parties (n=349); of those 349, 15.2% intended Likud and 8.0% Labor (Table 3B, p.77). 2006: Kadima 93.1%, Labor 96.4%, Likud 92.9% vs 79.7% for Meretz/NU-NRP/YB/Shas (n=360) (Table 3C, p.78). These are intentions, not ballots, and the 'minor' group includes mid-size lists. Implied minor-list retention is 0.61-0.80, which brackets the retired x0.7 realization ratio.
STR-F02.model_link: gevalt coupling and TRAIL_SAT_SOURCE (consolidation toward the bloc's large list); size of small-list desertion (NEW_STRADDLER mu; retired MICRO_REALIZE 0.7)

STR-F03.claim: Voters who expect their preferred party to stay out of the coalition often desert it for the least-bad viable partner. In Israel 2006 this held after controlling for ideological and coalition preferences, but only for the two bloc-defining parties (Labor, Likud). Support for Meretz, Shas, Yisrael Beitenu and the NRP did not move with coalition expectations. Coalition-targeted consolidation is therefore a large-party phenomenon, and small-list cores are insensitive to it.
STR-F03.quant: Same numbers. Reword the claim: consolidation responded to coalition expectations only for the two coalition-DEFINING parties (Labor, Likud). Support for Meretz (5 seats), NU-NRP (9), YB (11) and Shas (12, equal to Likud) did not move with Labor/Likud coalition expectations (pp.318-319).
STR-F03.model_link: gevalt coupling and trailing-Likud (consolidation is coalition-targeted and runs to the bloc-defining list); new_straddler and the sectarian distinction (small-list cores do not respond to coalition expectations)

STR-F04.claim: Under PR with a threshold there are three strategic-coalition contexts: (1) a rental vote by a major-party supporter for a junior partner at risk at the threshold, (2) avoiding a wasted vote for a small party not expected to pass, and (3) explicit coalition voting. An Austria 2006 survey supports all three. The paper's review of the Israeli work adds two points. In 2003, about one voter in ten met stringent conditions for coalition-motivated voting for a non-favourite party (Blais et al. 2006). Expectations did not affect the vote intentions of right-religious party supporters, but did affect them for the secular Shinui (Aldrich et al. 2004).
STR-F04.quant: Austria: nationally representative pre-election survey, 2006 election. Israel: 'about one in ten voters passes a series of stringent conditions' (p.340). The original Blais, Aldrich, Indridason & Levine (2006, Party Politics 12(6):691-705, doi 10.1177/1354068806068594) and Aldrich et al. (2004, in Arian & Shamir eds., The Elections in Israel 2003, pp. 180-211) were not opened. The Israeli figures here are UNVERIFIED beyond this secondary account.
STR-F04.model_link: both directions of the threshold mechanism (rental surge vs wasted-vote desertion); certainty-layer churn magnitude; the sectarian/ideological exemption

STR-F05.claim: Under an operational definition of strategic voting, Israeli strategic voters are a very small share of the electorate. They are better educated, more often support small parties, more often believe polls influence voters, and therefore delay their final decision. They do not switch parties between elections more than sincere voters, and they do not differ from sincere voters on which coalition should or will form.
STR-F05.quant: Abstract-level (full text not opened); no percentage retrieved. The abstract calls strategic voters 'a very small percentage of the entire electorate'.
STR-F05.model_link: ceiling on the size of desertion layers; timing (strategic decisions are late, so they fall in the poll-silence window)

STR-F06.claim: Across national election studies, the share of voters who actually vote strategically is typically 5-15% of the electorate. In a lab experiment embedded in two real German state campaigns, supporters projected their preferred small party 1.7-2.9 points above the poll they were shown. They still expected it to pass even in the 'failure' condition. Strategic-voting theory explained only a small number of the insincere votes. Wishful thinking damps desertion: supporters discount bad polls for their own small list.
STR-F06.quant: 'typically ranges between 5 and 15 per cent of the electorate' (p.638). The mean forecast for the preferred small party fell from 9.8% (10% poll) to 6.4% (4% poll condition), F=9.85, p<0.001, but participants added 1.7-2.9 pp to the polls (p.653). Abstract: theory supported 'only for a small number of voters' (p.636).
STR-F06.model_link: NEW_STRADDLER mu = -1.6 pp. Helps explain why realised ballot drift for first-cycle straddlers is only -0.42 pp (dossier s.46.1) against -1.6 seat-implied.

STR-F07.claim: In a three-wave Israeli panel spanning the 2019-2020 elections, voters abandoned a party they had voted for when they expected it to be left out of the next coalition. Voters who saw the race between the two would-be formateurs (Likud, Blue and White) as close were more likely to switch to a formateur party than voters who expected their side to win. This is the individual-level mechanism behind late consolidation into the bloc's largest list, and it is triggered by closeness, not by trailing.
STR-F07.quant: Waves: Apr 2019 n=1,206; Sep 2019 n=909; Mar 2020 n=801, each about a week before the vote; 1,104 observations from 655 respondents. Switching: 28.5% at the first opportunity, 18.1% at the second. Predicted switching probability is 47-58% when expected coalition chances are 0-2 (0-10 scale) vs 13% at 10. 8.6% moved non-formateur to formateur and 6.8% the reverse. 'None of the non-formateur party voters ... switched to the party of the unpreferred formateur' (fn 12). The close-race effect is significant in Model 3 but loses significance (keeping its size) in bootstrapped subsamples. Race perceptions: 61.9% expected their side to win, 24.6% saw it as close, 13.6% expected the other side to win.
STR-F07.model_link: TRAIL condition (trail/tie by 0.5 seats, cliff), TRAIL_RAMP_ON (held off, s.46.3), and the layer's one-sidedness (Likud only)

STR-F08.claim: In 2015, framed as Likud vs Zionist Union, both large lists gained on 2013, but almost all of their gains came from parties in their own bloc. Identity politics led each to court voters inside its bloc. The late Likud surge was a within-bloc transfer, not a bloc swing.
STR-F08.quant: Rahat et al. at abstract level: no transfer matrix. Corroboration (Brom, CAP, 22 Apr 2015): the right bloc was 42 in the Haaretz final-poll average of 13 Mar and won 44, so the bloc moved +2 while Likud moved +9 (21 to 30). Against 2013, Likud gained 12 while Bennett's and Lieberman's parties lost 11 combined.
STR-F08.model_link: TRAIL_SAT_SOURCE (beat sourced from own satellites); gevalt coupling as a zero-sum within-bloc transfer

STR-F09.claim: In the eight polls published 12-13 March 2015, the last before the legal poll silence, Likud stood at 20-23 seats and trailed Zionist Union (24-26). Likud won 30. Its satellites paid: Jewish Home fell from 11-12 to 8 and Yachad from 4-5 to 0. Zionist Union landed at the bottom of its range (24), so the other camp did not supply the surge.
STR-F09.quant: Eleven polls of 12-13 Mar 2015: Likud 20-23, ZU 24-26, JH 11-13, Yachad 4-5, Kulanu 8-11 (won 10), YB 4-6 (won 6).
STR-F09.model_link: trailing-Likud conditional (2015 fold); gevalt coupling; TRAIL_SAT_SOURCE

STR-F10.claim: In April 2019 both would-be formateurs beat their final polls by similar margins, each at the expense of its own bloc's smaller lists. Likud went from 26-31 to 35 and Blue and White from 28-32 to 35. On the right, New Right (5-6 seats in every final poll) and Zehut (4-6) both failed. On the centre-left, Labor (8-11) fell to 6 and Meretz (5-8) to 4. Consolidation in a close formateur race was two-sided, while the shipped trailing layer gives the beat to Likud only.
STR-F10.quant: Nine polls of 4-5 Apr 2019: Likud 26-31, B&W 28-32, New Right 5-7, Zehut 4-8, URWP 5-8, Kulanu 3.18%-6 seats, Labor 8-11, Meretz 5-8, Gesher 2.0-2.9% (one poll 4 seats). Zehut's result to final-poll ratio is at most about 0.84 (2.74/3.25) and about 0.45-0.8 across the range.
STR-F10.model_link: TRAIL (Likud-only beat); gevalt coupling; NEW_STRADDLER (New Right and Zehut are among the nine first-cycle failures); dossier s.15 Zehut row

STR-F11.claim: In September 2019 the formateur race was tied in the final polls (Likud 31-36, Blue and White 31-33), and both landed inside their ranges (32, 33): there was no trailing beat. Otzma Yehudit showed 4 seats (at least 3.25%) in five of the eight final polls and 2.9-3.1% in two others, yet won about 1.9%, after Likud and Yamina argued its votes would be wasted. An ideological-core right-flank list was deserted under a gevalt appeal.
STR-F11.quant: Otzma 83,609 votes (1.88%) against a threshold of about 144,200 (3.25% of 4,436,806 valid votes). Final eight polls: 4 seats in 5, 2.9-3.1% in 2, 1 with no figure.
STR-F11.model_link: dossier s.15 realization table (Otzma Sept 2019 row) and the site sentence on sectarian/ideological lists; gevalt coupling (Otzma in GEVALT_SAT_IDS); TRAIL (tie fold)

STR-F12.claim: In 2021 Likud led clearly (29-32 vs Yesh Atid 17-19), so there was no close formateur race. Every list sitting at the 4-seat floor of the final polls met or beat it: Blue and White 4-7 to 8, Meretz 4-5 to 6, Religious Zionism 4-5 to 6, Labor 4-6 to 7, and Ra'am, 4 in seven polls and 1.7% in one, to 4. The mid-sized first-cycle New Hope fell from 7-10 to 6. Near-threshold lists can surge as well as desert.
STR-F12.quant: Eight polls of 16-19 Mar 2021. Results: B&W 6.63%, Meretz 4.59%, RZP 5.12%, Labor 6.09%, Ra'am 3.79%, New Hope 4.74%, Yamina 6.21% (polled 8-10). The pattern matches the dossier's own 2021 straddler drift of +1.94 pp (s.36) and Ra'am entering the fidelity record as a D-21 straddler that passed (projected 3.16%, won 3.79%, s.46.1).
STR-F12.model_link: NEW_STRADDLER (one-signed desertion term); a desert/surge mixture; TRAIL (non-firing fold)

STR-F13.claim: In 2022 almost 9% of votes were wasted below the threshold. The Netanyahu bloc outpolled its rivals by about 30,000 votes, under one seat, yet won 64 seats. All four Netanyahu-bloc lists signed surplus agreements, against two in the other camp, where five lists were wobbling near the line. Measured against the final polls, Meretz (an established list, 4-5 seats in all eight final polls) failed with 3.16%, about 4,050 votes short. Jewish Home (polled 1.2-2.1%) took 1.19%. Balad, an Arab sectoral list polled at 1.0-2.75%, took 2.91%.
STR-F13.quant: Kenig: 'almost 9% of the votes were wasted below the electoral threshold'; Meretz and Balad together 'some 300,000 votes'. Final polls from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opinion_polling_for_the_2022_Israeli_legislative_election (eight polls of 23-28 Oct 2022). Results: Meretz 150,793 votes (3.16%), Balad 138,617 (2.91%), Jewish Home 56,775 (1.19%), of 4,764,742 valid votes. Jewish Home's ratio is about 0.6-0.65 (supports the old x0.7). Balad's is about 1.5 (supports a sectoral exemption). Meretz's is about 0.75-0.95, and Meretz is NOT first-cycle.
STR-F13.model_link: NEW_STRADDLER first-cycle restriction (Meretz 2022 is an established list that was deserted); sectoral exemption (Balad); surplus agreements as a coalition signal

STR-F14.claim: Gil (Pensioners), a first-cycle list polled at 0-2 seats under a 2% threshold, gained support in the days before the 2006 election. Contrary to all predictions it won 7 seats. This is a first-cycle near-threshold SURGE outside the graded 2009-2022 window. Inside the window the only surge among the eleven first-cycle straddlers is Yamina (Sept 2019).
STR-F14.quant: Bargsted & Kedar p.312 fn 11: Gil 'gained support in the days leading to the elections, and contrary to all predictions won seven seats'. Result: 185,759 votes, 5.92%, 7 seats; threshold 2%; pre-election polls 0-2 seats (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Israeli_legislative_election).
STR-F14.model_link: NEW_STRADDLER as a single normal with mu < 0 vs a desert/surge mixture

STR-F15.claim: Threshold insurance voting needs three conditions: the voter weighs government outcomes, the party is at risk of missing the threshold, and it is not the voter's first preference. All three held in Sweden 2010 for the Christian Democrats, the government coalition's small party at risk under the 4% line, which received strategic insurance votes. In the author's summary, a majority of KD voters named the Moderates (the senior partner) as their preferred party.
STR-F15.quant: Conditional logit on the 2010 Swedish National Election Study. KD won 5.6% (threshold 4%). The 'majority preferred the Moderates' wording is from Freden's LSE EUROPP post of 26 Feb 2015 (https://blogs.lse.ac.uk/europpblog/2015/02/26/evidence-from-sweden-shows-the-importance-of-parties-signalling-potential-coalition-partners-for-strategic-voting). Effect magnitudes were not retrieved (full text not opened).
STR-F15.model_link: surge component for straddlers embedded in a bloc with a senior partner (RZP-Zehut, Otzma, Amcha relative to Likud; Democrats or B&W relative to Yashar)

STR-F16.claim: In survey experiments with randomised polls and coalition signals, insurance voting for a small party depended on two things: polls putting it just below the threshold, and its membership of a clear pre-electoral coalition. Small parties outside a coalition benefited much less.
STR-F16.quant: Abstract-level (Lund University record); the experiment's magnitudes were not retrieved.
STR-F16.model_link: conditioning variable for a desert/surge mixture: coalition embedding of the straddler, not its age

STR-F17.claim: A 2022 Swedish survey experiment placed each of the three smallest parties below, at, or above the 4% threshold. Poll-induced insurance voting appeared for the party most tied to a government alternative (Christian Democrats), weakly for the Liberals, and not at all for the issue-focused Greens. None of the threshold parties was abandoned because of low poll levels.
STR-F17.quant: N=3,259 (fieldwork 31 Aug-9 Sep 2022; nine conditions). KD vote: 8.2% when shown at 2.5%, 7.3% at 4.0%, 4.1% at 5.5% (2.5 vs 5.5: t=4.88, p<.05; 4.0 vs 5.5: t=3.06, p<.05). Liberals 6.8 / 4.8 / 4.9% (n.s.). Greens 11.4 / 11.2 / 12.2% (n.s.) (p.6). Insurance came mainly from Moderate supporters; Sweden Democrat supporters mostly stayed. Authors: 'none of the smaller threshold parties were abandoned because of low poll levels'.
STR-F17.model_link: NEW_STRADDLER sign and conditioning; certainty-layer churn on near-threshold lists (low polls did not by themselves trigger abandonment)

STR-F19.claim: Supporters of the major German parties sometimes voted against their first preference on the PR (second) vote to raise the chance of a majority with the declared junior partner. Their party choice responded to expectations about the small party's chances of re-entering parliament.
STR-F19.quant: Two-step random-utility estimation on German election-study data. Abstract-level; magnitudes and elections covered not retrieved (full text not opened).
STR-F19.model_link: surge component (threshold insurance from the senior partner's voters)

STR-F20.claim: Because coalition bargaining waters down each party's influence on policy, outcome-oriented voters often back parties more extreme than themselves to pull the coalition's policy their way (compensational voting). The effect is stronger in consensual systems, such as the Netherlands and Norway, than in majoritarian ones (Britain, Canada). This is a standing counterforce to consolidation: some right-flank satellite support is held in order to pull a Likud-led coalition rightward, not merely parked.
STR-F20.quant: Four parliamentary democracies (Britain, Canada, Norway, Netherlands); the abstract states the theory and finds that institutional context conditions the weight on compensational voting. No pooled pp effect.
STR-F20.model_link: TRAIL_SAT_CAP 0.75 (a cap on how much satellites can lose to a Likud beat); the sectarian/ideological distinction

STR-F21.claim: Israeli law bars broadcasting or publishing the results of any election survey not already published from the END of the Friday before the polls open until the polls close. A survey published before that point may be repeated only with a prominent note that it is not current and says nothing about voting patterns on the day. For the 27 Oct 2026 election, Friday 23 Oct is the last legal day for new polls, which leaves about four unobserved days (Friday night to Tuesday 22:00).
STR-F21.quant: Elections Law (Propaganda Methods), 5719-1959, s.16E(h) (Hebrew 16ה(ח)), current text as published by the Central Elections Committee (reference 2022-000238). The same section requires filing every survey with the CEC (s.16E(e)).
