An IDI note of 15 Nov 2002 (https://www.idi.org.il/parliaments/7129/9017) described the October 2002 amendment as a one-day ban; the amendment history between that and the current end-of-Friday text was not traced. The Wikipedia 2022 polling page marks the silence from the end of Friday 28 Oct 2022 for a Tuesday 1 Nov election.
STR-F21.model_link: calendar (dossier s.5: 'Oct 23 (Fri) Poll blackout begins'); final refit on the 22-23 Oct polls; the forward random walk and gevalt/late-swing shocks cover a window no poll can observe

STR-F22.claim: In a post-election survey of 1,133 voters after the 2015 election, 15% said they decided on election day and another 13% in the campaign's final days. 62% of these late deciders voted for right-wing parties, 21% for centrist and 16% for left-wing parties. A large and right-leaning late decision fell inside the poll-silence window.
STR-F22.quant: n=1,133 (sponsor New Majority, pollster unnamed): 15% decided on election day (inside the window), 13% 'in the final days' (only partly inside). Late deciders (both groups) 62% right / 21% centre / 16% left.
STR-F22.model_link: poll-silence window variance; timing of the gevalt transfer; certainty layer (undecided lean)

STR-F23.claim: In a large Danish survey experiment (PR, eight parties), a news story showing a party gaining raised intended votes for it relative to a story showing it losing, for both a large party (about 21%) and a small one (about 4%). The loss story did not significantly lower support relative to the control. Bandwagon effects are real but small and asymmetric: a poll decline alone does not trigger measurable desertion.
STR-F23.quant: Gain vs loss p<0.05 for both parties; gain vs control joint p<0.05; loss vs control negative, n.s. (p<0.4); positive vs negative effect size difference n.s. (p<0.5). No heterogeneity by sociodemographics.
STR-F23.model_link: no poll-momentum (bandwagon) term in the projection; a falling straddler is not deserted by poll exposure alone

STR-F24.claim: In a Dutch survey experiment with real poll results, simply showing poll standings did not change later vote intentions. Framing a party as growing produced a small bandwagon effect, and that effect was no larger among undecided voters.
STR-F24.quant: N=23,421. Plain standings: no effect. Growth framing: modest positive effect. No moderation by indecision (abstract).
STR-F24.model_link: no bandwagon term; the undecided lean (certainty layer) need not track poll momentum

STR-F25.claim: Strong partisans react to a threatened electoral loss with anger and more campaign activity, and to reassured victory with enthusiasm. Holders of strong issue positions show no such arousal. This is the psychological basis of a 'gevalt' appeal: it works on identifiers when their party's standing is threatened, which fits a trigger based on the formateur race rather than a constant Likud premium.
STR-F25.quant: Four studies (APSR 109(1):1-17). Effects of threat and reassurance on anger and enthusiasm concentrate among strong identifiers (abstract). No vote-share magnitude.
STR-F25.model_link: TRAIL trigger (threat = trailing or tied) and the retired fixed anchors (a constant premium fired in two cycles out of eight)

SEC-F01.claim: The official Arab-and-Druze turnout series swings far more than national turnout, and the 2022 base the model scales from is a regular-station figure. Reuses atlas D2-F02 (verified with corrections) and D2-F07.
SEC-F01.quant: Arab lists 85.8% (423,877) / Jewish parties 14.2% (70,118): Bayan 28 Table 1; eligible/voters/regions: Table 2.
SEC-F01.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT_REC (harness), ARAB_TURNOUT base 0.538 (kalpi) vs 0.532 (s.43 disclosure e), regime tables A/B.

SEC-F02.claim: Peer-reviewed analysis of 2019-20 ties Arab turnout to list unity: when the Joint List broke up in April 2019, disappointed Arab voters stayed home and Arab seats fell from 13 to 10; the reunited list won 13 and then 15.
SEC-F02.quant: Seats: 13 (2015) -> 10 (Apr 2019, split) -> 13 (Sep 2019, reunited) -> 15 (Mar 2020). Turnout over the same cycles 63.5 -> 49.2 -> 59.2 -> 64.8 (SEC-F01).
SEC-F02.model_link: Regime structure of ARAB_TURNOUT (mean_unified vs mean_split; harness tables A/B).

SEC-F03.claim: The unity rule is conditional, not mechanical: Rudnitzky's peer-reviewed account frames 2019-21 as the Arab public disciplining the parties' configuration, and 2022 broke the rule (turnout rose 8.6 points despite a three-way split). Reuses atlas D2-F07.
SEC-F03.quant: Turnout 49.2% (Apr 2019) -> 64.8% (2020, a two-decade high) -> 44.6% (2021, record low); seats 10 -> 15 -> 10. 2022: 53.2% with three separate lists; Rudnitzky (Bayan 28): 2021 abstainers 'found an address', boycott declarations were reversed, tactical votes for Balad.
SEC-F03.model_link: Regime table B mean 0.580 (s.43): three four-party-unity years plus 2021. 2026 is a partial reunion (Hadash-Ta'al-Balad on one list, Ra'am separate).

SEC-F04.claim: Minority turnout in national elections falls when representation is descriptive but not substantive (no policy influence). In 2026 both prime-ministerial candidates rule out Arab parties in a coalition, while three in four Arab citizens want an Arab party in government: by this mechanism a downside risk to the 0.58 mean.
SEC-F04.quant: Rosenthal, Zubida & Nachmias: Muslim Arab turnout fell in national elections while rising in local ones. KAP May 2026: 77.2% support an Arab party joining the coalition (43.3% any government, 33.9% centre-left only). Xinhua, 11 Oct 2026: neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot willing to bring Arab parties into his coalition; Kan 4 Oct poll: Arab parties 13 seats.
SEC-F04.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT mean_unified 0.580 (enters the mean only through k = 0.247).

SEC-F05.claim: Disqualification fights are near-constant and leave no consistent turnout signature: the Central Elections Committee has moved against Arab lists or candidates in most elections since 2003, the Supreme Court reversed every one, and Arab turnout rose after four and fell after three. Configuration, not backlash, tracks turnout. Reuses atlas D2-F24 for 2026.
SEC-F05.quant: CEC disqualifications, all overruled: 2003 (Balad, Bishara, Tibi), 2009 (Balad, Ra'am-Ta'al), 2013 and 2015 (Zoabi), Apr 2019 (Ra'am-Balad), Mar 2020 (Yazbek) [IDI table]; 2022 Balad (CEC 9-5, Court 9-0, Adalah); 2026 Joint List and Ra'am (Court unanimous, 2 Oct 2026, atlas D2-F24). Arab turnout change in those elections: 2003 -13.0, 2009 -2.9, 2013 +3.1, 2015 +7.0, Apr 2019 -14.3, 2020 +5.6, 2022 +8.6 points.
SEC-F05.model_link: No disqualification/backlash term in ARAB_TURNOUT; the T draw's spread carries it.

SEC-F06.claim: The 2025-26 KAP/Stat-Net surveys bracket the model's 0.58: about 53% if the parties run separately, 62-67% if all four reunite; 2026 is in between (a Joint List without Ra'am). Crime dominates the agenda. Verifies the November 2025 figures the atlas desk could not open (atlas D2-F19).
SEC-F06.quant: Nov 2025 (Stat-Net, phone in Arabic, n=500, 13-18 Nov): 52.4% separate (Hadash-Ta'al 5.3, Ra'am 3.9, Balad 2.6 seats) vs 61.8% four-party Joint List (15.5 seats); June 2025 survey 57%; the authors link the Nov dip to the Monitoring Committee dispute. May 2026 (Stat-Net, n=500, 26 Apr-3 May): 53% separate (5.3 / 4.6 / 1.8) vs 67% four-party (16.3 seats). Nov 2025: violence and crime the top issue for 74%; 76.6% report weak personal security; Arab homicides 244 (2023), 237 (2024), 228 (to Nov 2025).

SEC-F07.claim: Survey-based Arab turnout forecasts have missed by 4 to 15 points in both directions, so they cannot tell 0.53 from 0.62. KAP's 'expected turnout' re-weights stated intention by respondents' past voting.
SEC-F07.quant: Final pre-election KAP surveys: +15.1 (Mar 2021), -4.2 (Oct 2022); early-campaign readings: KAP Aug 2022 -11.2, Statnet/Kan Aug 2022 -14.2, KAP Nov 2020 +11.0; Coalition 17/9 (Sep 2019) -3. Range 3-15 points.
SEC-F07.model_link: s.20 rule that turnout-intention series do not drive SECTOR_TURNOUT; ARAB_TURNOUT sd; Afkar 1.6x noise multiplier.

SEC-F08.claim: Stated intention to vote overstates Arab turnout by 15-35 points, and stated certainty does not rank sectors by actual turnout (haredim, the highest-turnout sector, report the least certainty). Reuses atlas D2-F21 (corrected).
SEC-F08.quant: Stated intention above actual: +16 to +38 points (IDI Sep 2022 70 vs 53.2; KAP Oct 2022 69 vs 53.2; KAP Mar 2021 82.5 vs 44.6). Khalaily: 'optimistic' reading ~50%.
SEC-F08.model_link: s.20 participation dial; certainty layer (undecided lean) should not use stated turnout certainty by sector.

SEC-F09.claim: Afkar's September 2026 Arab-sector poll is a mixed-mode stratified sample with low response rates, converted to seats at an assumed 60% turnout. No published Afkar turnout or seat track record was located; IDI has used Afkar for fieldwork (2022 special survey, 2026 first-time voters).
SEC-F09.quant: IDI first-time voters (May 2026): n=576, 443 Jewish / 133 Arab, fieldwork firm not named; Afkar-IDI link documented for 2022 special survey and 2025 Democracy Index only.

SEC-F10.claim: The under-count is Ra'am-shaped, not proportional: sector surveys admit they miss Ra'am's Negev Bedouin base, sector pollsters' Ra'am scenarios were wrong in 2021, and national final polls under-counted Ra'am in both cycles it ran alone.
SEC-F10.quant: KAP Nov 2025: sampling misses Negev Bedouin tribes, so Ra'am's strength is underestimated (p.11). Ra'am took 73.9% of the Negev Arab vote in 2022 (Bayan 28); Negev 144,860 eligible, 51.0% turnout; tribal stations 38% (atlas D2-F09). Makladeh, Mar 2021: Ra'am likely fails near 55% turnout and passes near 59% (Times of Israel, 23 Mar 2021); actual turnout 44.6% and Ra'am won 4 seats. KAP Oct 2022 gave Ra'am 3.7 seats from Arab votes; it won 5. Own record, final-poll mean minus result: Ra'am -2.29 (2021), -0.57 (2022); Joint List +2.29 in 2021 (family error 0.00).
SEC-F10.model_link: Arab family term allocates the shift by base share (JL and Ra'am move together); Ra'am pass probability 0.752; LOYAL_SD raam 1.8; harness merges 2021 JL+Ra'am (s.43 disclosure i).

SEC-F11.claim: Most 2026 national polls are Hebrew-language online panels of 500-610 with single-digit to mid-20s response rates, so their Arab subsamples are small and self-selected. Tatika's raw sample was 11% Arab, close to the Arab share of 2022 voters but well below the ~16% Arab share of the electorate. Channel 13's consortium alone runs a separate StatNet phone sample of Arabs (101-221) and converts to seats 'by sector weights in the population'.
SEC-F11.quant: Ch13 Arab phone samples 100-230 across Jul-Oct filings; drop 'Hebrew-language' (not stated in filings).
SEC-F11.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT base comment: 'National panels weight the Arab sector to the last election's turnout (0.538)'; house effects.

SEC-F12.claim: The national election study itself found online panels yield too few Arab respondents and supplements them by telephone in Arabic; in 2020 it commissioned Statnet for the Arab sample. This is independent support for the claim that mainstream panels under-reach the sector.
SEC-F12.quant: INES 2022 and 2025: Cohen Institute online probability panel, with phone interviews added among Arabic speakers to raise Arab numbers; 2019: phone, Arab households stratified by district and religion; 2020: Statnet random cellular sample after the pre-election survey produced few Arab interviews. Arab subsample sizes are given only in images (not read).

SEC-F13.claim: Houses embed different Arab turnout assumptions, so 'polls weight Arabs to 2022 turnout' is true for some firms only. Maariv's pollster says Arab lists would reach 17 seats at Jewish-level turnout while his polls show about 12; Afkar converts at 60%; Channel 13 shows 13-15.
SEC-F13.quant: Lazar (JPost, 13 Sep 2026): Arab turnout 'not increasing'; 17 seats at Jewish-level turnout; Ra'am steady at 5; his CEC filings show Joint List 7 + Ra'am 5 = 12 (implied Arab turnout about 0.7x Jewish, roughly 0.50-0.53). Afkar: 60% (SEC-F09). Ch13 / Midgam Project: Joint List 8-10 + Ra'am 5-6 = 13-15 seats across Aug-Oct filings. Range of house totals 12-15 seats is about what Arab turnout of 0.50-0.60 implies.
SEC-F13.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT base 0.538 used as the poll average's implicit turnout in r = 1 + k(T_mean/base - 1).

SEC-F14.claim: National polls absorb most of a turnout swing but under-count the Arab lists on average, matching the graded term. In 2022 the press consensus expected Arab turnout in the low 40s and about 8 Arab seats; turnout was 53.2% and Arab lists won 10 seats, with Balad's 2.9% wasted. In 2021 the polls caught the turnout collapse exactly.
SEC-F14.quant: AP, 26 Oct 2022: Arab turnout expected 'in the low 40s', Arab parties about 8 seats, Ra'am polling 4. Own record, Arab family final-poll mean minus result (seats): 2009 -2.78, 2013 -0.27, 2015 -0.38, 2019a +1.22, 2019s -0.71, 2020 -1.00, 2021 0.00, 2022 -1.57; mean -0.69. Harness fit (s.43): slope k 0.247 (se 0.21, strict-LOO 0.10-0.32), intercept -0.634 (se 0.41), n=8.

SEC-F15.claim: A pre-2015 audit of every published poll found Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties under-estimated and Likud and Labor over-estimated. Its author warned that house corrections stop working when pollsters change methods, which matters because 2026 firms now run dedicated haredi and Arab samples.
SEC-F15.quant: Project 61 (Nehemia Gershuni-Aylho): all polls of the 2006, 2009 and 2013 elections up to 30 days out, compared with results. Directional finding only; no published magnitudes in the article.
SEC-F15.model_link: Signs of ARAB_TURNOUT_INTERCEPT and the haredi FAMILY_SHOCK mean; case for down-weighting pre-2019 cycles.

SEC-F16.claim: The haredi population grows about 4.2% a year, but the haredi lists' realised vote share has grown about 0.2 points a year (about +1 seat per four-year term), well below the dossier's '+1.5-2 seats' demographic drift.
SEC-F16.quant: Realised Shas+UTJ share growth: 1992-2022 ~+0.2 pt/yr; 2009-2022 ~+0.1; 2015-2022 ~+0.43. Mechanical pool estimate ~+1.0-1.3 seats per 4 years.

SEC-F17.claim: Haredi turnout is high and nearly flat. 2022 rebounded to the 2019-20 level after a 2021 dip; it was not a surge. Reuses atlas D2-F12 (corrected) and D2-F22.
SEC-F17.quant: Clearly haredi polling stations: 76% (2013) -> 72.5% (2022) at regular stations, offset by +3.5 points of envelope voting, so about 79% including envelopes in both years (Malach). Project kalpi haredi cluster (304,123 eligible in 2022): 76.4, 76.8, 76.6, 72.8, 75.8% (2019a-2022). Arab and haredi cluster turnout swings correlate 0.88 over four transitions, carried by both sectors' 2021 dip. Local elections 2018->2024: haredi -0.5 points (atlas D2-F23).
SEC-F17.model_link: KALPI_HAREDI_FLOOR turnout 0.74; s.4 haredi 78-82%; KALPI_FAMILY_RHO 0.5 (+0.92 measured); dossier s.34 line 'haredi lists beat their final polls by +1.35 seats ... and 2022's haredi turnout surge is the reason'.

SEC-F18.claim: The mechanism for haredi under-polling is coverage: haredim are less likely to answer polls, especially online ones, and only 69% use the internet regularly. The 2026 filings show the cost: haredi online samples answer at 3.6-26%, and only the Channel 13 consortium adds a phone haredi sample.
SEC-F18.quant: Regular internet use, ages 20+: haredi 69% vs other Jews 94% (IDI 2025 yearbook p.15). IPF: weekly polls of about 500 have MoE over 4 points; super-sampling Arabs or haredim is costly and not typical. CEC filings, Ch13 / Midgam Project: haredi online invitations 5,530 at 3.6% response (28 Jul), 1,031 at 22.3% (30 Sep), 1,899 at 15.4% plus 220 by phone (23 Sep). Tatika raw sample 8% haredi (42/500).

SEC-F19.claim: The 'haredi' under-poll is almost entirely Shas. UTJ's final-poll errors average about zero. Shas draws a large share of its vote from traditional and national-religious non-haredi voters, the low-SES Mizrahi base that online panels also under-reach. The model spreads the family shift across Shas and UTJ by base share.
SEC-F19.quant: Own record, final-poll mean minus result, seats: Shas 2009 -1.11, 2013 -0.55, 2015 +0.38, 2019a -2.67, 2019s -1.00, 2020 -0.25, 2021 -0.43, 2022 -1.43 (mean -0.88); UTJ +0.67, -1.09, +0.50, -1.67, +0.71, +0.38, -0.29, 0.00 (mean -0.10). IDI pooled surveys, 2022 vote (12,322 Jews): haredim 58% UTJ / 28% Shas / 7% RZP-Otzma / 4% Likud; Shas 10% of traditional-religious and 10.5% of national-religious voters. Malach (2019): about a third of Shas voters are not haredi.
SEC-F19.model_link: FAMILY_SHOCK['haredi'] allocated by base weights (w_f / w_f.sum()) to Shas and UTJ alike.

SEC-F20.claim: The -1.35 mean is fragile. It is the post-bloc-swing (e1) mean, carried by two misses (2013 -3.44, Apr 2019 -4.41). The April 2019 miss had a structural cause: Yahad's late withdrawal and a record wasted vote, on top of young first-time voters. Without that cycle, or on the raw scale, or in the last four cycles, the mean is -0.6 to -1.0.
SEC-F20.quant: Haredi family e1 by cycle: 2009 -0.93, 2013 -3.44, 2015 +0.91, 2019a -4.41, 2019s -1.24, 2020 +0.12, 2021 -1.33, 2022 -0.50 (mean -1.35, median -1.09, sd 1.77). Raw e0 mean -0.98; last four cycles e0 -0.58, e1 -0.74; ex-2019a e1 -0.92. Malach (IDI, 17 Apr 2019): haredi seats 13 -> 15; pollsters expected Shas to shrink; UTJ about 250,000 votes vs about 240,000 expected from 4% growth; wasted ballots at least 8% (from 4%); Yahad withdrew at the last minute.

SEC-F21.claim: The election-day machine that produced past haredi over-performance is constrained in 2026. The High Court unanimously barred party polling-station agents from passing who-has-voted data to their parties. The Likud and the ultra-Orthodox parties had relied on that data heavily.
SEC-F21.quant: Ruling of 17 Sep 2026 (Justice Willner, with Stein and Kabub). It overturned the full Committee's decision allowing the practice; per other press reports, not opened, that decision had reversed chairman Sohlberg's August ban. Grounds: no legal authority, and a breach of the Protection of Privacy Law. Per the same unopened reports, the CEC will publish aggregate per-station turnout during the day. No quantitative estimate of the GOTV effect exists.
SEC-F21.model_link: Haredi FAMILY_SHOCK mean (election-day beat); s.4 note on machine-party GOTV.

SEC-F22.claim: 2026 polls already contain haredi leakage and a new haredi list. In Channel 13's dedicated haredi sample, Shas plus UTJ hold about 73% of decided respondents, against 86% of haredi voters in 2022. The Haredi Public takes 7.8% and Otzma 8.3%. If the small list fades late, as Yahad did in 2019, the gain goes to Shas and UTJ beyond the polls.
SEC-F22.quant: CEC filing 4182 (29-30 Sep 2026, haredi online sample n=230): UTJ 47.8, Shas 17.0, Otzma 8.3, The Haredi Public 7.8, Likud 4.3, undecided 6.5, won't vote 4.3. 16 Sep (n=263): UTJ 41.8, Shas 19.4, The Haredi Public 7.2. IDI 2022 haredi vote: 58 UTJ / 28 Shas / 7 RZP-Otzma / 4 Likud (SEC-F19). The model's 15 Oct draws: The Haredi Public mean 0.06 seats.
SEC-F22.model_link: Haredi family shock; small-list desertion; withdrawn-list rule.

SEC-F23.claim: Druze turnout has fallen for 25 years, and Druze votes go overwhelmingly to Zionist lists. Druze are effectively absent from national poll samples (Tatika: 2 of 500). Reuses atlas D2-F11 (corrected; the unverified '2021-22 average 48.7%' is dropped).
SEC-F23.quant: Druze turnout: 1996 76.8, 1999 78.9, 2003 64.2, 2006 64.9, Sep 2019 53.2 (Shanan & Eilat); 2015 57.7, Apr 2019 60.1, Sep 2019 54.5 (Brake). About 90% of Druze-town votes went to Zionist parties in 2022 (Bayan 28). Druze are about 1.5-1.6% of the population (CBS, reported via secondary tables; not opened).
SEC-F23.model_link: Druze are outside the Arab family and the KALPI_ARAB_CAP cluster; they sit in the general Jewish/Zionist residual.

SEC-F24.claim: Russian-speaking (FSU) voters turn out less and are said to be harder to poll, but the FSU party's final-poll record shows no systematic bias. No FSU family term is warranted. Reuses atlas D2-F13 and D2-F27.
SEC-F24.quant: YB final-poll e0: mean -0.06, sd 1.62 (7 standalone cycles); D-60 sd 1.71 (s.7).
SEC-F24.model_link: LOYAL_SD yisrael_beytenu 2.2; absence of an FSU family shock.

SEC-F25.claim: The Arab capacity ceiling is loose. Its formula implicitly assumes every Arab-town voter backs an Arab list and uses a 0.78 concentration. Measured values (at most 94% in-sector Arab-list share; concentration 0.81-0.85) and 2020's record, scaled to the 72% maximum turnout, put the physical bound near 14.8-15.4% of the vote, not 16.3%. Turnout must be compared on one basis: envelopes add about 3 points to Arab and 7.5-10 points to Jewish and settlement turnout (atlas D2-F04).
SEC-F25.quant: Production (mixture_draws, 15 Oct): P(Arab>=19) 9.75%, >=20 6.06%, p95 20. Cap clip rate now 2.9% (haredi floor 0.06%); at cap 0.150, 7.9%. Arab family final-poll sd: e0 1.17, e1 1.45.
SEC-F25.model_link: KALPI_ARAB_CAP 0.163 (839k x 72% / 0.78); ARAB_TURNOUT max 0.72; KALPI_HAREDI_FLOOR 0.066 (Shas+UTJ get only 28% of their votes from the haredi cluster, so the floor is a judgement, not a physical bound).

COA-F01.claim: Martin & Stevenson's conditional logit over every potential cabinet estimates large effects for a pre-electoral pact (+2.72) and a public refusal to govern together (-4.10), alongside incumbency (+1.89) and being the largest party (+1.40) (Table 1, M&S Model 7 as reprinted by Glasgow, Golder & Golder 2012). The paper reports the coefficients; it does not rank the predictors.
COA-F01.quant: 220 formation opportunities, 33,256 potential governments, 14 democracies including Israel, mid-1940s to mid-1980s. Model 7 coefficients (as replicated exactly by Glasgow, Golder & Golder 2012, Table 1, p.258): pre-electoral pact +2.72 (SE 0.62), anti-pact -4.10 (1.04), incumbent coalition +1.89 (0.20), largest party +1.40 (0.27), minimal winning +0.55 (0.26), number of parties -0.31 (0.14), minority where investiture required -0.91 (0.34), anti-system party -19.13 (3.71). Log-likelihood -558.74. Sample description: Glasgow, Golder & Golder 2012, p.256. The 2001 original was not opened; all figures come from that exact replication.
COA-F01.model_link: Formation-tree architecture: the bloc-first ordering of gates, the pledge gates (centre_defects, raam_joins, ZIONIST_ONLY) and the incumbency assumption built into NB_CORE.

COA-F02.claim: Public refusals bind in the comparative record. In the Martin & Stevenson sample only 1 of the 220 cabinets that formed contained parties that had publicly refused to govern together. Anti-pact and anti-system values almost perfectly predict that a cabinet will not form, so their coefficients are poorly identified. Debus (2009) confirms that pre-electoral commitments, both pacts and rejections, significantly shape formation after controlling for endogeneity (atlas D10-F08, verified). Israel 2020-21 is an outlier: both governments formed in the 2019-21 sequence broke public refusals (Gantz's 2020 entry under Netanyahu; Bennett's 2021 government with Lapid and Ra'am), and both came only after three or four elections.
COA-F02.quant: Anti-pact cabinets that formed: 1 of 220. Cabinets with an anti-system party: 6 of 220. Potential cabinets with a pre-electoral pact: 30 of 33,256, of which 7 formed (Glasgow, Golder & Golder 2012, p.256). Israel: both governments formed in the 2019-21 sequence (2020, 2021) broke a public refusal. At the sequence's first election (April 2019) no one broke a pledge and no government formed.
COA-F02.model_link: centre_defects 0.12 (pledge-break), raam_joins 0.40 (every Jewish change list's 'Zionist government' framing acts as a soft anti-pact), res_right 0.12 and ZIONIST_ONLY. Dossier s.3 already argues that pledge-break is endogenous to the number of elections.

COA-F03.claim: The incumbency advantage in government formation is conditional. Coalitions are more likely to form when their parties have recently governed together, but the incumbent's advantage disappears completely when partners became mired in public conflict or lost seats. A cabinet that collapsed through internal conflict is one-tenth as likely to re-form immediately as one that did not. Seat gains raise every potential coalition's odds, and incumbents' odds about twice as much.
COA-F03.quant: 256 formation opportunities and 65,320 potential coalitions in 17 West European countries (p.509). Outgoing coalitions immediately re-formed about 35% of the time in the 2001 sample (p.503). A conflict-collapsed cabinet is 1/10 as likely to re-form and 1/4 as likely as an alternative coalition (p.515). A 1% average seat gain raises a non-incumbent coalition's odds by about 10%, and the effect for incumbents is about twice that (p.516).
COA-F03.model_link: NB_CORE counts Shas and UTJ as unconditional members of a Netanyahu coalition. Yet UTJ quit Netanyahu's government in July 2025 over the draft-exemption law and Shas's ministers resigned (atlas D10-F28, corrected). That is the 'public conflict' condition under which the incumbency advantage disappears. The 2026 haredi mood to recommend no one (atlas D10-F29) points the same way.

COA-F04.claim: Even the best statistical models of formation predict the exact cabinet only about one time in three in Western Europe. Most of that predictive power comes from the status-quo (incumbent) indicator. The authors argue for combining large-n prediction with case study of the deviant cases.
COA-F04.quant: 'We cannot predict more than about one-third of the Western European governments' (abstract). Martin & Stevenson (2010, p.504) report Bäck & Dumont's predictive efficiency, the share of predicted cabinets that are correct, as 12% without the status-quo indicator and 32% with it.
COA-F04.model_link: Formation outcome intervals (p05-p95) and the BEHAVIOR_NEFF concentrations. The model predicts 9 coarse outcome classes rather than exact cabinets, which is easier, but the literature's ceiling argues against tight formation intervals.

COA-F05.claim: Conditional-logit formation models violate independence of irrelevant alternatives. A mixed logit with random coefficients fits better and shows that key effects vary sharply across formation opportunities. For example, incumbency is an advantage in about 63% of formations and a disadvantage in 37%. The best-fitting model's log-likelihood gives the field's benchmark for scoring formation forecasts.
COA-F05.quant: CL LL -558.74 (220 opportunities; mean -2.54 per formation in-sample). MXL Model 1 LL -532.99 (LR 51.50); MXL Model 2 LL -533.75 (LR 49.98), where incumbent mean 1.47, SD 4.50, 62.8% / 37.2%. Uniform baseline: at least -5.02 (exact value needs each opportunity's choice-set size).
COA-F05.model_link: Hierarchical Beta/Dirichlet parameter draws (dossier s.13). These are the scenario-tree analogue of random coefficients, and the literature supports carrying behavioural heterogeneity rather than fixed gates. Also validate_formation.py's choice of score.

COA-F06.claim: A poll-driven coalition-formation forecast has a peer-reviewed analogue. Kayser, Orlowski & Rehmert combine monthly polls with an empirical formation model chosen by out-of-sample testing to estimate each party's probability of entering government. Held out of sample, the model picks the cabinet that actually formed in about 48% of formation opportunities, against at most 45% for the competitor specifications.
COA-F06.quant: Formation data: 454 opportunities, 116,484 potential cabinets, 31 democracies (130 single-party majorities excluded from the benchmark). Non-majority sample 324 = 262 training + 62 test. Out-of-sample 30/62 = 48% correct vs at most 45% for competitors. Party-level AUC 0.89. CIPs computed for 21 democracies. Israel in neither.
COA-F06.model_link: The whole pipeline: seat draws, then a formation model, then outcome and PM probabilities. A party-level 'inclusion probability' (P(Shas in government), P(Ra'am in government)) is a natural extra output and is easier to validate than coalition classes.

COA-F07.claim: The multiparty poll-forecasting literature reports probabilities of coalition seat majorities, not of which government forms. Stoetzer et al.'s dynamic Bayesian model (polls plus fundamentals) gives the probability of a plurality and of majorities for given coalitions, and stops there. Formation has no likelihood in that framework.
COA-F07.quant: Two ex ante forecasts of 2017 elections. The model outperforms fundamentals-only models on accuracy and on calibration of uncertainty (abstract).
COA-F07.model_link: The site's split between arithmetic (P(NB>=61), change alone, with Ra'am) and politics (the formation tree). The government_formation.py docstring ('this layer cannot be estimated from data ... scenario analysis') matches the field's practice.

COA-F08.claim: The logarithmic score is strictly proper for categorical forecasts, so the formation harness's choice of score is sound. The harness itself has three weaknesses. It grades a parameter set that is not the shipped one. Three of its eight cycles are scored as certainties. It floors probabilities at 1e-3, so the score is not strictly logarithmic. Its -0.93 vs -0.92 comparison therefore cannot discriminate between trees.
COA-F08.quant: Gneiting & Raftery (2007): proper scoring rules, including the logarithmic score for categorical variables (abstract, Savage representation). Harness (src/validate_formation.py; data/processed/formation_validation.csv): BEHAVIOR there has haredi_defect 0.30, raam_joins 0.55, raam_supports 0.40, jl_supports 0.25, likud_sans_bibi 0.15. The shipped tree has shas 0.10, utj 0.15, raam_joins 0.40, raam_supports 0.60, jl_supports 0.45, likud_sans_bibi 0.18. 2009, 2013 and 2022 get P(realized)=1.0 (log score 0), so the informative n is 5. On those 5 the with-defection tree averages -1.48, against -1.95 for uniform over 7 (desk computation from the CSV).
COA-F08.model_link: validate_formation.py and dossier s.19. The site's sentences 'log score -0.93 vs -0.92' and 'average log-loss -0.92 ... highest probability in five of eight cycles' rest on the stale parameter set.

COA-F09.claim: Exchange-traded markets give an external benchmark for the formation layer, and on 15 Oct 2026 they price a repeat election far below the model. Kalshi's 'Prime Minister of Israel after the 2026 election?' contracts resolve to 'No one' if new elections are called before a government forms, which is the same definition as the model's repeat outcome. Its candidate prices leave little room for that outcome. Polymarket's larger market resolves to the next PM sworn in following the 2026 election. That appears to include one sworn in after a repeat election, since it resolves 'Other' only if no PM is sworn in by 31 Dec 2027, so its prices are not directly comparable to the model's.
COA-F09.quant: Kalshi (15 Oct re-pull): mids Eisenkot 0.455, Netanyahu 0.265, Bennett 0.13, Liberman 0.045; sum bids 0.85, asks 1.13, mids 0.99; implied P(no one) about 0.01 (mid), range 0 to 0.15; no explicit 'No one' strike. Likud-alternative mids about 0.04 (Kalshi), 0.006 (Polymarket).
COA-F09.model_link: Repeat-election residual (outcome 7, 0.453 [0.35-0.54]) and the 'rotation / Likud successor' PM row (0.061; markets price Likud alternatives at about 0.01-0.02 in total).

COA-F10.claim: Prediction markets typically produce fairly accurate forecasts that beat most moderately sophisticated benchmarks, and well-designed contracts can reveal probabilities. Market design matters, and thin markets and contract wording limit what prices mean. This makes a liquid, same-definition market a legitimate benchmark for the formation layer, not a target to fit.
COA-F10.quant: Review across prediction contexts (abstract). No coalition-specific accuracy figures. Coalition-formation markets have no peer-reviewed track record that this desk could locate.
COA-F10.model_link: How to use COA-F09: as a pre-registered external benchmark scored with the same log score on resolution, not as an input.

COA-F11.claim: Failed formation is rare in the Israeli record. Of 25 Knesset elections from 1949 to 2022, 23 produced a government; the only two that did not were April and September 2019. Since 1996 the count is 10 of 12. In the parliamentary era since 2003 it is 8 of 10. Formation takes about seven weeks and has lengthened. Every government since 2009 took 49 days or more from election to start date, and 2020-22 took 58-82 days.
COA-F11.quant: ParlGov, first non-caretaker cabinet: n=23 formed of 25; median 51 days, mean 53.8 (51.5 / 54.3 only if 1949 is dropped); max 100 (1955). Since 1996: median 52.5 (2003 = 34 in ParlGov, 31 by the 28 Feb 2003 formation date).
COA-F11.model_link: P(repeat election) = 0.453 (p05-p95 0.35-0.54), the largest single outcome in the 15 Oct build. Also the site's formation calendar.

COA-F12.claim: Delays in forming a government come from uncertainty about which cabinets are acceptable. Bargaining complexity (more parties, more polarisation) lengthens formation only when that uncertainty is present. Bäck et al. (2024; atlas D10-F09, verified) add that pre-electoral blocs short of a majority delay formation and can cause breakdown. Both describe the 2026 configuration: two blocs, each short of 61.
COA-F12.quant: 16 West European countries, 1944-1998 (abstract). Bäck et al.: 17 countries 1945-2019, plus the Swedish 2018-19 case.
COA-F12.model_link: Supports a higher-than-historical repeat risk and a long formation window for 2026. It explains delay, not failure, so it does not license a 61% conditional failure rate (see COA-F11 and the challenges).

COA-F13.claim: Basic Law: The Government sets the sequence that the tree collapses into one step. After consultations the President tasks an MK within 7 days, choosing by recommendations and list size; neither binds him. That MK has 28 days, extendable by 14. A second MK may then get 28 days. After that, a 21-day window lets 61 MKs name a candidate in writing, who gets 14 days. Failure means deemed dissolution, with an election within about 90 days (atlas D10-F16, verified). The first mandate need not go to the largest list: Netanyahu got it in 2009 with 65 recommendations to Livni's 28, although Kadima had won 28 seats to Likud's 27 (atlas D10-F17, corrected). Recommendation counts were 55-54 in Sept 2019 and 61 for Gantz in March 2020 (atlas D10-F18, corrected).
COA-F13.quant: s.7: 7 days. s.8: 28+14 days. s.9: second MK, 28 days. s.10: 21 days, then 14 days. s.11: dissolution. 2026 calendar (atlas D10-F16): results about 4 Nov, mandate about 11 Nov, first mandate ends 9 Dec or 23 Dec with extension, second ends about 23 Jan 2027, s.10 window ends about 13 Feb; a repeat election falls between April and May 2027.
COA-F13.model_link: Outcome 7 (repeat) is the end of a three-stage process. The tree has no 'who is tasked first' stage: PM_ALLOC is drawn within outcome classes, so formateur advantage and the President's discretion do not enter. Glasgow, Golder & Golder (2011) find that presidents can influence PM choice.

COA-F14.claim: Investiture rules decide whether minority governments are a live option. A requirement to hold an investiture vote does not by itself reduce minority cabinets; only an absolute-majority decision rule does. Israel's investiture needs only a simple majority of those voting, held after the government is formed (Akirav 2022; Basic Law s.13(d), atlas D10-F21). The Bennett-Lapid government was approved 60-59-1.
COA-F14.quant: 26 European countries since 1946 or democratisation: absolute-majority investiture rules make minority governments considerably less likely, while other investiture features do not (abstract). Israel: approval by a simple majority; Bennett-Lapid 60-59 with one Ra'am abstention (13 June 2021; atlas D10-F21). Akirav (2022, Journal of Legislative Studies 30(1):1-24, doi:10.1080/13572334.2021.2024397) classifies Israel's rule as a simple-majority, ex-post vote.
COA-F14.model_link: Outcome 5 (centre minority backed by the Joint List) and its arithmetic minority_ce > present/2 with abstainers removed. That is legally correct for Israel's plurality rule.

COA-F15.claim: Minority governments are a normal outcome in parliamentary democracies. They are not a sign of crisis: they form when opposition parties can influence policy and when governing carries an electoral cost (Strøm 1990; Strøm 1984 puts them at about 35% of postwar governments in 15 democracies, atlas D10-F11). With written support agreements they last as long as majority governments (atlas D10-F12). Israel has done this: Rabin's government lost its majority in Sept 1993 and survived about two years on Hadash and Arab Democratic Party votes from outside (atlas D10-F23). Peres's new government of 22 Nov 1995 was formed on the same Labor-Meretz-Yi'ud coalition, below 61 seats.
COA-F15.quant: Peres II (22 Nov 1995): Labor-Meretz-Yi'ud, 58 seats (Wikipedia) or 59 at 1992 election sizes (ParlGov); Hadash + ADP (5) supported from outside.
COA-F15.model_link: Outcome 5 and jl_supports 0.45, raam_supports 0.60, liberman_minority_ok 0.25. Challenges the site's sentence that 'no Israeli minority government has been sworn in from day one'. That holds for post-election formations but not for the mid-term Peres government of Nov 1995.

COA-F16.claim: Israel has signed three premiership-rotation agreements, and their record is mixed. Peres-Shamir (1984) was honoured on the two-year date. Netanyahu-Gantz (2020) was never executed: the government collapsed over the budget in Dec 2020, before the Nov 2021 rotation date. Bennett-Lapid (2021) transferred the premiership early, on 1 July 2022, through the statutory trigger added in 2020-21. The Basic Law now makes rotation legally enforceable, with dissolution and budget-failure triggers (atlas D10-F19, verified; D10-F24; D10-F26).
COA-F16.quant: Rotations agreed: 3. The premiership passed in 2 of them (1986 on schedule; 2022 early, by law) and never passed in 1 (2020). ToI (18 Nov 2020): Netanyahu 'is to serve as prime minister until November 17, 2021, when Gantz will succeed him', and 'if the government falls due to failure to pass the state budget, Netanyahu retains the premiership'. The budget-failure dissolution came in Dec 2020 (IDI 2021 election page, atlas D10-F25). Amendment No. 10 later added budget failure as an early-rotation trigger (atlas D10-F19).
COA-F16.model_link: PM_ALLOC: the 'rotation / Likud successor' column and the Together-vs-Yashar flip rule. The model's PM is the first PM sworn in, which the record supports, because second-half rotations are often not reached.

COA-F17.claim: The largest party usually supplies the prime minister, but not always. Across 28 European countries the largest party took the premiership in 72.8% (West) and 77.5% (East) of PM selection opportunities, and the largest-party bonus varies sharply across cases. Israel since 1996 matches: the largest list's leader became PM in 7 of 10 governments formed. The exceptions were 1996 (direct election), 2009 (Kadima first, Netanyahu PM) and 2021 (Bennett with 7 seats). Formateurs also gain a bonus over their seat weight in portfolio share (Ansolabehere et al. 2005; atlas D10-F10).
COA-F17.quant: 369 PM selection opportunities, 2,412 potential PM parties (p.944). Largest party PM: 72.8% West, 77.5% East (p.945). In Western Europe the largest party is advantaged about 67% of the time and disadvantaged about 33% (random-coefficient SD 4.73 around a mean of 2.11, p.945). Israel 1996-2022 from ParlGov seats and cabinets: 7/10; 6/8 since 2003.
COA-F17.model_link: PM_ALLOC change rows: Eisenkot, leader of the largest change list, gets 0.64-0.85, flipping to Bennett when Together outweighs Yashar. These shares match the comparative rate.

COA-F18.claim: UTJ and its components historically refused full ministerial posts on principle, with exceptions since 2015. Since the 1990s their only non-Likud-led government was Barak's in 1999, which they left in September 1999 over Sabbath work. Shas has been far more mobile. It sat in the 1984 unity government (Peres PM for the first two years), joined Rabin in 1992, Barak in 1999 and Olmert in 2006 (atlas D10-F28, corrected), and stayed out in 2003, 2013-15 and 2021. When a non-Likud premier was viable, Shas joined 3 times in 4 (1992, 1999, 2006 yes; 2021 no). UTJ joined once in 4 (1999).
COA-F18.quant: Shas, non-Likud premier viable: joined 1984 (Peres unity), 1992, 1999, 2006; declined 1990 (Peres), Oct 2008 (Livni), Feb 2009 (recommended Netanyahu), 2021. That is 4 of 8, or 3 of 6 excluding unity and the direct-election 1999; 0 of 3 since 2008. UTJ/components: joined 1999 only (about 1 of 6 on the same cases).
COA-F18.model_link: shas_defects 0.10 (NEFF 30) and utj_defects 0.15 (NEFF 16), with COND anchors 'Shas 1992, Shas+UTJ 1999'. The anchors omit Shas-Olmert 2006, which fits the pivot pattern, and the 2021 refusal.

COA-F19.claim: Since 2019 the haredi parties have tied themselves to Netanyahu's bloc in writing. After the September 2019 election Likud, Shas, UTJ and Yamina agreed to negotiate as one 55-MK bloc headed by Netanyahu. On 16 Feb 2020 Shas, UTJ and Yamina signed a letter declaring 'We'll only support Netanyahu'. In 2021 both haredi parties stayed in opposition rather than join the change government. Nissim Leon's chapter title, 'From Preference to Default' (Purdue UP 2024, pp.203-226, doi:10.2307/jj.22177844.13), states the thesis that haredi alignment with the right hardened over time; its abstract was not available, so treat it as unverified. The 2026 counter-signal is the reported mood to recommend no one and sit out for about a year (atlas D10-F29, verified).
COA-F19.quant: Bloc of 55 MKs (Likud 32, Shas 9, UTJ 7, Yamina 7; Sept 2019). Loyalty letter: 16 Feb 2020, signed by Shas, UTJ and Yamina and initiated by Deri. In the bloc era (2019-22) the haredi parties joined 0 non-Likud governments.
COA-F19.model_link: This is the evidence for the low haredi defection priors (and why COA-F18's pre-2019 rate should be down-weighted, not adopted). It also bears on a missing branch: haredi abstention or later entry rather than defection at formation (UTJ_ABSTAINS is coded but set to 0).

COA-F20.claim: Liberman's vetoes are real but have bent once under pressure. In 2019 his refusal to compromise on the haredi draft law caused Israel's first-ever failure to form a government (atlas D10-F25, corrected). He has not sat with the haredi parties since. In March 2020, facing a fourth election that he called 'the worst of all possible scenarios', he softened his earlier refusal to work with the Joint List while talking with Gantz about a minority government. That government was blocked instead by two of Gantz's own MKs, Hauser and Yoaz Hendel. In 2021 he sat in a coalition with Ra'am inside.
COA-F20.quant: March 2020: the JL-backed minority government lacked 61 once three centre-left MKs refused: Levy-Abekasis (10 Mar), Hendel and Hauser.
COA-F20.model_link: liberman_haredi_ok 0.20 (supported by 0 of 5) and liberman_minority_ok 0.25 (one softening in two tests). The binding 2020 veto came from Hendel, whose 2026 'Zionist government only' rule the model now encodes (ZIONIST_ONLY), so the minority branch faces two independent vetoes.

COA-F21.claim: Ra'am's 2021 entry was a first, and it came at the end of a deadlock sequence. INSS described the Bennett-Lapid coalition as the first time an Arab party joined an Israeli coalition (atlas D10-F26: first independent Arab party in decades). INSS warned the precedent would be reversible if the government proved short-lived. In the same 2021 deadlock Netanyahu also courted Ra'am: Deri offered Abbas 'exclusivity' on Arab-sector issues at the Interior Ministry, and the talks failed over Smotrich's opposition and the May 2021 Gaza operation. After four elections, both blocs treated Ra'am as available.
COA-F21.quant: Ra'am 4 seats in 2021; coalition 61 including Ra'am; investiture 60-59-1 (atlas D10-F26). The government lasted about one year (dissolved 30 June 2022). Netanyahu-Ra'am contacts: ToI, 11 Aug 2022, citing Channel 12.
COA-F21.model_link: raam_joins 0.40 and raam_supports 0.60. The only Israeli precedent for an Arab party inside a coalition followed three repeat elections, so it says little about the first election of a new sequence.

COA-F22.claim: Mainstream parties shut a party out when they have no pressing need to cooperate with it and can credibly say its ideology is beyond accepted norms. Size and ideology are the main determinants. When mainstream parties do take in formerly excluded partners, office, policy and votes all drive the choice, enabled by electoral shifts and convergence of positions (de Lange 2012, Political Studies 60(4):899-918, doi:10.1111/j.1467-9248.2012.00947.x).
COA-F22.quant: Logistic regression on 31 Western European anti-immigration parties (abstract and repository record). Full text not opened.
COA-F22.model_link: raam_joins is conditioned only on arithmetic: it fires when the centre is short and Ra'am's seats close the gap. The literature says the decisive condition is 'pressing need', which in Israel rose with each repeat election in 2019-21. A first-election raam_joins should sit below the 2021-derived level.

COA-F23.claim: The 2026 signals on Ra'am are 'not at the outset'. On 16 Sept 2026 Channel 12 reported Bedouin council heads saying Eisenkot had promised to bring Ra'am into his coalition. Yashar denied it ('These things were never said, not even by implication'). Yashar restated three tests for partners: accepting the Declaration of Independence, recognising Israel as Jewish and democratic, and serving all citizens. It added that partners must recognise Hamas as a terrorist organisation Israel must destroy, a test aimed at Abbas's July interview. Bennett and Lapid launched Together in April 2026 pledging a 'Zionist government', and Hendel rules out Arab-dependent coalitions (atlas D10-F30).
COA-F23.quant: Yashar tests: Declaration of Independence values; Israel as Jewish and democratic; 'service for all'; Hamas recognised as a terrorist organisation. Bennett (JNS 27 Apr 2026): a government 'composed solely of Zionist parties, ruling out reliance on Arab parties'.
COA-F23.model_link: raam_joins 0.40 versus raam_supports 0.60. The code comment 'every Jewish party still pledges no Arab party INSIDE at the outset' is now sourced as a soft anti-pact (no explicit 'never Ra'am' quote), which supports joins < supports.

COA-F24.claim: No Israeli party has ever dropped its sitting leader after an election in order to form a government. All three unity governments kept both leaders: Peres-Shamir in 1984 and Shamir-Peres in 1988 (atlas D10-F24, verified), and Netanyahu-Gantz in 2020. The 1988 case was not a deadlock: the right-religious bloc held 65 seats and Shamir chose unity anyway. The closest comparative precedent is Spain in October 2016. After two inconclusive elections, PSOE's leader Pedro Sánchez was pushed out, and the party's federal committee voted 139-96 to abstain so that Rajoy could govern, explicitly to avoid a third election in under a year.
COA-F24.quant: Israeli precedents for 'party drops leader to form': 0 in 25 Knessets (desk reading of the IDI election pages and atlas D10-F24/F25). Spain: second election June 2016; leader out 1 Oct 2016; abstention vote 23 Oct 2016 (139-96, 2 abstentions); Rajoy invested 29 Oct.
COA-F24.model_link: likud_sans_bibi 0.18 (NEFF 20) and its COND anchor 'unity resolved the deep deadlocks (1984/1988)' in dossier s.19, which overstates the case: 1988 was not a deadlock and neither unity dropped a leader. The comparative precedent fired only after a second failed election.

COA-F25.claim: Laver & Schofield set the agenda the tree implements. Coalition outcomes depend on who the actors are and what motivates them (office, policy), on which coalitions form, how long they last, how payoffs are shared, and on constitutional, behavioural and historical constraints on bargaining. Their framework treats formation as constrained bargaining among motivated actors rather than seat arithmetic. That is the case for an explicit behavioural tree over a pure 'who reaches 61' rule.
COA-F25.quant: Book: 328 pages, 27 tables, with case studies of European coalitions (publisher description). The original OUP 1990 edition was reissued by the University of Michigan Press in 1998.
COA-F25.model_link: Design of government_formation.py: actor-level behavioural gates (motivations, vetoes, institutional signatories) layered on seat arithmetic.

COA-F26.claim: The outgoing government stays in office until a new government is constituted. Under Basic Law: The Government (2001), s.30, when a new Knesset has been elected the outgoing government continues to carry out its functions until the new government is constituted, and a prime minister who has resigned continues pending the new government. So if no government forms and a repeat election is held, the sitting prime minister heads the outgoing government through it.
COA-F26.quant: s.30(a)-(b): 'the outgoing Government shall continue to carry out its functions until the new Government is constituted'; s.30(c): a PM who has resigned continues pending the new Government; s.30(d): it may appoint a Knesset Member as a minister in place of one who ceased to serve.
COA-F26.model_link: formation outputs: 'Netanyahu still prime minister after formation' = Netanyahu forms the government + repeat election

DYN-F01.claim: Across 45 countries, polls become steadily more informative about the final vote as election day approaches. Early in the cycle they predict parliamentary elections better than presidential ones, and by election day the two are indistinguishable. Differences between PR and plurality systems are small. Whether Israel is in the published dataset could not be confirmed.
DYN-F01.quant: More than 26,000 vote-intention polls, 45 countries, 312 electoral cycles, 1942-2013. Per the authors' AJPS summary, early-cycle error is about 4 points (RMSE) in parliamentary elections against about 6 in presidential ones; PR-vs-plurality differences are 'very small' and only intermittently significant. Israel is not in the 41-country Table 1 of the 2013 working-paper version (p. 28, see DYN-F02). The published country list is in the Dataverse codebook (doi:10.7910/DVN/28856), which was not opened.
DYN-F01.model_link: Forward random-walk calendar (campaign_vol_weight): backs a forward variance that shrinks as the election approaches, rather than uniform sqrt(weeks).

DYN-F02.claim: In the full-text working-paper version, the share of vote variance explained by polls reaches 0.9 four to five months out but keeps rising, 'particularly during the last month'. Systems with more than four effective parties are the least predictable: polls barely improve between about 150 and 50 days out, then become more informative over the final ~50 days. In fragmented systems a real share of crystallisation happens late.
DYN-F02.quant: More than 23,500 polls, 41 countries, 245 cycles (p. 1). R-squared about 0.9 at 4-5 months, still rising in the final month (p. 15). Where the effective number of parties exceeds 4, R-squared is about 0.15 lower a year out than where it is below 3, flat from about 150 days out, then rising over the final 50 days (p. 18). Israel is not among the 41 countries in Table 1 (p. 28). Israel's effective number of parties is well above 4 in every cycle since 2009.
DYN-F02.model_link: campaign_vol_weight(<=35 d) = 0.64. Informs the shape: in a fragmented system the final weeks still carry real, lasting movement, so the calm-zone weight should not be cut further. The blackout days have to be carried somewhere, and they are, by the election-day shocks.

DYN-F03.claim: In US presidential races 1952-2008, preferences are most volatile in the convention season and most stable in the final weeks, and debates rarely produce dramatic change. Final-week polls track the vote closely (r = 0.98), yet leads shrink between the final week's polls and the vote, partly because some respondents who say they will vote do not.
DYN-F03.quant: Leader shrinkage in Israel (D-14..D-4, complete polls): 2009 Likud 27.9 -> 27 (-0.9); 2015 Zionist Union 24.2 -> 24 (-0.2); 2019a Blue and White 30.5 -> 35 (+4.5).
DYN-F03.model_link: Supports the calm final-weeks calendar. The 'lead shrinkage' finding (a mean reversion that a zero-drift random walk lacks) does not transfer to Israel: the leading list in 2009, 2015 and April 2019 did not shrink (see DYN-F09). No change recommended.

DYN-F04.claim: Polls taken in the final three weeks have total error about twice what their reported margins imply. A large part of it is an election-level bias that all polls of the same race share, so averaging more polls does not remove it.
DYN-F04.quant: 4,221 polls, 608 US state-level races 1998-2014, all in the final three weeks. RMSE about 3.5 percentage points, about twice the reported margin of error. Average absolute election-level bias about 2 points.
DYN-F04.model_link: Election-day shock stack (bloc swing sd 3.36, family shocks), fitted on final-poll errors rather than on sampling noise. Backs treating the last four days (D-4 to E-day) as a shared industry error plus real movement, not as sampling noise that more polls would average out.

DYN-F05.claim: In Israel the final weeks' poll movement is mostly real signal. In 6 of 8 cycles the per-list error of the final-window average is lower than that of the average 3-6 weeks out. The exceptions are 2009 and April 2019, and 2015 barely improved: the three cycles whose decisive move came after the last published poll.
DYN-F05.quant: Per-list mean absolute error, seats: 3-6 weeks out 1.89, final window 1.53 (mean over 8 cycles). Improvement by cycle: 2009 -0.15, 2013 +0.51, 2015 +0.03, 2019a -0.40, 2019s +0.65, 2020 +0.80, 2021 +1.29, 2022 +0.20.
DYN-F05.model_link: Forward random walk: late poll moves are persistent, not bounces to mean-revert, which supports a zero-drift walk. It also shows that what the walk cannot see (the blackout) is where the large misses live, which the election-day shocks must carry.

DYN-F06.claim: Two-wave surveys covering 62 elections in 10 countries show that a sizeable share of voters settle their choice in the final two months. Their shifts track which issues they rank as important and their beliefs about candidates, while their policy preferences stay stable. TV debates and exogenous disasters had no detectable effect on vote choice.
DYN-F06.quant: 17-29% of voters decide in the final two months. About 253,000 observations, 56 TV debates, null debate effect.
DYN-F06.model_link: Certainty layer soft-support churn (defection d ~ Beta(mean 0.25, sd 0.12) among soft supporters). A quarter-ish movable share two months out is the right order. By D-12 the still-movable share should be smaller, which the layer gets only if the CERTAINTY inputs are refreshed.

DYN-F07.claim: In 2015 more than a quarter of voters decided at the last minute, and they broke right. The legal ban on polls in the closing days meant the published polls missed a late Likud surge, which commentators saw continuing into election day.
DYN-F07.quant: Post-election survey of 1,133 voters, commissioned by New Majority, an anti-Netanyahu group: 15% decided on election day and 13% in the final days (28%). Late deciders voted 62% right-wing, 21% centrist, 16% left-wing. Final published polls had Likud at 20-23; the result was 30.
DYN-F07.model_link: Certainty-layer undecided lean and the gevalt layers. The one Israeli measurement of where late deciders went points right, opposite to the 2026 lean the layer applies. The blackout window carries real movement.

DYN-F08.claim: Israeli law bans publishing any new poll from the end of the Friday before polling day until the polls close. In 2026 that runs from the end of Friday 23 October to 22:00 on Tuesday 27 October. In every cycle 2009-2022 the last published pre-election fieldwork ended 3-4 days before election day, so about four days of opinion movement are never observed by a published poll.
DYN-F08.quant: Section 16(h) of the Elections (Propaganda Methods) Law 5719-1959. Last pre-election fieldwork by cycle (poll archive): 2009, 2013, 2015, 2019a, 2019s, 2021, 2022 D-4; 2020 D-3. Comparative: WAPOR/ESOMAR 2017 (133 countries), 32% have no blackout; the median among those with one is 4.5 days.
DYN-F08.model_link: Projection horizon. The final refit uses the 22-23 Oct polls. The four blackout days are carried by election-day shocks fitted on final-poll-vs-result errors (dossier s.5), which is the right vehicle (see challenge 4 for a small horizon mismatch).

DYN-F09.claim: Every Israeli list that beat its final polls by 4 seats or more since 2009 was either in a close race for first place or a new centrist list. Three of the five trailed for first place, and three of the five were not Likud. Every shortfall of 4 seats or more was a smaller list in the surging leader's own bloc, often at the threshold. When Likud surged, its own satellites paid. The bloc-level moves were small: the right-wing bloc beat its final polls by 0.7 seats in 2015 and fell 1.7 short in April 2019. In other years the right-wing bloc beat its final polls when Likud led.
DYN-F09.quant: D-14..D-4, complete polls (seat sum 108-122), seats beat (result - polls): 2009 Kadima 23.3 -> 28 (+4.7), Likud 27.9 -> 27 (-0.9; Kadima trailed by 4.6); 2013 Yesh Atid +8.4, Likud-Beytenu -3.0; 2015 Likud +8.0, Jewish Home -3.8, Yachad -4.1; 2019a Likud +6.9, Blue and White +4.5, New Right -6.0, Zehut -5.9, Labor -3.5; 2019s Likud -0.1, Blue and White +1.1; 2020 Likud 33.6 -> 36 (+2.4) trailing Blue and White 33.8 -> 33 (-0.8) by 0.2; 2021 Blue and White +3.9 (+4.1 on the desk's all-rows method), Meretz +2.5; 2022 Meretz -4.6. NB bloc (Likud + right satellites + haredim, +Kulanu 2015/2019a): 2015 +0.8, 2019a -1.9 (+0.4 with Yisrael Beytenu), 2019s -3.0, 2020 +1.4, 2021 +3.0 (about 0 with Yamina), 2022 +3.7.
DYN-F09.model_link: Gevalt coupling (GEVALT_SD 2.0, NB-only) and the trailing-Likud conditional (TRAIL mu 5.0, sd 4.9, half strength). Supports the zero-sum Likud-satellite structure. Challenges the Likud-only scope: the trailing beat appeared on the other side too (Kadima 2009).

DYN-F10.claim: In 2015 both Likud and the Zionist Union gained compared with 2013, but almost all their gains came from parties in their own bloc. Identity campaigns targeted voters inside each bloc and kept bloc boundaries clear. Kulanu was the pivotal exception.
DYN-F10.quant: Qualitative: nearly all big-party gains were within-bloc.
DYN-F10.model_link: Gevalt coupling and the bloc-swing/residual split. Backs a zero-sum, within-bloc transfer for the late surge rather than a bloc-level shift.

DYN-F11.claim: A three-wave Israeli panel during the 2019-2020 repeat elections finds that voters switch parties to influence who becomes formateur, and abandon parties they expect to be left out of the coalition. The effect is stronger when the race between potential formateurs is seen as close.
DYN-F11.quant: Three online panel waves, 2019-2020. The abstract reports no effect sizes. Companion evidence: Bargsted & Kedar (AJPS 2009, atlas D1-F24) find coalition-directed desertion significant for Likud and Labor only, not for sectoral parties.
DYN-F11.model_link: Trailing-Likud conditional. The mechanism (formateur optimisation when the race for first place is close) is not Likud-specific. It applies to whichever bloc's leader trails. 2026 has a close Yashar-Likud race for first.

DYN-F12.claim: The closest Israeli precedent for a security-credentialed centrist list drawing soft Likud voters is Kadima in 2006, and its soft intention faded heavily before polling day. The voters it lost did not mostly return to Likud: most went to the Pensioners party.
DYN-F12.quant: In December 2005, 53% of 2003 Likud voters who stated an intention said Kadima; 31% actually voted Kadima. Kadima's vote was 42% ex-Likud. Individual switching reached 63% in 2006 (record). The verifier adds that most ex-Likud votes Kadima lost went to the Pensioners party.
DYN-F12.model_link: Certainty layer for Yashar (declared CERTAINTY 0.65) and the churn destination split (change bloc 72.5% within / 10.3% cross / 17.2% abstain). Supports material fade of a new list's soft support and a destination that is mostly not 'home'.

DYN-F13.claim: Not all undecided Israeli voters are alike. Sophisticated undecideds (high interest and knowledge) consume more campaign news, decide on policy, are more often choosing between parties inside one bloc ('internal floaters'), and are more likely to vote than less sophisticated undecideds.
DYN-F13.quant: Two panel surveys before and after the April 2019 election, N = 1,427 and N = 912. The abstract gives no turnout percentages.
DYN-F13.model_link: U_TURNOUT = 0.65 haircut on the undecided pool (the code cites 'GIQ'). The paper backs the direction (less sophisticated undecideds under-vote) but not the 0.65 magnitude, which is the model's own derivation. It also implies the informed part of the pool mostly moves within a bloc.

DYN-F14.claim: The latest 2026 measurement puts 11% of voters undecided, but only 5.4% of those (about 0.6% of all respondents) are torn between the blocs; the rest are choosing within a bloc. Self-reported bloc switching favours the change bloc (5% of Netanyahu-bloc intenders vs 2% the other way). In July, N12 described about 10% undecided, the same share as four years earlier.
DYN-F14.quant: N12 Ulpan Shishi, published 9 Oct 2026 (pollster and n not stated): 11% undecided; 5.4% of the undecided between blocs or unsure of bloc; 5% NB->change vs 2% change->NB, 70% unchanged. N12/mako 28 Jul 2026 (atlas D5-F07): about 10% undecided, 8-10 seats; 1.3% of the undecided potential cross-bloc movers.
DYN-F14.model_link: Certainty-layer undecided transfer (U_LEANED_FRAC 0.71, lean 0.775 anti). The cross-bloc undecided pool is tiny, so any bloc-level transfer from the undecided must come from the bloc composition of within-bloc undecideds being allocated proportionally across all lists. That composition has not been published since July.

DYN-F15.claim: In July 2026 a JPPI survey found 53% of voters completely sure of their vote, 29% fairly sure and 14% undecided. Certainty was lowest in the centre: 71% of left-identifiers were completely sure, 58% of the right and 44% of the centre.
DYN-F15.quant: JPPI Israeli Society Index, July 2026 (TheMadad panel; Afkar for the Arab sample). Completely sure 53%, fairly sure 29%, undecided 14%, not voting 4%. Completely sure by ideology: left 71%, right 58%, centre 44%. n and margin not given in the report.
DYN-F15.model_link: CERTAINTY tiers and the soft-centre asymmetry (Together 0.47, Yashar 0.65 declared). Supports softer certainty for centre lists than for the right.

DYN-F16.claim: The official inquiry into the 2015 UK polling miss found the primary cause was unrepresentative samples, not late swing or 'shy' voters. It recommended pollsters review how they allocate 'don't know' and refusing respondents, calling existing procedures ad hoc and lacking a coherent theoretical rationale. The peer-reviewed version (JRSS-A 2018) confirms unrepresentative sampling as the primary cause of an average 7-point error on the Conservative lead.
DYN-F16.quant: Average error on the Conservative-Labour lead about 7 points. Late swing contributed at most about 1 point to the lead error, per the report's executive summary as quoted in search results (the PDF itself returned 403). Don't-know allocation was named in Recommendation 3.
DYN-F16.model_link: Certainty-layer undecided transfer. A non-proportional allocation is a modelling choice the polling profession itself regards as unsettled, so a single lean measurement should carry little weight. Also informs 'shy' voters: deliberate misreporting was not the cause.

DYN-F17.claim: Proportional allocation of undecided voters, a 'cleaner' ballot question and even allocation produced no significant difference in poll accuracy. Allocating undecideds neither adds to nor detracts from a poll's accuracy.
DYN-F17.quant: 54 polls in 20 states, 2018 US midterms; absolute error, statistical accuracy and predictive accuracy compared; no significant differences.
DYN-F17.model_link: Certainty-layer undecided transfer. Proportional, the model's prior, is a defensible default. A departure needs a lean measurement with a track record, which no Israeli house has.

DYN-F18.claim: Camil Fuchs, a leading Israeli pollster, said in July 2020 that undecided respondents leaned centre-left. When asked a forced bloc choice, undecideds without a party said centre-left, and the blocs drew level at 55-56 seats each. Measurement of this kind preceded, rather than predicted, the following elections: the right-wing bloc beat its final pre-blackout polls in 2021 and 2022 (DYN-F09). This is a precedent, not a test, because the remark came eight months before the 2021 election.
DYN-F18.quant: Right-wing bloc vs final pre-blackout polls (D-14..D-4): 2020 +1.4; 2021 +3.0 to +3.5 for the Netanyahu bloc proper, about 0 including Yamina; 2022 +3.7.
DYN-F18.model_link: Certainty-layer undecided lean (N12 55/16, 30 Jul 2026). The same kind of evidence (undecideds leaning anti-Netanyahu) has no validated record of predicting final-poll error in Israel, and the record runs the other way.

DYN-F19.claim: The 2026 pool has been resolving without the drift the July lean implies. Within the same pollster, from late July to early October the polled Netanyahu bloc rose about 1 seat while the undecided pool shrank from about 12% to the 9.65% the model now measures. Likud itself fell about 1.7, so its satellites gained. If the leaned undecideds had resolved 77.5/22.5 against Netanyahu into houses that drop undecideds, the gap should have moved about 1 seat the other way.
DYN-F19.quant: Within-pollster NB change Jul->Oct: mean +1.0 seats (median +0.75, se 0.63, 7 firms). Expected under the model's pooled lean about -0.17 per side; under the raw July lean with the 0.65 turnout haircut about -0.34; the desk's -0.5 omits the haircut.
DYN-F19.model_link: Certainty-layer undecided transfer. This is a falsification check the layer can run every build, and so far it does not support the anti-ward drift.

DYN-F20.claim: The worst miss in Quebec polling history (2018) was mainly a 'polling miss' rather than a methodological 'poll failure': a post-election poll attributes most of the gap to last-minute shifts and to how non-disclosers voted, with regional variation.
DYN-F20.quant: Qualitative in the abstract: changing voter behaviour explains 'most of the discrepancy'. Non-disclosers voted differently from disclosers. Israeli counterpart, an anecdote only: Midgam's Mina Tzemach blamed the April 2019 Channel 12 exit-poll miss (Likud 33 vs 35, Blue and White 37 vs 35) on Likud voters lying (Times of Israel, 11 Apr 2019). That is a claim, not a finding.
DYN-F20.model_link: Election-day shocks and the Likud anchor. In multiparty races, late shifts and non-disclosers can produce one-sided final-poll errors. This backs fitting E-day shocks on the final-poll record, including its right-ward Likud mean (anchor -2.30), rather than assuming the undecided break mirrors stated leans.

DYN-F21.claim: Terror attacks raise right-bloc support, and more so near an election. A local attack within three months of an election adds about 1.35 points to the right bloc's share of the two-bloc vote in that locality. Fatalities also move places beyond the attacked locality, more strongly closer to the election. At the national level, Berrebi & Klor (2006) find relative support for the right rises after periods of high terrorism and falls after calm.
DYN-F21.quant: +1.35 points right-bloc share per local attack within 3 months (APSR 2008). National poll evidence 1990-2003 (Berrebi & Klor, Journal of Conflict Resolution 50(6):899-925, 2006, doi 10.1177/0022002706293673). Rocket-range localities: +2 to +6 points right (Getmansky & Zeitzoff, APSR 2014; atlas D1-F30), about +4 points per 1,000 damage claims (Elster, JEBO 2019).
DYN-F21.model_link: EVENT_RISK on the bloc swing. Backs some election-proximate event risk, larger the closer the event is to the vote, and with a typical right-ward sign for terror.

DYN-F22.claim: War can cut support for incumbents. The unexpected 1973 war and its casualties reduced support for incumbent parties and leaders and raised opposition support, despite military victory. Wars over a country's core territory can be politically costly.
DYN-F22.quant: Oct 7 2023, within-pollster (archive): 0-35 d one firm only (Lazar): Likud -8.8, NB -11.2; 35-70 d (3 firms): Likud -8.9, NB -8.7; 70-120 d (5 firms): Likud -8.0, NB -5.6.
DYN-F22.model_link: EVENT_RISK. The sign of a security shock is not fixed (right-ward for terror and rallies, anti-incumbent for failures), which backs the dossier's choice of variance inflation with no mean shift.

DYN-F23.claim: Israeli public reactions to violent escalation are immediate but brief. Long-run change in Jewish conflict attitudes follows non-violent signals (failed negotiations, leadership changes), not violence levels. For the prime minister specifically, the 2014 Gaza war produced a rally behind Netanyahu, but after October 7 trust in him tracked blame rooted in prior judicial-reform views and did not rally.
DYN-F23.quant: Monthly Israeli data 2001-2020 (conflict attitudes, not vote intention). Feinstein & Ben-David (POQ 90(3), 2026): waves Mar-Apr 2023 n=1,552, Oct 2023 n=1,012, Dec 2023 n=969; the 2014 doubling of Netanyahu approval to about two-thirds is reported in that paper.
DYN-F23.model_link: EVENT_RISK horizon. Event effects decay, so the event-risk premium belongs to the share of the remaining calendar in which an event can occur and still matter on election day. It is not a constant.

DYN-F24.claim: In this cycle's own poll archive, security events moved the Netanyahu bloc little and briefly. The one exception is the October 7 failure. War rallies lifted Likud 1-3 seats for up to five weeks, mostly at its satellites' expense, and were gone within 5-10 weeks. Ordinary two-week bloc movement has sd 1.2 seats.
DYN-F24.quant: EVENT_RISK 1.2 adds about 2.9 seats of bloc sd (t5 scale 3.36 -> sd 4.33). Hazard-scaled multiplier with sigma 4.33: 1.02-1.14 at D-58, 1.005-1.036 at D-12. Events listed: 8 in about 36 months (about 0.0073/day). Oct 7 0-35 d figures from 1 pollster. Persistence at 70-120 d: Lebanon Sep 2024 Likud +2.7; Gaza ceasefire Oct 2025 NB +2.4.
DYN-F24.model_link: EVENT_RISK = 1.2 adds about 2.2 seats of bloc sd (sqrt(4.03^2 - 3.36^2)) to every draw. On this record the hazard-weighted event variance over 12 days is 0.17-1.41 seats^2 (excluding or including an Oct-7-class shock), equivalent to a multiplier of 1.01-1.06. The same arithmetic at D-56, when 1.2 was set (30 Aug), gives 1.03-1.22. The forward tau, fitted on this war-era archive, already carries some event movement.

EVAL-F01.claim: A scoring rule is strictly proper when issuing one's true predictive distribution uniquely maximises the expected score, so proper scores reward careful, honest forecasts. For a central (1 - alpha) prediction interval [l, u] the proper score is the interval score S = (u - l) + (2/alpha)(l - x)1{x < l} + (2/alpha)(x - u)1{x > u}: a narrow interval is rewarded and every unit by which the outcome misses is charged 2/alpha. In the paper's case study three 95% interval forecasts all had close to nominal coverage, the sharpest was not the best, and the interval score (not coverage) ranked them.
EVAL-F01.quant: Eq. (43), Section 6.2, p. 370; case study Section 6.3 and Table 2, p. 371 (100,000 one-step forecasts of a bilinear process). Model: validate_bayes.py and validate_horizon.py compute exactly this score at alpha = 0.10, i.e. (hi - lo) + 20 x miss in seats. Restated baseline (CLR latent, ballot-fidelity windows, 3 seeds, dossier s.46): eve 9.280, D-7 9.430, D-21 9.622 seats per list.
EVAL-F01.model_link: Harness metric interval_score (validate_bayes.py, validate_horizon.py). Also bears on the shipping rule, which uses coverage, an improper criterion, as a pass/fail constraint (see EVAL-F03).

EVAL-F02.claim: Brier proposed scoring probability forecasts of a binary event by the mean squared difference between the stated probability and the 0/1 outcome (0 is perfect, lower is better). It is the standard verification score for yes/no events and is what the model uses for threshold passage and for the bloc-majority probability. Because it is an average over events, pooling many near-certain events (lists sure to pass) shrinks it without saying anything about the hard cases, so it needs a stratified or skill-score companion.
EVAL-F02.quant: Monthly Weather Review 78(1):1-3. Brier defined P = (1/n) sum_i sum_j (f_ij - E_ij)^2 over all r classes (0 perfect, 2 worst); for a binary event twice the one-component (p - o)^2 score now called the Brier score (per secondary sources; original scan not opened).
EVAL-F02.model_link: threshold_brier and bloc Brier in the harness; the site's 'Threshold Brier score, election eve' tile.

EVAL-F03.claim: Probabilistic forecasts should maximise sharpness subject to calibration. Calibration (statistical consistency between forecasts and outcomes) comes first, and among calibrated forecasts the sharper one is better. A hump-shaped PIT or rank histogram signals overdispersed forecasts whose prediction intervals are too wide on average, and sharpness is read from the average width of the central 50% and 90% intervals. Over-coverage is therefore a calibration failure, not a safety margin.
EVAL-F03.quant: Summary p. 243; PIT shapes p. 253; Section 3.3 (sharpness via 50% and 90% interval widths) p. 255. Model: 90% coverage .981 (eve), .990 (D-7) and .990 (D-21) on the s.46 yardstick. In the 13 Oct horizon file 7 of 8 cycles cover 100% at both D-7 and D-21, with 1-2 misses in about 91 list-cycles where 9 are expected (binomial P(<=1 miss | 10%) = 0.0008, ignoring within-cycle dependence). s.46 width grid: every leave-one-cycle-out fold picks a residual width of 0.6 or 0.7. At 0.6 the scores are MAE 1.609, Brier .043, interval score 8.773 and coverage .960, all better than the shipped 0.9 (1.626 / .047 / 9.302 / .981).
EVAL-F03.model_link: Per-list residual shock width (RESID_SCALE 0.9), the shock stack and the forward random walk. Also the site caption 'above it, the intervals are conservative' and the claim that 0.9 'wins every leave-one-cycle-out fold'.

EVAL-F04.claim: When forecasts are issued as central intervals, the weighted interval score (WIS) combines the absolute error of the median with interval scores at K levels, using weights w0 = 1/2 and wk = alpha_k/2. It is proper for any non-negative weights, approximates the CRPS as K grows, generalises absolute error, and decomposes into a dispersion term plus over- and under-prediction penalties. The COVID-19 Forecast Hub scores the median plus K = 11 intervals (nominal 98%, 95%, 90%, ..., 10%). Inverse-U PIT histograms mark overdispersed forecasts.
EVAL-F04.quant: Eqs. (1)-(3) and the Forecast Hub specification (arXiv 2005.12881, p. 4); PIT discussion p. 9. Model: the harness scores one level only (90%, alpha = 0.10). The 50% and 80% ranges, where most list outcomes are decided, are never graded.
EVAL-F04.model_link: interval_score in the harness (single 90% level); the published seat ranges.

EVAL-F05.claim: For count (ordered discrete) outcomes the ordinary probability integral transform is not uniform even when the model is correct, so calibration checks designed for continuous variables mislead. The authors give a nonrandomised PIT histogram, marginal calibration diagrams and proper scores (such as the predictive deviance) for counts, usable with any Bayesian or classical model.
EVAL-F05.quant: Biometrics 65(4):1254-1261. Model: seats are integers, and harness coverage counts a hit when the actual count is >= the 5th and <= the 95th percentile of integer seat draws. A calibrated discrete forecast therefore covers at least 90%, usually more, and a list whose range starts at 0 is covered whenever it fails. Part of the 98-99% coverage is this artefact. The rest is real overdispersion, which the s.46 interval-score gains from narrower widths show.
EVAL-F05.model_link: coverage_90 in validate_bayes.py and validate_horizon.py; the site's coverage-by-horizon chart.

EVAL-F06.claim: Point forecasts are meaningful only when the scoring function is fixed in advance, or the forecaster is told which functional (mean, median, quantile) to report, and the scoring function must be consistent for that functional. Mismatches can produce grossly misguided comparisons. Quantiles, including the median, are elicited by generalised piecewise-linear scores such as absolute error; means are elicited by Bregman scores such as squared error.
EVAL-F06.quant: JASA 106(494):746-762 (abstract). Model: s.28 reports the median beating the mean by ~0.09 seats per list 'in every configuration'. Under absolute-error scoring that is the expected result, not independent evidence. The published central count is a third object (the median share vector, renormalised and D'Hondt-allocated). MAE per list in the 13 Oct horizon harness, published central vs per-list seat median: D-7 1.696 vs 1.628, D-21 1.887 vs 1.831, D-56 2.558 vs 2.511. The shipping rule grades the per-list median, not what the site prints.
EVAL-F06.model_link: The central seat count (median share vector) and the shipping rule's median-MAE criterion (harness_compare.py).

EVAL-F07.claim: Few proper scores exist for multivariate forecasts. The energy score is the usual choice for sample (ensemble) forecasts but has limited power to detect a wrongly specified correlation between components. Variogram-based scores, built from pairwise differences between components, were distinctly more sensitive to errors in the correlation structure in simulations and in a five-site wind case study. They are proper but not strictly proper, so the authors use them alongside other scores.
EVAL-F07.quant: Monthly Weather Review 143(4):1321-1334 (abstract; Sec 2 p.1324; Sec 3d p.1327; Sec 4 p.1330; Sec 5 pp.1332-1333).
EVAL-F07.model_link: Correlated bloc swing, gevalt coupling, trailing-Likud sourcing, family shocks: the layers that produce P(NB>=61).

EVAL-F08.claim: Election forecasts are hard to evaluate for calibration. 95% intervals cannot be checked even on 10 back-tested elections, and sub-unit results are correlated, so pooling them adds less than it seems. Implausible conditional predictions are a practical check. They can come from adding independent long-tailed errors on top of a correlated model, which lowers the effective correlation, and the authors found bugs in their own model by inspecting such predictions. Because calibration is so hard to verify, forecasters face incentives toward underconfidence, which hedges against the reputational cost of a miss. FiveThirtyEight's political 20% events happened 14% of the time and its 80% events 88%.
EVAL-F08.quant: Judgment and Decision Making 15(5):863-880. Sec 2.1 pp.866-867; Sec 2.3 pp.867-868; Sec 3.1-3.2 pp.872-873; p.873: per the Boice & Wezerek (2019) calibration plot, 538's political '20% really means 14%, and their 80% really means 88%', flagged as based on few elections.
EVAL-F08.model_link: Validation scope (8 cycles), the bloc headline, residual vs bloc-swing structure, and the site's framing of over-wide intervals as 'conservative'.
