EVAL-F09.claim: Calibration means that events given X% happen about X% of the time across many forecasts; FiveThirtyEight checks it over thousands of its own forecasts since 2008. Calibration alone is not skill: giving every NCAA team a 1-in-68 chance is calibrated and useless, so FiveThirtyEight also reports Brier skill scores. Its election forecasts have historically leaned underconfident.
EVAL-F09.quant: FiveThirtyEight, 4 Apr 2019: of 5,589 events forecast at 70%, 71% happened; of 55,853 near 5%, 4% happened; candidates given 75% won 83% (generally not statistically significant).
EVAL-F09.model_link: The site's track-record section (calibration, then sharpness) and the threshold reliability chart.

EVAL-F10.claim: In survey experiments, people shown a win probability were more confident about who was ahead and who would win than people shown a vote-share projection with a margin of error, and participants in every format misjudged the chance of winning. In an incentivised voting game, higher win probabilities (but not larger vote-share leads) reduced paying to vote. Small vote-share leads map to large win probabilities, which readers misread.
EVAL-F10.quant: Journal of Politics 82(4):1530-1544 (Oct 2020). Study 1 n = 4,151 (hypothetical Senate race, three formats); study 2 n = 1,171 (economic game). Design and n from the Pew Research summary of 6 Feb 2018; citation from Crossref.
EVAL-F10.model_link: Site headline probabilities: P(NB>=61), bloc and PM probabilities.

EVAL-F11.claim: In a repeated decision experiment on transit predictions, quantile dotplots (50 discrete outcomes) and CDF plots led to better and more consistent decisions than textual interval displays. Dotplots reached about 97% of the optimal expected payoff, 5 points above the no-uncertainty control. Text displays were sensitive to which interval level was communicated.
EVAL-F11.quant: Proc. ACM CHI 2018; dotplot gain over control +5 percentage points of optimal payoff (95% CI 2 to 8); within-subject SD 4 points lower than control.
EVAL-F11.model_link: Site display of seat ranges and the bloc distribution.

EVAL-F12.claim: Leave-one-out cross-validation estimates pointwise out-of-sample predictive accuracy. Computed per held-out unit, it also gives approximate standard errors for each model's predictive error and for the difference between two models, which should accompany any comparison.
EVAL-F12.quant: Statistics and Computing 27(5):1413-1432 (abstract). Model: leave-one-cycle-out is the grouped (leave-one-group-out) form with 8 groups. harness_compare.py prints pooled deltas and win/tie/loss counts but no standard error of the paired difference across folds.
EVAL-F12.model_link: The leave-one-cycle-out harness design and harness_compare.py reporting.

EVAL-F13.claim: When data have temporal, spatial or hierarchical structure, random cross-validation seriously underestimates predictive error. Folds should be blocked on the dependence structure, even when fitted residuals look uncorrelated, though blocking can force extrapolation and so overstate error.
EVAL-F13.quant: Ecography 40(8):913-929, abstract p. 913. Model: whole cycles are the right block. But 2019a, 2019s, 2020 and 2021 fell within 23 months with largely the same lists, so those four folds are not independent of each other; s.43 notes that the Arab slope k 'rests on 2019a'.
EVAL-F13.model_link: Fold design of validate_bayes.py and validate_horizon.py.

EVAL-F14.claim: For time series, leave-one-out cross-validation lets future observations inform predictions of the past, so it is over-optimistic as a measure of forecasting skill. Leave-future-out cross-validation respects time order, and Pareto-smoothed importance sampling can approximate it without one refit per step.
EVAL-F14.quant: Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation 90(14):2499-2523 (2020), abstract. Model: when 2015 is graded, the trailing-Likud mean comes from 2019a and 2019s (only 3 trailing years exist; s.36). The Arab a and k, the new-straddler drift and the industry shocks also borrow later elections. The site says each election 'was forecast again ... using only the polls published before each date', which is true of the polls but not of these parameters.
EVAL-F14.model_link: LOO parameterisation in decompose(), trailing_likud_params, new_straddler_params, arab_turnout_params and the firm scorecards; the site's track-record sentence.

EVAL-F15.claim: When cross-validation is used both to tune a model and to report its error, the reported error is substantially optimistic. On null datasets with no real signal, tuned classifiers showed low CV error while their independent-test performance was at chance. Nested CV (tuning inside an inner loop, error estimated in an outer loop) was nearly unbiased, so every selection step must be repeated inside each fold.
EVAL-F15.quant: BMC Bioinformatics 7:91 (2006), abstract: the tuned shrunken-centroid classifier's CV error was below 30% on 18.5% of null training sets. Model: arab_regB was chosen among nine graded arms (s.43c), trail_sat among five variants (s.41) and the residual width from a 6-point grid, each graded on the folds that chose it. The exception is the width grid's printed 'LOO width choices', which is already a nested selection.
EVAL-F15.model_link: Arm selection in validate_bayes.ABLATIONS; the restated baselines; the width grid.

EVAL-F16.claim: Even without deliberate fishing, analysis choices that would have gone differently had the data come out differently create a 'garden of forking paths': many implicit comparisons, whose winner looks better than it is.
EVAL-F16.model_link: The harness ablation list, restated baselines and the round-by-round candidate process.

EVAL-F17.claim: Pre-registration, which fixes the questions and the analysis plan before the outcomes are seen, separates testing predictions from generating postdictions, a line that hindsight bias otherwise blurs. Partial strategies keep it usable when the data already exist.
EVAL-F17.quant: PNAS 115(11):2600-2606 (abstract). Model: the dossier already pre-registers some choices. trail_sat was the PRIMARY arm with the others marked sensitivity (s.41). The combine plan's G1/G2 gates were applied as written and dropped the ramp (s.46). The undecided half-weight was fixed in advance (s.11). The 2026 election is the one truly unseen outcome.
EVAL-F17.model_link: Candidate grading protocol; the final 2026 build.

EVAL-F18.claim: The Diebold-Mariano test was meant for comparing forecasts, not models. The belief that pseudo-out-of-sample analysis is the best insurance against in-sample overfitting in model comparison is largely false, and in finite samples it widens the scope for data mining (for example over the choice of sample split). Its legitimate use is learning about comparative historical predictive performance.
EVAL-F18.quant: JBES 33(1):1-9 (2015); NBER WP 18391 (2012), abstract and the discussion of split-point mining (WP PDF p. 13). Model: the eight-cycle harness is a pseudo-out-of-sample exercise used as the model-selection device, so its numbers for the shipped configuration are selection-affected.
EVAL-F18.model_link: Use of the harness as both selector and scorer; the site's statement of backtest accuracy.

EVAL-F19.claim: Election forecasts built on a few historical elections usually overstate their certainty, because they ignore uncertainty in coefficient estimates and in specification choices; with limited data, many models are empirically justifiable. Once those sources were accounted for, 95% intervals widened to about +/-10 points of vote share at the state level and +/-7 nationally.
EVAL-F19.quant: new-straddler drift re-measured at -0.42 pp on CEC vote shares (n 11, s.46.1; -0.33 pp was s.41 on nine lists)
EVAL-F19.model_link: Arab turnout term (ARAB_TURNOUT_K, ARAB_TURNOUT_INTERCEPT), the trailing-Likud layer and the new-straddler layer.

EVAL-F20.claim: Rank-normalised split-R-hat should be below 1.01 (the old 1.1 rule passes chains that have not converged), with at least four chains. Rank-normalised bulk ESS should exceed 400 for stable Monte Carlo standard errors. When intervals or quantiles are reported, the tail-ESS (at the 5% and 95% quantiles) must also be adequate, and the MCSE should be checked for every quantity of interest.
EVAL-F20.quant: Bayesian Analysis 16(2):667-718, doi 10.1214/20-BA1221; arXiv Sec. 2 pp. 4-5. Site renders 'r-hat <= 1.02, bulk ESS >= 261' (from fit_summary.json; 332 is only the template fallback).
EVAL-F20.model_link: bayes_model.REFIT_GATES and diagnostics(); harness fits (600/600 draws at eve, 400/400 at the horizons); headline precision.

EVAL-F21.claim: The No-U-Turn Sampler removes Hamiltonian Monte Carlo's hand-tuned path length by extending trajectories until they begin to double back, and adapts the step size by dual averaging. It performs at least as efficiently as well-tuned HMC without costly tuning runs.
EVAL-F21.quant: JMLR 15(47):1593-1623 (abstract). Model: PyMC NUTS with 4 chains, target_accept 0.92 and 800/800 production draws (bayes_model.fit).
EVAL-F21.model_link: Posterior sampler for the state-space poll model.

EVAL-F22.claim: Divergent transitions flag regions of high curvature that the numerical integrator cannot resolve. Any divergence should prompt suspicion of the estimates, and divergences that persist as the step size shrinks indicate bias that calls for reparameterisation (for example non-centred forms) or stronger priors. These diagnostics are necessary but not sufficient for valid inference.
EVAL-F22.quant: arXiv 1701.02434 v2: Section 6.2, p. 45; Section 6.3 (limitations of diagnostics). Model: 0 divergences in production fits and in 23 of 24 CLR-fidelity harness windows; 2020 D-7 has 1 (s.46).
EVAL-F22.model_link: Divergence monitoring in diagnostics() and in the harness (divergences column).

EVAL-F23.claim: Model fit is assessed by posterior predictive checks with realised discrepancies T(y, theta): functions of the data and the parameters, chosen to probe the aspects of the model that matter, and computed as a by-product of the posterior simulation.
EVAL-F23.quant: Statistica Sinica 6(4):733-807 (abstract and issue record). Model: the production PPC is one in-sample number, the share of poll observations inside a 95% band built from the 2.5th percentile of draw-wise lower bounds and the 97.5th of upper bounds (bayes_model.posterior_predictive_check); docs/bayesian_workflow.md reports ~98% inside. No discrepancy targets the forecast's use, such as final-fortnight house-effect residuals, within-firm residual autocorrelation or the spread of final-week polls.

EVAL-F24.claim: A Bayesian workflow validates computation with fake-data simulation (refitting data simulated from known parameters) and, more thoroughly, with simulation-based calibration, which needs many refits. It also warns that picking one model from many similar ones by minimising cross-validation error overfits and gives suboptimal choices, and recommends projection-predictive selection or stacking instead.
EVAL-F24.quant: arXiv 2011.01808 (2020): Sections 4.1, 4.2, 8.2 and 8.3. Model: there is one fake-data replicate, from 29 Aug, with 6 lists x 20 weeks (90% of true trajectories inside 90% CIs; tau recovery r 0.88; house effects 0.94; docs/bayesian_workflow.md s.3), on the earlier ALR model. The production model has since gained the CLR latent, structural breaks, CEC raw-share filings and an undecided-noise term, and now has 21 lists x 45 weekly bins.
EVAL-F24.model_link: workflow_bayes.py (recovery stage); candidate selection among arms.

EVAL-F25.claim: Pareto-smoothed importance sampling stabilises importance weights, and its fitted Pareto shape k-hat is a reliability diagnostic. Estimates are trustworthy when k-hat < min(1 - 1/log10(S), 0.7). Above 0.7 they should not be trusted, and the affected leave-one-out folds should be refit exactly (PSIS-LOO+) or replaced by K-fold CV.
EVAL-F25.model_link: Model ladder (PSIS-LOO M0-M3) in workflow_bayes.py; any future poll-level LOO-PIT.

EVT-F01.claim: On deadline day (Friday 16 Oct, D-11) the surplus-vote map is exactly the model's five pairs. Signed: Likud with RZP-Zehut, Together with Yisrael Beytenu, Yashar with the Democrats, Shas with UTJ, and Ra'am with the Joint List. Three lists near the threshold have no pact. Otzma has none: Ben-Gvir refused Amcha on 13 Oct, and Likud had already signed with RZP-Zehut. Blue and White says it will sign with no list in either bloc. The Reservists have none, because Hendel would not sign with Winter.

Model, computed by this desk from mixture_draws.parquet (8,000 draws, 16 Oct): P(NB6>=61) 0.136, P(change4>=61) 0.078, either 0.214; P(NB6>change4) 0.528, tie 0.033; means NB 53.1, change 51.8.
EVT-F23.model_link: Bloc headline (mixture_blocs.csv: p_nb_61 0.139, p_anti_61 0.078). An external check that passes; no change.

EVT-F24.claim: On which list finishes first, the markets disagree with each other, and the model sides with the minority. Polymarket's deep 'winner' market (most seats, $886k) moved from Likud 0.545 (4 Oct) to Yashar 0.665 (16 Oct). Kalshi's seat ladders imply Likud's median about 24 against Yashar's about 22, closer to the model's P(Likud > Yashar) 0.601. Every network poll of 11-15 Oct had Yashar ahead.
EVT-F24.quant: Polls with fieldwork 11-15 Oct (polls.csv): Yashar ahead in 7 of 8; Filber/Channel 14 (12 Oct) had Likud 29, Yashar 20.
EVT-F24.model_link: TRAIL (trailing-Likud beat, mu 5.0 seats) and the anchors decide P(Likud largest). The deepest market contradicts the model's 0.63, the thinner seat ladders agree. TRAIL is the model's deliberate historical bet (2015, 2019a), so this is a flag, not a fix.

EVT-F25.claim: On thresholds, markets and every October poll put RZP-Zehut, Otzma and Ra'am far safer than the model does, and the Reservists far likelier to pass. Seat-win prices: RZP-Zehut 0.875-0.905 vs model 0.555; Otzma 0.975-0.987 vs 0.783; Ra'am 0.945-0.96 vs 0.764; Reservists 0.45-0.46 vs 0.209. Amcha (0.225-0.245 vs 0.245) and Blue and White (0.047-0.085 vs 0.011) roughly agree. The archive supports the markets on the all-cycle base rate and the model in Likud-trailing cycles.
EVT-F25.quant: Likud-trailing cycles (2015, 2019a), right-bloc lists averaging 4-6.3 seats in the final 3 weeks: 3 of 6 failed excluding haredi lists (Yachad 4.2, New Right 5.9 and Zehut 5.6 failed; Yisrael Beytenu 2015 5.6, URWP 6.3 and Kulanu 4.1 passed), and 3 of 8 with Shas and UTJ 2019a. All three failures were first-time lists. Reservists at 4+ in 8 of 8 polls since 11 Oct.
EVT-F25.model_link: p_pass layer: TRAIL_SAT_SOURCE (Likud's trailing beat taken from Otzma/RZP, capped at 75%), GEVALT_SD 2.0, the Arab turnout term (T 0.58, pass-through 0.247) for Ra'am, and new-straddler desertion (-1.6 pp) for the Reservists. The model is betting on a 2019a-style right-satellite collapse. That bet has a record (3 of 5 in trailing cycles), but neither exchange prices it.

EVT-F26.claim: Election administration figures for 27 Oct. 7,331,981 eligible voters; 12,018 polling stations; about 450m ballots for 38 lists and about 4m outer envelopes. More than 800 military stations, including the first-ever voting by troops across the border, with soldiers' early voting from the evening of 20 Oct. Abroad voting opened 15 Oct at 101 stations in 99 missions (about 4,800 eligible). Evacuees vote by double envelope at designated stations. The poll-publication ban runs from midnight 23/24 Oct to the close of polls, and final results are due 4 Nov.
EVT-F26.quant: Maariv 14 Oct 14:42 (CEC logistics centre; Sohlberg: 'every shipment leaving here is checked thoroughly'): 7,331,981 eligible, 12,018 stations, ~450m ballots, ~12m envelopes, ~4m outer envelopes, emergency 'freeze the count' tables. JNS 14 Oct: 'more than 800 military polling stations'; early voting 'the evening of Oct. 20'. ToI liveblog 15 Oct 7:41 am: abroad voting at 101 stations / 99 missions, about 4,800 eligible. ToI 2 Sept (Livne): evacuees vote by double envelope at designated stations; about half a million double envelopes counted centrally in Jerusalem and broadcast live. Maariv 18 Aug: ban 'from midnight between 23 and 24 October'; official final results 4 Nov 2026.
EVT-F26.model_link: Turnout layer denominators (registered voters 7.33m); kalpi layer (double envelopes, about 0.5m or ~10% of votes, are not in the station panel and are counted last); DYN-F08's blackout dates are confirmed. The final pre-blackout refit should use polls published through Friday 23 Oct.

EVT-F27.claim: Likud and RZP-Zehut say they will send about 2,000 activists to polling stations in Arab communities, citing 'a long series of fraud incidents'. The CEC's director general had earlier said: 'There is no fraud in Israel. If it exists, it is on the margins.' This brings back the 2019 monitoring fight in the final fortnight.
EVT-F27.quant: ToI liveblog 15 Oct 11:40 am: about 2,000 activists; CEC director Dean Livne: 'There is no fraud in Israel. If it exists, it is on the margins.' Model's Arab turnout term: mean T 0.580, pass-through 0.247.
EVT-F27.model_link: Arab turnout term (graded, s.43). A visible monitoring campaign is a possible mobiliser in Arab towns. There is no 2026 measurement and the 2019 effect was not verified by this desk, so do not move T on it.

TRN-F01.claim: The 2026 register is 8% larger than 2022's, with 12,018 polling stations. Election day is a paid national day of rest with free intercity buses and trains, the same arrangement as 2022, so the date itself adds no new turnout effect.
TRN-F01.quant: Eligible voters 7,331,981 (2022: 6,788,804), so +543,177 (+8.0%), the figure the article gives as voters 'added to the register since 2022' (it equals the net change). Polling stations 12,018; accessible 6,208, of which 3,620 special accessible stations (double-envelope capable); 250 hospital stations (hospitals with 50+ beds); 55 prison and detention stations; 102 stations in 100 missions abroad (state employees only). Hours 07:00-22:00 (small communities, hospitals, prisons, nursing homes 08:00-20:00). Day of rest under Basic Law: The Knesset; employees who work are paid 200%. Intercity buses (15 km+) and Israel Railways free from 26 Oct 20:00. Final results by 4 Nov. The CEC chairman's figure is reported elsewhere as 7,336,553 (secondary GitHub citation, not opened); Arutz 7 (14 Oct) gives '7.33 million' and 12,018 stations.
TRN-F01.model_link: National turnout prior (s.4: 70.5 +/- 2.5); electorate size used for vote-per-seat arithmetic and the threshold in votes.

TRN-F02.claim: Against the 2022 baseline, 2026 has more stations of every special type, and double-envelope voting had already grown from 5.5% to 9.6% of ballots between 2015 and 2021. The official CEC-based Arab series differs from the Dayan Center series by up to about 2 points.
TRN-F02.quant: 2026 vs 2022: accessible 6,208 vs 5,116 (+21%); special accessible 3,620 vs 2,939 (+23%); hospital 250 vs 222 (+13%); prison 55 vs 55 (no change); missions 102 at 100 vs 103 at 101 (one fewer). Not 'every special type'.
TRN-F02.model_link: Double-envelope layer and the election-night vs final split (s.4: 600-700k envelopes, 12-13%); ARAB_TURNOUT base (0.538 kalpi vs 0.532 Dayan; the CEC-based series is a third definition).

TRN-F03.claim: Double-envelope ballots lean right and away from the Arab and haredi lists, so more envelope voting moves the final count rightward after election night. Soldiers are the largest group.
TRN-F03.quant: 2021 envelopes: Netanyahu camp (incl. Yamina) 48.76% vs anti 48.56%; IDI expects 'negligible impact' on bloc seats except through the threshold. The lean is by list (RZ +25%; Shas/UTJ up to a third lower; Arab lists under half), not by bloc.
TRN-F03.model_link: s.4 double-envelope lean ('RZ/right lists overperform, haredi and Arab lists 1/3-1/2 under'); election-night engine.

TRN-F04.claim: The IDF is running its largest field vote: at least 850 military polling stations, a quarter of them mobile, including positions in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, with voting from the evening of 20 October. Inference: the soldier envelope pool is likely at least as large as in 2022.
TRN-F04.quant: At least 850 military stations (about a quarter mobile), voting from the evening of 20 Oct to 27 Oct; the source makes no 2022 comparison ('largest' unsupported).
TRN-F04.model_link: Double-envelope layer (night-to-final drift of about +0.5-1 seat right, s.4); threshold straddlers near 3.1-3.5%.

TRN-F05.claim: Special-population voting is small in seat terms. About 14,000 people are still displaced; nursing-home stations reached about 30,000 voters last time. Dedicated stations will serve the evacuated Gaza-border communities.
TRN-F05.quant: CEC at the Knesset committee (23 Jun 2026): about 14,000 people still displaced from their homes (about 0.2% of the register); a dedicated 'election address' was proposed. Nursing homes and sheltered housing last election: stations in 226 institutions, about 37,000 eligible, about 30,000 voted (about 81%). The CEC deputy director opposed permanent cameras in polling stations because they 'could discourage voters'. Per ynet's guide (15 Oct), dedicated stations will serve the communities evacuated from Be'eri, Kfar Aza, Nir Oz and Holit; evacuees may also vote at their original station or an accessible station.
TRN-F05.model_link: None directly; bounds the evacuee effect on turnout as negligible (<0.1 seat).

TRN-F06.claim: Net emigration since 2022 inflates the register's denominator. About 125,000 more Israelis left long-term than returned between January 2022 and August 2024, and those still registered lower measured turnout by about 1.2 points if nothing else changes.
TRN-F06.quant: Net Israeli migration (all ages): -29,700 (2022), -58,600 (2023), -36,900 (Jan-Aug 2024), -125,200 cumulative. Turnout denominator effect about 0.9-2.1 points (adults-only in the desk's window, to all ages through Oct 2026 at the 2024 pace); treat as about -1 to -1.5.
TRN-F06.model_link: National turnout prior (s.4: 70.5 +/- 2.5); s.4 'emigration -1-1.5 centre-left seats'.

TRN-F07.claim: Arab localities have 89 fewer polling stations than in 2022, although their electorate grew about 10%. In 2026 an average Arab-locality station serves 672 voters against 578 in Jewish localities; in 2021 the two were about equal.
TRN-F07.quant: Stat-Net position paper and appendix, from CEC station lists as of 31 May 2026: Arab-locality stations 1,628 (2022) to 1,539 (2026), -89; Jewish-locality stations 7,886 to 8,482, +596. Eligible voters in Arab localities about +96,000 (+10.2%) vs +8.1% in Jewish localities. Voters per station 672 vs 578 (gap about 16%); 2021: about 528 vs 539. 52 of 147 Arab localities (35%) have fewer stations despite more voters (Jewish localities: 3%). Examples: Kafr Bana 15 to 9 stations (6,492 eligible); Ma'ar 31 to 25. Stat-Net: about 250 more Arab-locality stations would close the gap. Unrecognised Negev villages: 30-45 minutes' travel; some tribal assignments up to 65 km. The CEC says the Interior Ministry places stations through the CBS. Inference: 938,401 (2022 Arab and Druze eligible, Bayan 28) x 1.102 gives about 1.03 million Arab-locality eligible voters in 2026, about 14.1% of the register.
TRN-F07.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT['mean_unified'] (0.58): a new 2026 headwind outside the regime table; KALPI_ARAB_CAP denominator (Arab eligible about 1.03m).

TRN-F08.claim: Peer-reviewed natural-experiment evidence: consolidating polling places cut overall turnout by 1.85 points, and in-person turnout by 3.03 points. Israel has no civilian absentee voting to absorb the loss, so the in-person figure is the closer analogue.
TRN-F08.quant: Los Angeles County, 2003 California gubernatorial recall (precinct consolidation): overall turnout -1.85 points, polling-place turnout -3.03, absentee +1.18. Both transport costs and search costs (finding the new place) contributed; Democrats responded more. Transfer to Israel is an analogy, not a measurement: Arab-locality station load rose about 16% relative to Jewish localities (TRN-F07).
TRN-F08.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT mean: size of a possible station-load adjustment.

TRN-F09.claim: Peer-reviewed boundary-discontinuity evidence: one standard deviation more distance to the polling place (0.245 miles) cuts ballots cast by 2-5%. The effect is about three times larger in high-minority areas in lower-salience elections.
TRN-F09.quant: Nine municipalities in Massachusetts and Minnesota, four elections (2012-2016): +1 sd distance gives -2% to -5% of ballots; in non-presidential elections the effect is about 3x in high-minority vs low-minority areas. The paper's counterfactuals remove the distance effect for +1.6 to +4 points turnout. A Knesset election is high-salience (closer to the presidential case, where the minority gap was not significant), so the upper end is unlikely to apply.
TRN-F09.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT mean: station-load adjustment bound (Negev tribal assignments up to 65 km, TRN-F07).

TRN-F10.claim: Likud and Religious Zionism say they will station about 2,000 activists at hundreds of polling stations in Arab communities, on top of the formal observers, citing fraud claims the CEC has rejected. The 2019 precedent cuts both ways. A similar camera operation in April 2019 coincided with a record-low Arab turnout, which its organiser claimed as his doing, though no independent study links the two. Five months later Arab turnout rebounded 10 points.
TRN-F10.quant: 2026 (announced 15 Oct, D-12): nearly 2,000 activists (Haaretz: religious-nationalist activists and yeshiva students); 'hundreds of polling stations' chosen by a 'special mapping' of fraud risk; no official function. CEC director Dean Livne in June: 'There is no fraud in Israel. If it exists, it is on the margins.' 2019 (Times of Israel, Jacob Magid, 8 Aug 2019): about 1,200 activists with hidden body cameras, about 40 coordinators; the organiser posted that 'voter turnout dropped below 50%'. IDI: Arab turnout 49.2% (Apr 2019) vs 63.8% (2015, IDI basis). Police investigated only two stations, neither targeted by Likud. Likud doubled the budget to about NIS 2 million for September 2019, when Arab turnout was 59.2% (Dayan series, SEC-F01). Neither article gives a causal estimate.
TRN-F10.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT spread (0.05): an event that can move Arab turnout either way. No directional intimidation term; the precedent supports a symmetric spread.

TRN-F11.claim: Channel 13's Arab seat numbers assume 60% Arab turnout, according to the head of Stat-Net, which fields its Arab sample. He says 72% would lift the Arab lists from 14 to 16 seats, about 0.17 seats per point at full pass-through. This answers the sector desk's open question on Channel 13's conversion.
TRN-F11.quant: Channel 13 poll published 3 Sep 2026: Joint List 9, Ra'am 5 at a 60% Arab-turnout assumption (Yousef Makladeh, Stat-Net). At 72% with all else equal: Joint List 10, Ra'am 6. If Amcha Yisrael fails the threshold: Joint List 11, Ra'am 6-7. Desk arithmetic for comparison: 1 point of Arab-locality turnout is about 10,300 voters x 0.858 Arab-list share (2022), about 8,900 votes, about 0.22 seats at about 40,000 votes per seat. Through the model's k = 0.247 that is about 0.05 seats per point. Makladeh (Kul al-Arab interview, 28 Apr 2026) also said a four-party list would 'automatically' add about 10 points of turnout.
TRN-F11.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT base and ratio: Channel 13 embeds 0.60, so its Arab seats already sit above a 0.538 base. ARAB_TURNOUT_K (0.247) and the house-effect layer.

TRN-F12.claim: The Afkar institute's director, whose firm fields Arab-sector polls, puts expected Arab turnout at 59-61% after the disqualification fight. He says about 15 Arab seats would need at least 65%.
TRN-F12.quant: 59-61% from Jubran's poll (no n, dates or method); '65% for ~15 seats' is the article's unattributed estimate.

TRN-F13.claim: The parties' own numbers are higher still: the Joint List's internal poll shows 61% two weeks out, and the list and Hadash both target 70%. Activist reports also cut both ways: more willingness to vote overall, but Balad's base was demobilised when its leader withdrew under threat of disqualification.
TRN-F13.quant: Local Call, 12 Oct 2026: Joint List internal poll about two weeks before election day projects 61% Arab turnout; target near 70%; no pollster, n or dates. Field activists (Yafia; Standing Together in the Southern Triangle) report more willingness to vote. Sami Abu Shehadeh's withdrawal 'reduced motivation among some Balad activists'; others say the threat raises motivation. Al-Araby (4 Oct): Hadash secretary-general Amjad Shbeita is 'working toward 70%', which he says would give the Joint List more than 10 seats.
TRN-F13.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT['mean_unified']: party claims; treated as an upper bound, not a signal.

TRN-F14.claim: Channel 13's sector samples (official CEC filings) give stated certainty of voting by sector over the last three waves. The Arab phone sample's 'certain' share is 73-80%, flat within noise. The haredi share depends on mode: 80% by phone, 66-67% online. Haredim report the least certainty, as in past cycles, so stated certainty cannot rank sectors by turnout.
TRN-F14.quant: Drop 'as in past cycles' (no prior series). Haredi cluster turnout 72.8-76.8% (2019a-2022, regular stations), level with the religious-Zionist cluster: 'among the highest', not 'the highest'.
TRN-F14.model_link: Certainty layer; sector_stream; FAMILY_SHOCK['haredi']. Supports s.20 (do not drive the turnout dial from surveys).

TRN-F15.claim: Afkar's survey of young Arabs for the Abraham Initiatives (January 2026, before the lists formed) projects 59% turnout among 18-34s. Stated intention collapses among past abstainers and first-time voters, the groups whose turnout decides the sector.
TRN-F15.quant: Past voters 70% definitely. The other two groups are 43% definitely (16% probably) and 15% definitely (42% probably); the slide's text and legend assign them to past abstainers and first-time voters in opposite ways.
TRN-F15.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT['mean_unified']; youth composition (Points: 118,000 first-time Arab voters, TRN-F19).

TRN-F16.claim: Stat-Net's February 2025 Arab survey for the Abraham Initiatives ran two turnout models on the same data: 53% and 47%. A 6-point spread from modelling choice alone, before the list configuration was known.
TRN-F16.quant: n=750, telephone in Arabic, 10-17 Feb 2025, sample weighted by previous voting patterns, religion and geography. Expected turnout 53% ('Bias Model'); 47% under the 'Motivation Model', which drives all of its demographic breakdowns. Abraham Initiatives summary: 89% support a four-party joint list; 18% name division among Arab parties as the top barrier to voting; 30% name lack of impact.
TRN-F16.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT sd (0.05): method uncertainty inside one firm is as large as the sd.

TRN-F17.claim: The Dayan Center's unity-year forecast for 2015 was close (64.7% expected vs 63.5% actual). With the misses the sector desk recorded, the four KAP forecasts that could be checked have a mean error near zero and a spread of about 11 points: unbiased but very noisy.
TRN-F17.quant: KAP final surveys: +1.2, +15.1, -4.2 (mean +4.0, sd 10.0, n=3). All six readings including early-campaign ones: mean -0.4, sd 11.8.
TRN-F17.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT['mean_unified']: weight of the 2026 survey signal (about 60%) against the 58% prior.

TRN-F18.claim: IDI's May 2026 first-time-voter survey: 87% of young Arabs and 92% of young Jews say they will or think they will vote. Haredim are again the least certain group.
TRN-F18.quant: Ages 18-22, first Knesset vote in 2026; fieldwork May 2026. Jews n=422 online (iPanel), weighted by religiosity; Arabs n=154 online and phone (Afkar); maximum sampling error +/-4.08%. 'Do you intend to vote in the upcoming Knesset elections?': Arabs 62% certain + 25% think so = 87%; Jews 63% + 29% = 92%; total 63% + 28%. Secular Jews are most emphatic (72% certain); the chart reads about 52% certain for haredim. The English summary gives n=576 (443 Jews, 133 Arabs), which differs from the Hebrew PDF.
TRN-F18.model_link: s.4 first-timer cohort (about 8.7% of the electorate); confirms stated intention is uninformative for levels.

TRN-F19.claim: A geo-demographic analysis counts a record 595,000 first-time voters (8.7% of the register): about 118,000 Arab (10.6% of the Arab sector) and about 105,000 haredi (one in six haredi eligible voters). The haredi figure implies about 630,000 haredi eligible voters. The source's total register (6.8m) conflicts with the CEC's 7.33m, so treat its counts as approximate.
TRN-F19.quant: 595,000 first-time voters = 8.1% of the CEC register (8.7% only on Points' 6.8m). Haredi eligible implied 630-656k (IDI yearbook suggests about 0.69m aged 18+); 10% relative dip = 1.0-1.2 seats.
TRN-F19.model_link: Haredi turnout arithmetic (seat value of a haredi turnout drop); KALPI_HAREDI_FLOOR; s.4 first-timer cohort 8.7% (matches).

TRN-F20.claim: IDI's August 2026 Voice Index: only 1.2% of Jews and 8.7% of Arabs volunteer that they do not intend to vote, against actual non-voting of roughly 28% and 47% in 2022. Crime in Arab society is the top vote factor for Arab respondents.
TRN-F20.quant: 2022 non-voting: non-Arab registrants about 27%, Arab-locality about 47%. Survey: a 'don't intend to vote' option on a vote-consideration item (Q7), 1.2% Jews / 8.7% Arabs.
TRN-F20.model_link: Certainty layer and undecided pool; supports not reading turnout levels from surveys.

TRN-F21.claim: Channel 12's analyst reports haredi parties' internal polls showing about a 10% fall in willingness to vote. UTJ's campaign headquarters is paralysed by a rift between the two leading Lithuanian rabbis, and Shas is losing voters over the draft-exemption stance, some of whom are staying home.
TRN-F21.quant: 'Internal polls' of unspecified ownership show 'about 10%' lower willingness to vote (relative or points not stated); no n, dates or wording.
TRN-F21.model_link: FAMILY_SHOCK['haredi'] mean (-0.98 e0, i.e. polls under-count haredi lists); s.4 haredi turnout 78-82% 'near-invariant'.

TRN-F22.claim: A haredi-sector pollster finds only 75% of haredim say they will certainly vote (69% under 30), against 80-88% turnout claimed in past cycles. Young haredi support for Shas has fallen to 13%.
TRN-F22.quant: 75% 'certain' (69% under 30): a certainty share with no baseline, in line with Ch13 Jewish adults (73-75%). Measured past haredi turnout 72.8-76.8% at regular stations, not 80-88%.
TRN-F22.model_link: FAMILY_SHOCK['haredi']; leakage to The Haredi Public / Achi (threshold waste).

TRN-F23.claim: IDI's haredi specialists document that internal disputes have cost UTJ before, in 2009, 2015 and 2021, and that haredi party loyalty is far higher than the public's. Haredi turnout dips are tied to rabbinic disputes, not just demography.
TRN-F23.quant: IDI documents UTJ share losses in 2009, 2015 and 2021 (2015 with partial Jerusalem Faction abstention); it gives no haredi turnout figures.
TRN-F23.model_link: FAMILY_SHOCK['haredi'] sd and tail; dossier s.4 'haredi 78-82% near-invariant with a small protest-under-vote tail'.

TRN-F24.claim: The Jerusalem Faction (Peleg), which has abstained since 2015, tried in August to split Gur from UTJ into a hard anti-draft list to draw non-voting haredim; Gur refused. A separate anti-draft list (Tzeva Shachor) is on the ballot but polls near zero. No haredi vehicle is drawing new voters in, so draft anger shows up as abstention, not as a new list.
TRN-F24.quant: Ch13 haredi sample (6-7 Oct): Tzeva Shachor 0.6%, The Haredi Public 5.2%, Otzma 5.4%, 'other' (all Achi) 0.8%. Draft anger shows partly as switching, not only abstention.
TRN-F24.model_link: FAMILY_SHOCK['haredi']; small-list realisation for The Haredi Public (s.15).

TRN-F25.claim: Both camps are running organised turnout drives. Likud and Religious Zionism have set up a joint election-day operation to raise right-wing turnout, headed by the Yesha Council chairman, while the High Court's ban on real-time voter tracking (SEC-F21) limits the party machines' traditional tool.
TRN-F25.quant: Times of Israel, 7 Oct 2026: Netanyahu and Smotrich hold a joint 'Saving the Right' conference with Religious Zionist rabbis and yeshiva heads; the parties are setting up a joint operation to raise right-wing turnout, headed by Yesha Council chairman Israel Gantz (Channel 12). Otzma Yehudit was not invited; Likud signed a surplus agreement with RZP the day before. No scale or budget published.
TRN-F25.model_link: Correlated bloc swing; gevalt coupling (Likud <-> satellites); RZP near the threshold.

TRN-F26.claim: In 2022 turnout rose 3.2 points overall, and the rise was differential: right-leaning cities gained 3-7 points while centre-left cities stayed flat. The right-wing bloc's vote share rose only 1.3 points; its 64 seats came mostly from wasted centre-left votes.
TRN-F26.quant: 2022 below-threshold votes: Meretz 3.16% and Balad 2.91% (anti-bloc) vs Jewish Home 1.19% (right). The '64 seats from waste' reading is desk inference, not INSS, and the waste was about half Arab.
TRN-F26.model_link: Correlated bloc swing (t, df 5, x1.2); whether a Jewish-sector turnout term is warranted (no: the 2022 effect is about one bloc point).

TRN-F27.claim: Peer-reviewed locality analysis of 2022 (all 1,215 localities): settlements in Judea and Samaria and localities with many haredim have higher turnout; development towns and larger localities lower. Distance from the centre matters only in Arab localities.
TRN-F27.quant: Eight socio-demographic and geographic predictors, 2019-2022: SES predicts turnout in both Jewish/mixed and Arab localities; peripherality is not significant in Jewish and mixed localities but is significant in Arab localities; locality size is inversely related to turnout; development towns lower; Judea and Samaria and high-haredi-share localities higher. National turnout about 70%.
TRN-F27.model_link: kalpi capacity bounds; sector turnout priors (haredi high); supports making peripheral Arab (Negev) station access part of the station-load test.

TRN-F28.claim: The only wartime election held since October 2023, the February 2024 municipal elections, saw turnout fall most among Arabs (-10 points vs 2018) and non-haredi Jews (-4.5), and hardly at all among haredim (-0.5). Election day was a holiday both times.
TRN-F28.quant: IDI analysis of the 2024 local elections: turnout in 2024 was lower than in 2018 but higher than in 2003, 2008 and 2013; change from 2018: Arab localities -10 points, non-haredi Jewish localities -4.5, haredi localities -0.5. Arab local turnout stayed close to the haredi level. Proposed reasons: the war diverted attention (haredim less affected, as few serve). Closing-night national turnout was about 49% vs 59.5% in 2018 (press figure, not in the IDI text).
TRN-F28.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT spread and left tail (wartime demobilisation); KALPI_FAMILY_RHO (Arab and haredi turnout need not co-move in wartime).

TRN-F29.claim: The security backdrop is live but not restrictive. The government is extending the nationwide 'special situation on the home front' to 3 November, past election day, citing a 'high probability' of attack from Iran or Lebanon. No binding civil-defence restrictions are in force, and the CEC has emergency procedures for sirens during voting and counting.
TRN-F29.quant: Current declaration (in force since February) was due to expire 20 Oct; the Defence Minister asked to extend it to 3 Nov, with Knesset FADC approval needed. Defence officials: 'still a high probability' of an attack on the civilian population; uncertainty mainly on the Iranian and Lebanese fronts. The declaration lets Home Front Command restrict schools and gatherings, but 'no such directives are currently in effect'. CEC logistics (Arutz 7, 14 Oct): emergency kits let poll workers move counting to a protected space; asked whether a confrontation with Iran could cancel the vote, the logistics chief said it is 'not a logistical issue'.
TRN-F29.model_link: Event-risk multiplier (x1.2) on the bloc swing; ARAB_TURNOUT and national turnout left tails (an attack near election day).

TRN-F30.claim: Crime is the Arab public's top issue and the 2026 campaign's main Arab mobiliser. A general strike over police failures preceded the four Arab parties' January unity pledge, and killings remain at record levels.
TRN-F30.quant: Times of Israel, 22 Jan 2026: nationwide Arab general strike and Sakhnin march over police failure to curb violent crime; 2025 was the deadliest year on record (252 homicide victims). The same day the four parties signed a pact in Sakhnin (JNS and Jewish Chronicle reports, not opened); Ra'am later ran separately. AP (15 Oct 2026, opened): the Abraham Initiatives count 184 crime-related killings in Arab communities so far in 2026; 12% of first-half killings solved. IDI Aug 2026: crime the top vote factor (TRN-F20).
TRN-F30.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT['mean_unified']: mobilising issue context (no separate term).

HAR-F01.claim: UTJ is running as one list but three registered parties. On 8 Sept 2026 it filed a joint slate of Degel HaTorah, Agudat Yisrael and a new party, Chomat Torat Yisrael. Meir Porush (Shlomei Emunim) and the Belz representative Elyakim Stark left Agudat Yisrael and registered separately. Per Davar, they did so to avoid being bound by the Gerrer Rebbe, to draw their own party funding and to keep the option of splitting from UTJ in the Knesset. Ger, Vizhnitz and Sanz signed with Degel separately. Davar says no third party has sat on the UTJ list since the 1992 Moriah episode.
HAR-F01.quant: Filed slate (Davar, updated 8 Sep 2026 23:42; YWN 9 Sep): 1 Yaakov Asher (Degel), 2 Yitzhak Goldknopf (Agudah/Gur), 3 Yitzhak Pindrus (Degel), 4 Meir Porush (Chomat Torat Yisrael), 5 Moshe Rosenthal (Degel), 6 Elyakim Stark (Chomat/Belz), 7 Yehuda Weissfish (Degel), 8 Yaakov Tessler (Agudah/Vizhnitz). Per YWN, slots 9-12 go to Ohana or Zeltz, Baruchi and Roth, but its list and its running text disagree on slot 9. Joint statement by Shlomei Emunim and Belz (YWN): 'merely a technical measure intended to ensure an equitable partnership within Agudas Yisrael.' At 7 seats: Degel 4, Agudah 1, Chomat 2. At 8 seats: Degel 4, Agudah 2, Chomat 2.
HAR-F01.model_link: Formation layer: AGUDAH_SHARE = 4/7 and the UTJ_ABSTAINS channel; utj_defects (a crossing by one faction is now institutionally separable). Registration mixture: no open UTJ event (filed as one list).

HAR-F02.claim: Degel HaTorah's rabbis removed party chair Moshe Gafni and MK Uri Maklev from the slate. Yaakov Asher replaced Gafni and heads the joint list. Reports tie the shake-up to the failed exemption law and to a dispute over relations with Netanyahu: Gafni and Maklev favoured dialogue and compromise, while Rabbi Dov Lando's camp pushed for confrontation.
HAR-F02.quant: Decision confirmed Saturday night, 5-6 Sep 2026. Lando's office: 'due to the need to refresh the Knesset members, the two will leave the Knesset'. Gafni was first elected in 1988. 'No major changes are expected within Agudat Yisrael' (led by Goldknopf). Lists closed 8 Sep.
HAR-F02.model_link: utj_defects (0.15): the new leadership is more confrontational toward Netanyahu but also less willing to compromise on the draft, which cuts both ways for a centre deal.

HAR-F03.claim: Before filing, Agudah's smaller courts threatened to run apart from Degel. Senior figures in Shomrei Emunim and Belz said Gur 'does not represent us', denied any negotiation with Degel, and said Agudah was examining a technical bloc with another party. Early feelers went to Noam. The threat was resolved by registering Chomat Torat Yisrael inside UTJ (HAR-F01), not by a separate run.
HAR-F03.quant: Kikar HaShabbat, 25 Aug 2026 (12 Elul): Gur held talks with Degel through Bnei Brak mayor Chanoch Zeibert and Moshe Shipman. A dispute over UTJ's 5th slot (Gur vs Tzanz). About two weeks remained before lists closed.
HAR-F03.model_link: Registration mixture: a separate Agudah or Belz run was a live pre-filing event. It is now closed, because UTJ filed one list.

HAR-F04.claim: Two commentators expected UTJ to run as a 'purely technical bloc' and split after the vote, with each faction negotiating its own coalition terms. In mid-August the Jerusalem Faction and allied activists pitched Gur on leaving UTJ to form a hard-line anti-draft party, arguing it would win an extra seat from current non-voters. Gur's Moti Bebchik rejected the pitch. Degel MK Pindrus called the split reports 'meaningless'.
HAR-F04.quant: N12 (Amit Segal, 16 Aug 2026): 'run as a technical bloc only and split after the elections'; Gafni was expected to split from Goldknopf's Agudah after the vote. The meeting took place at the home of Peleg member Eliyahu Goldstein. INN, 14 Aug 2026: columnist Yaakov Rivlin forecast a post-election split into two factions; Pindrus on Kol Chai: 'These reports are meaningless.'
HAR-F04.model_link: UTJ_ABSTAINS and utj_defects: the formation tree treats UTJ as one actor, apart from the Agudah abstention sensitivity row.

HAR-F05.claim: Twelve days before the vote, Gur, UTJ's largest Hasidic bloc, is withholding its campaign. Activists were told not to engage in any election activity, and the Rebbe has made no public call to vote. The stated aim is to keep Belz's Elyakim Stark (slot 6) out of the Knesset. Belz dismisses the threat, and the prevailing expectation is a compromise followed by a Gur vote for UTJ.
HAR-F05.quant: INN, 15 Oct 2026 09:13: 'we have been instructed not to engage in any election-related activity'; 'there has been no public call from the Gerrer Rebbe'. Gur is put at 25,000-30,000 votes. INN states 'UTJ could potentially lose two Knesset seats' (unsourced). Belz: UTJ's natural voter growth is about 55,000, and a work-to-rule protest 'won't manage to affect even the seventh seat.' Kikar HaShabbat (Shaul Kahana, 15 Oct): Hamodia carries no campaign; Goldknopf has skipped every official election gathering; Belz has its own share of election funding for the first time.
HAR-F05.model_link: Haredi family shock (symmetric t, base-share allocation): it has no UTJ-specific left tail for an organised abstention. utj_defects and UTJ_ABSTAINS: the rupture strengthens the case for faction-level behaviour.

HAR-F06.claim: Gur's vote is worth about half a seat to UTJ, not the one to two seats the press quotes. Gur has about 30,000 eligible voters (ynet). At 2026 seat prices that is roughly 19,000-24,000 votes, or 0.5-0.65 seats.
HAR-F06.quant: Gur's full abstention is worth about 0.5-0.7 UTJ seats (up to 0.8 if the 25-30k are votes, not eligible voters). Seat price 37.4-40.2k on 4.82M valid votes with 0-7% below-threshold waste; 2022: 36.2k per passing seat.
HAR-F06.model_link: Size of a Gur-abstention left tail on UTJ: about -0.6 seats if Gur stays home entirely, about -0.3 if half complies.

HAR-F07.claim: The Gur rupture moved to the field on 15 Oct. Gur refused to take part in the joint Agudah election headquarters agreed that morning. Shlomei Emunim and Belz then set up their own headquarters without Gur and Vizhnitz. No instruction not to vote UTJ was given. Separately, i24 reports Gur's fallback: if no call to vote UTJ goes out, a 'quiet instruction' to vote Code Black.
HAR-F07.quant: Emes (Shalom Stein, 16 Oct 2026 00:30): the joint headquarters was to cover Shlomei Emunim, Belz, Ger and Vizhnitz; Gur 'will not take part'; 'no instruction was given not to vote for Yahadut HaTorah'. Emes calls Tessler's (slot 8) Knesset seat 'imaginary'. i24 Hebrew (Ari Kalman, Wednesday 14 Oct): Gur's condition is that roles are settled before election day. Precedent: in the 2008 Jerusalem mayoral race Gur backed Barkat over the haredi candidate Meir Porush.
HAR-F07.model_link: UTJ election-day turnout machine; ties to SEC-F21 (17 Sep High Court ban on real-time voter tracking): both weaken the GOTV mechanism behind past haredi beats.

HAR-F08.claim: Channel 12 reported that Netanyahu fears Gur will not vote, staying home or casting protest votes for sub-threshold lists. Likud and Religious Zionism are pressing The Haredi Public to withdraw, because it could siphon votes from Shas and UTJ. The Haredi Public refused.
HAR-F08.quant: ToI, 15 Oct 2026 00:40: about 30,000 potential Gur voters. Haredi Public: 'There is no point in pressuring the Haredi Public to drop out of the elections'. It says it speaks for 'the tens of thousands of Haredim who want new and responsible leadership'.
HAR-F08.model_link: Withdrawn-list rule and registration mixture: a Haredi Public withdrawal is a live event with no entry today. Its polled share would go to UTJ and Shas (kalpi transfer haredi_public: utj 0.5, shas 0.5).

HAR-F09.claim: On 11 Oct, N12 reported that UTJ insiders treat 8 seats as 'a miracle' and would not be surprised by 6. It said the campaign was frozen by a rift between Degel's two leading rabbis, and that internal party polls show haredi willingness to vote down about 10%. Three days later both rabbis publicly called for an all-out UTJ effort: Lando said there is 'no room to stand aside' and Hirsch called a UTJ vote binding under Torah law. New campaign headquarters opened. The Degel side of the rift looks bridged; the Gur side (HAR-F05, F07) does not.
HAR-F09.quant: N12 (Amit Segal, 11 Oct 2026 23:27): Shas+UTJ won 18 seats last time and poll 14-15 now; with sector growth 19-20 could have been expected; internal polls show '~10% drop in willingness to go to the polls'. Some Shas voters went to Yesh Atid or Otzma, others stay home. HaMehadesh (Shuki Katz, 14 Oct): Hirsch said each person must 'do the maximum' and vote UTJ (letter Gimel); new headquarters in Petah Tikva (6,000-7,000 votes), Achisamach and for FSU immigrants.
HAR-F09.model_link: Haredi family shock and the UTJ seat distribution. Model UTJ mean 8.8 (mixture, 15 Oct) vs UTJ insiders' 6-8.

HAR-F10.claim: Code Black – Shield of the Torah World is a single-issue anti-draft list headed by kollel heads, including men labelled deserters. Hebrew Wikipedia identifies it with the Jerusalem Faction. Its stated purpose is to turn protest against UTJ into votes. It says it will back no government without a full arrangement for the whole yeshiva world, and it attacks the established parties over a '50% law'. No rabbinic body has endorsed it. Its polling is negligible outside one pollster.
HAR-F10.quant: Named list (JDN 16 Oct): Baumrind, Rabin HaKohen, Yehonatan Yissachar, Miller (founder); no Dagani. Itemised by Kantar 0.5-0.7% (4 filings) and Maagar Mochot 0.2% (4151, 15 Sep).
HAR-F10.model_link: Code Black is modelled as an ordinary latent list (p_pass 0.016) outside the haredi family. Its realistic ceiling is the Peleg base (HAR-F11) plus any Gur protest vote (HAR-F07).

HAR-F11.claim: The Jerusalem Faction's national electoral record is withdrawal, boycott or abstention. Its 2013 list (Netzah) withdrew five days before the vote after a Gur-Auerbach deal. In 2015 it campaigned against voting UTJ. In 2019 its rabbis announced it would not take part. Its municipal vote is the best measure of its size: 14,000-22,000 votes, about 0.3-0.45% of a national electorate.
HAR-F11.quant: Hamichlol 'Bnei Torah (party)': Netzah registered for the 19th Knesset and its candidates withdrew on 6 Shevat 5773 (17 Jan 2013), five days before the vote, under an agreement between the Gerrer Rebbe and Rabbi Auerbach. In 2015 a rally two days before the vote declared 'one may not assist transgressors', read as a ban on UTJ; about 4,000 supporters cast invalid ballots or voted Shas or Yachad. Municipal votes: ~14,000 (2013, three cities), ~22,000 (2018, six cities), ~18,000 (2024). Wikipedia: the Peleg has abstained since the 20th Knesset, and Rabbi Tzvi Friedman's strict stream forbids voting.
HAR-F11.model_link: Code Black's ceiling. Historical analogue for the haredi family mean: the 2013 withdrawal preceded UTJ beating its final polls by 1.09 seats, and the 2015 boycott year saw UTJ over-polled by 0.50 (HAR-F28).

HAR-F12.claim: The Haredi Public is a modern, integrationist haredi list led by Moti Leitner, a Beit Shemesh councillor (deputy mayor per +972). It supports military service tracks, secular education and workforce integration, and has women on its slate. It began in July by demanding a UTJ slot and announced an independent run on 23 Aug. Its national polling is 0.2-0.9%, but its haredi-sample strength is mostly an online-sample effect (HAR-F25).
HAR-F12.quant: Haredi Public online vs phone among decided haredim: 6.0% vs 2.1% in ONE phone wave (≈4 of 220 respondents; z≈2.1). Treat as suggestive; it does not establish an online-only effect.
HAR-F12.model_link: MICRO_REALIZE['haredi_public'] = 1.0 ('sectarian core holds') is doubtful for a list whose support is concentrated among online respondents. Withdrawal event (HAR-F08).

HAR-F13.claim: Ahi is the haredi-adjacent list the brief leaves out. It is the movement of the late Rabbi Yoram Abergel, a Sephardi traditional-haredi network based in Netivot, headed by Yuval Elimelech. It runs alone by decision of Rabbi Chaim (HaIDA) Abergel, targets about 170,000 votes, and draws on Shas's southern, traditional base. A haredi-sector survey puts it at 9% of haredim. National polls give it 0.1-1.1%.
HAR-F13.quant: Babli (David Klein, 8 Sep 2026): Rabbi Abergel decided on an independent run after talks 'that collapsed at the last moment'. List: Elimelech, Yisrael Eplalo, Rabbi Erez Reuven, Avi Dayan (former deputy mayor of Elad). Target ~170,000 votes (the threshold). he.wikipedia: Ahi won 7 of 17 seats in Netivot (Feb 2024) vs 5 for Shas+UTJ; national run announced 16 Jun 2026. Super Data (14 Oct): Ahi 9% of the haredi public, 12% under 30. CEC filings: Kantar 0.7% (4 Oct), 0.5% (11 Oct); Filber 0.1%. polls.csv: Lazar 1.1% (9 Sep), 0.8% (17 Sep). Ch13 7 Oct: every free-text 'other party' answer in the haredi sample (0.8%) named Ahi.
HAR-F13.model_link: List 'ahi' ('Ahi - Back to the Roots', p_pass 0.009) sits outside the haredi family. Its sub-threshold vote is a Shas leak, which matters for the Shas side of the family shock and for the withdrawn-list rule if it folds.

HAR-F14.claim: Tzomet Beit Yisrael is not a haredi list. It merges the old secular-right Tzomet party (Moshe Green) with Beit Yisrael, the party of former Likud MK Gadi Yevarkan, under the label 'the Third Camp on the Right'. The model correctly keeps it out of the haredi family.
HAR-F14.quant: he.wikipedia: merger announced 20 Aug 2026; list led by Yevarkan, then Green and Yaniv Ashtamker; ballot letters בי. Lazar 0.2-0.4% (CEC 4158, 4164, 4177, 4197); Midgam and Maagar Mochot 0.0%.
HAR-F14.model_link: Classification of the small lists. The model's lists 'beit_yisrael' and 'code_black' are not in bias_audit.FAMILY['haredi']; haredi_public is.

HAR-F15.claim: Shas's spiritual leader, former chief rabbi Yitzhak Yosef, was reported in August to have privately told students not to vote Shas, after the bloc failed to pass the exemption law. Yosef denied it. He then reconciled with Deri on 20 Aug, gained a larger say in decisions and publicly called for a Shas vote.
HAR-F15.quant: ToI (Sam Sokol, 20 Aug 2026): per Haaretz, Yosef demanded a student 'promise not to vote for Shas'. Under the reconciliation, Rabbi Moshe Maya's letter asked Yosef to carry on Ovadia Yosef's legacy, and the two meet weekly on Fridays. Shas launched its campaign the same day in Holon (slogan 'Derech Emunah Bacharti', he.wikipedia). +972 (15 Oct): Deri has been booed at rallies organised by the party's own rabbis; 'distrust remains'.
HAR-F15.model_link: shas_defects (0.10, NEFF 30): the 'psak mechanism' rationale (Yosef newly empowered) is confirmed. No change to Shas's vote is implied beyond what polls carry.

HAR-F16.claim: Yosef's new power is real. Shas's Council of Torah Sages, led by Yosef, overruled Deri's attempt to drop MK Yoav Ben-Tzur. Shas put a reservist, Dror Amos, sixth to soften its anti-draft image. Commentators describe a shrinking traditional base: Deri's face is absent from billboards, which show only Ovadia Yosef.
HAR-F16.quant: N12 21 Aug: Rabbi DAVID Yosef thinks Shas should not rule out working with Gadi EISENKOT if he can form a majority government (not Yitzhak Yosef / Gantz).
HAR-F16.model_link: shas_defects; Shas's non-haredi share (SEC-F19: about a third of its voters are not haredi) is the segment online panels reach least well and the one most exposed to the draft issue.

HAR-F17.claim: Shas competes with Otzma Yehudit and Likud for young haredi and traditional voters. The leak to Otzma among self-identified haredim is visible in 2026 polls but is not clearly larger than in 2022. Otzma itself claims a pool of 2-4 seats of haredim 'not locked' to the haredi parties.
HAR-F17.quant: N12/Midgam first-time voters (15-22 Sep 2026, online, n=301, MoE 4.4): haredi first-timers UTJ 45%, Shas 20%, Otzma 13% (haredi subsample size not reported). Ch13 haredi samples (decided respondents): Otzma 6.1-9.3% online, 3.6% phone (23 Sep). IDI 2022 benchmark: RZP-Otzma 7% of haredim (SEC-F19). Maariv (2 Sep): Shas runs a digital campaign in 'hundreds of groups'; Otzma's estimate of 2-4 seats is a party claim.
HAR-F17.model_link: The gevalt coupling covers Likud and its satellites, not Shas and Otzma. Shas's under-poll (SEC-F19) may partly be late returns from Otzma and Likud flirters.

HAR-F18.claim: Haredi sources have floated recommending nobody to the president and sitting in opposition for 'the first year', until a draft law is settled; after that, 'the haredim could enter any government'. These are moods reported by unnamed sources, not decisions by the rabbis. By 13 Oct the line was that they would not actively help replace Netanyahu or Speaker Ohana either.
HAR-F18.quant: JPost (Anna Barsky, 17 Sep 2026, from Maariv): 'The feeling right now is that we won't recommend anyone'; 'intention of sitting in the opposition for the first year'; 'Shas won't do something different from United Torah Judaism'; yeshiva funding demand of NIS 1.2-1.5bn. Eisenkot's framework allows deferral for up to 3% of each cohort for one year. JPost (Barsky, 13 Oct): 'neither party is inclined to recommend a candidate to the president'; unclear whether they would vote against, abstain or skip a vote to replace Ohana.
HAR-F18.model_link: Formation tree: the Netanyahu path treats haredi membership as certain once the bloc reaches 61 (the site already lists 'haredi membership treated as certain' as a weakness). The centre-haredi branch (utj_defects 0.15, shas_defects 0.10) is a crossing at formation, but the reported plan is delayed entry.

HAR-F19.claim: Both party leaders have now made the same condition public for ANY government: no support or participation until the status of yeshiva students is regulated in a law that survives the courts. Asher: 'We do not belong to any bloc.' The two parties signed a surplus-vote agreement on 11 Oct.
HAR-F19.quant: Deri (14 Oct): no government with Shas support or participation 'unless the status of yeshiva students is regulated' (no 'law/courts' qualifier, no timeline). Asher (12 Oct): UTJ won't ENTER a government that does not pass the law. 'Survives the High Court' is Rosenthal's (UTJ), conditioned on 'whoever commits'.
HAR-F19.model_link: SURPLUS_PAIRS ('shas','utj') is confirmed as signed. Formation: the Netanyahu VI gate needs a law passed first (feasible for Netanyahu, so a delay rather than a block). A centre crossing needs Eisenkot to legislate an exemption, which he rejects (he said on 28 Sep that no haredi party meets his conditions; ToI 29 Sep). This supports low shas_defects and utj_defects.

HAR-F20.claim: The single report of an Agudah abstention on an Eisenkot-led minority government still has no second source; Asher denied it the same night. The report named Goldknopf and Tessler as Gur, but Tessler represents Vizhnitz. Under the filed list order, Agudat Yisrael holds slots 2 and 8. Its Knesset faction is therefore 1 seat if UTJ wins 7 and 2 if UTJ wins 8-10, far below the 4/7 share the formation tree assumes.
HAR-F20.quant: ToI (Ariela Karmel, 29 Sep 2026): unsourced Ch12 report that UTJ MKs Goldknopf and Tessler plan to abstain on swearing in an Eisenkot-led minority government; Asher: the party 'has no desire to topple or install anyone' and no UTJ faction backs any government until the exemption is 'legally settled'. Wikipedia: Tessler was chosen in 2019 as 'the main representative of the Vizhnitz community'. List order: HAR-F01. The model's AGUDAH_SHARE = 4/7 implies about 4.6 abstainers at UTJ 8; the filed list gives 2. Chomat Torat Yisrael (Porush, Stark) holds 2 more seats and is a separate party.
HAR-F20.model_link: UTJ_ABSTAINS = 0.0 (headline), 0.25 sensitivity; AGUDAH_SHARE = 4/7 is wrong for the filed list.

HAR-F21.claim: Arrests of haredi draft evaders are rare relative to the pool, so the campaign's anger comes from the threat, sanctions and a few arrests rather than from mass enforcement. From mid-January to mid-June 2026, 16 of 165 proactive military-police arrests were haredi, against roughly 74,000 haredi men declared draft dodgers or issued an Order 12.
HAR-F21.quant: Haaretz (Chen Maanit, Noa Shpigel, 1 Jul 2026), from the Attorney General's High Court filing: 165 proactive arrests 16 Jan-11 Jun 2026, 16 haredi; 81 more detained in chance encounters; 294 indictments Jan-mid-June, ~32 haredi; 92,080 declared draft dodgers or Order 12 as of 10 May, ~80% haredi (IDF sources); Brig. Gen. Shai Tayeb: 'we are on our way to 90,000 draft dodgers'. Code Black's party claim of '730 held in military prison in the past year' is unverified.
HAR-F21.model_link: Context for any haredi turnout or anger term: the exposure is broad (tens of thousands of families with a 'deserter') but enforcement is thin.

HAR-F22.claim: Enforcement eased as the vote approached, but anger stayed visible. Kan reported that proactive arrests stopped in August, which the IDF denies. The High Court unanimously struck down the coalition's arrest-ban law in early September. Election day is arrest-free by agreement. Two arrests in early October set off Peleg protests that blocked Highway 4 and surrounded a Shas campaign event in Modiin Illit.
HAR-F22.quant: ToI (26 Sep 2026): Kan, citing judicial sources, says the IDF and police were 'deterred' by protests; police sources told Haaretz arrests were suspended in August; about 80,000 haredi men aged 18-24 eligible and not enlisted. The arrest-ban law passed 14 Jul and was frozen 15 Jul; the High Court struck it down 'earlier this month' (JPost, 16 Sep), with 8 of 9 justices also finding it unconstitutional in substance. ToI (23 Jun): the CEC chair, AG and police chief agreed there will be no draft-evader arrests on election day, at the haredi parties' request. JPost (8 Oct): two evaders arrested in Beersheba and Eilat; protesters surrounded a Shas conference with Deri in Modiin Illit; Shas called the violence a 'desecration of God's name' and the Committee to Save the Torah World attacked Shas.
HAR-F22.model_link: Haredi turnout: the anger has two outlets with opposite signs. One mobilises a protective vote for the haredi parties; the other is the Peleg/Code Black channel of protest against them. The election-day moratorium removes a direct deterrent to voting.

HAR-F23.claim: The only phone-based, repeated haredi-sector survey with a 2022 baseline finds an electorate that is undecided rather than defecting. Among decided haredi voters, UTJ+Shas hold 83.2% against 85.6% at the same point in 2022, a difference that is not statistically significant. The undecided share has more than doubled. The firm estimates the haredi parties at about 1 seat (0.5-1.5) below 2022, all of it Shas, and less if undecided voters return as they did in 2022.
HAR-F23.quant: Askaria (CEO Dudi Dror), three telephone polls per cycle; n=1,300 (Sivan-Elul 5786) vs 1,355 (2022 cycle). Decided voters: UTJ 57.2 (55.5), Shas 26.0 (30.1), non-haredi parties 16.8 (14.4). Whole public: UTJ+Shas 63.8 vs 71.5 (significant), Shas 19.9 vs 25.2, UTJ 43.9 vs 46.4, undecided 13.2 vs 5.9, not voting ~10 (unchanged). Undecided leaners: ~1/3 UTJ, few Shas, ~1/2 non-haredi parties. New haredi parties ~2% of haredim in September. Assumes haredim = 10.8% of valid votes. Quote: 'a sector that is dawdling, not disconnecting'. Askaria also fields Ch13's haredi sample.
HAR-F23.model_link: Haredi family mean and allocation (the decline is Shas's); turnout term not indicated (non-voting intention unchanged).

HAR-F24.claim: A haredi-community pollster (Super Data) reports that only 75% of haredim say they will definitely vote (69% under 30), against historical turnout of 80-88%. It also reports a youth swing away from Shas (13% from 33-36%) and UTJ (41% from 50%) toward Ahi and Leitner. No sample size, method or field dates are published, and SEC-F08 shows stated certainty does not rank haredi turnout, so this is weak evidence for a turnout drop.
HAR-F24.quant: Kikar HaShabbat 'Super Data' (Eli Gotthelf; analysis by Avi Widerman, 14 Oct 2026). Under-30s who will not vote: 36% say the existing haredi parties 'do not represent them'; 33% will not vote for another party against the gedolim. 62% think askanim control the gedolim's homes (70% of Hasidim). Widerman: 'the situation is not good, and the campaigns are not working.' Benchmarks: Ch13 haredi sample 7 Oct, 66.2% 'certain' + 21.2% 'fairly sure' vs 74.6% certain among Jewish adults (CEC 4193); actual haredi-cluster turnout 76.4/76.8/76.6/72.8/75.8% for 2019a-2022 (SEC-F17).
HAR-F24.model_link: A haredi turnout term is not warranted on this evidence; at most a widening of the left tail.

HAR-F25.claim: Channel 13's dedicated haredi samples show a large mode effect for the haredi family. Online haredi respondents give Shas+UTJ 72-78% of decided votes (mean 74.8% over six waves). The one phone wave (23 Sep, n=220) gives 84.9%, in line with Askaria's phone survey (83.2%) and IDI's 2022 vote (86%). With haredim at 10.8% of the vote, the gap is worth 1.0 seat against the same-day online wave (z = 2.1) and 1.3 against the pooled online mean (z = 3.6). That is a concrete mechanism for the recorded haredi under-count. How the gap splits between the two lists is not robust: on the same day it is even (Shas 3.8 points, UTJ 4.1), but against the pooled online waves it is Shas-heavy (6.4 vs 3.7), as it is with Askaria's phone figures (5.5 vs 2.9). The Haredi Public and Otzma are two to three times stronger online.
HAR-F25.quant: Phone-online gap for Shas+UTJ among decided haredim: 7.9 pts same-day (z 2.1; ~1.0 seat), one phone wave n=220 fielded by the same house as the Askaria benchmark. The pooled 10.1 pts (~1.3 seats) mixes waves across five weeks. A plausible mechanism, not a measured one.
HAR-F25.model_link: Supports the sign and size of the haredi family under-count (0.98 raw; the mode gap implies 1.0-1.3). It gives only weak support to a Shas-heavy allocation, which rests mainly on the list record (SEC-F19, HAR-F26). It argues against MICRO_REALIZE 1.0 for The Haredi Public.

HAR-F26.claim: Pollsters disagree on Shas far more than on UTJ, and the record favours the high end. In 2026 house effects on Shas range from +1.87 seats (Filber) to -0.98 (Midgam Project), while UTJ polls sit at 7-8 everywhere. In the five cycles 2019a-2022, no pollster's final two-week average ever over-stated Shas: 34 of 38 pollster-cycles under-stated it and 4 were exact. UTJ's pollster-cycle errors are centred near zero. Filber is online, so mode does not explain the house spread.
HAR-F26.quant: house_effects_lists_2026.csv, Shas (seats): Filber +1.87 (12 polls), Maagar Mochot +1.31 (3), Tatika +0.57 (13), Direct Polls +0.19 (9), Midgam -0.63 (15), Kantar -0.74 (17), Lazar -0.95 (11), Midgam Project -0.98 (10). CEC raw shares since 20 Sep: Shas 5.0-8.6% (mean 6.2; 5.7 without Filber) vs 8.25% in 2022; UTJ 5.0-6.6% (mean 6.0) vs 5.88% in 2022. October seat polls (n=18): Shas mean 7.7 (7.3 without Filber), UTJ 7.9. Record (polls.csv, final 14 days, by pollster): Shas 38 pollster-cycles, mean error -1.66 seats, 0 positive / 4 zero / 34 negative; UTJ mean -0.26, 10 positive / 16 zero / 12 negative. Filing 4192: Filber collects via a 'digital internet system'.
HAR-F26.model_link: Sum-to-zero house effects centre the Shas latent on the house average. A pollster that has never over-polled Shas is treated as no more right than the others. The family term (0.98) partly compensates, but by base share, so about half goes to UTJ.

HAR-F27.claim: Before the electoral threshold rose, haredi splits added seats rather than wasting them. In 1988, Rabbi Shach's Degel HaTorah split from Agudat Yisrael and he also backed Shas. Agudah rose from 2 seats to 5, Degel entered with 2 and Shas rose from 4 to 6: the haredi total went from 6 to 13 seats under a 1% threshold.
HAR-F27.quant: 1988 haredi seats 13 (Shas 6, Agudah 5, Degel 2) vs 6-7 in 1984 (Agudah 2, Shas 4, plus Morasha's PAI seat); Agudah's +3 is credited to the Lubavitcher Rebbe's late endorsement, not to the split.
HAR-F27.model_link: Historical analogue for infighting. Not transferable to 3.25% (the 2026 splinters are all sub-threshold), but it shows that rabbinic competition can raise mobilisation.

HAR-F28.claim: Under a threshold, the record splits by what the splinter does. When a rival haredi list or boycott campaign stayed active through election day, the splinter was over-polled and its votes wasted, and the list it targeted was not under-polled (Shas 2013 -0.55, Shas 2015 +0.38, UTJ 2015 +0.50; mean +0.11). When a splinter withdrew late, the beneficiary beat its polls heavily (UTJ 2013 -1.09 after Netzah withdrew 5 days out; April 2019 UTJ -1.67 and Shas -2.67 after Yachad withdrew 13 days out and endorsed UTJ; mean -1.81). The other 10 list-cycles average -0.28. With n=3 per group this is suggestive only, but it ties the family's big misses to withdrawals, not to infighting as such.
HAR-F28.quant: Active-splinter list-cycles +0.11 (n=3); withdrawal-beneficiary cycles -1.81 (n=3), but -1.38 (n=2, UTJ only) if Shas 2019a (Yachad endorsed UTJ) is excluded; the largest non-splinter misses (Shas 2022 -1.43, 2009 -1.11) fit neither story.
HAR-F28.model_link: FAMILY_SHOCK['haredi'] mean (0.98 under-count): its large-miss cycles are withdrawal cycles, and 2026's configuration resembles the active-splinter cycles. Withdrawn-list rule: a late withdrawal of a haredi splinter should move votes to UTJ/Shas beyond the polls.

HAR-F29.claim: The last big UTJ feud before 2026 ended in UTJ's best result. In the October 2018 local elections Degel and Agudah ran against each other, often acrimoniously, and Degel won almost twice as many council seats. The factions formally split in January 2019 (a 'procedural' move for separate funding), then reunited within a week on an equal 50/50 slate. In April 2019 UTJ won 8 seats, 1.67 above its final polls.
HAR-F29.quant: ToI (Raoul Wootliff, 16 Jan 2019): Agudah took the odd slots and Degel the even ones; in 2015 Agudah had held 60% of the list. Gafni called it an 'unprecedented historic agreement'. April 2019: UTJ polled 6.33 and won 8 (project record).
HAR-F29.model_link: There is no evidence that intra-UTJ infighting alone lowers UTJ's vote or raises its poll error. That counts against adding an 'infighting penalty' unless a faction actually withholds its vote (the Gur case).

HAR-F30.claim: Peer-reviewed work on 2013 describes the haredi parties' 'emergency campaign' to hold voters once treated as automatic. The open, assertive battle between UTJ and Shas produced 'an uneasy electoral stability' rather than defection. The same pattern fits 2026: insiders and sector surveys report anxiety and indecision, while phone-based measures of decided haredi voters are close to 2022.
HAR-F30.quant: Leon (2015), Israel Affairs 21(2): 230-244. Abstract only: 'The battle was fought openly and assertively'. In 2013 UTJ won 7 seats (5.16%) and Shas 11 (8.75%); final polls had 5.91 and 10.45 (project record).
HAR-F30.model_link: Supports keeping a positive (under-count) haredi family mean rather than a crisis-driven negative shift, and not adding a separate haredi turnout-collapse term.
